en: Now begins the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter.
Since the distinction between rituals has been established in the second [chapter], [this section] now concerns distinct actions themselves.
Therefore, the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (śeṣa-śeṣi-bhāva), which is desired to be known, is here set forth.
By this, the sequence of the second and third chapters has been established.
(Sūtra in the first section concerning the thesis:
Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary (śeṣa).
Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.1.

In the first section (adhikaraṇa) of the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter, he formulates the following: "Is the status of being a subsidiary (śeṣatā) non-verbal or verbal? It is not verbal, because it is not directly perceived; for the acquisition of linguistic competency (vyutpatti) occurs only with respect to the relation between an action and its factors (kriyākāraka). (Mīmāṃsājñānakāṇḍa 3.1.2)
This [subsidiary character] is included within the category of "association" (saṃsarga) by virtue of its being subordinate to the principal;
because it is possible to derive its meaning through grammatical analysis, it possesses the status of being expressed by words (śābdatā), just like the action (kriyā) and so forth.
That which is to be established as "subsidiarity" (śeṣatva) in this third chapter—
That is not based on verbal testimony.
Why?
Because subsidiarity (śeṣatva) is not perceived through any word whatsoever.
For it is only a word whose meaning has been mastered (*vyutpanna*) that conveys a sense;
and such mastery is never observed in the case of the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*).
This is because in all worldly cases, it is observed that the basis for mastery [of a word's meaning] is exclusively the connection between an action and its factors (*kriyākārakānvaya*).
If it is argued that this chapter need not be commenced because the status of being a subordinate (śeṣatā) is not explicitly stated by the words [of the Veda], we say:
not so;
for the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva) is included within the category of "concomitance" (anvaya).
For syntactic connection (anvaya) is not possible without a relationship of subordinate and principal;
this is because two subordinate elements, being devoid of mutual expectancy, lack the fitness for connection,
and the same applies to two principal elements.
Therefore, since its derivation is possible, just as the action, the factors of action (*kāraka*), and their mutual relations are verbal (*śābda*),
so too the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), which is included within those relations, is also verbal. Consequently, this chapter must be commenced.
(Regarding the second section on the definition of the subsidiary, the sūtra states: "The subsidiary is that which exists for the sake of another. (Jaimini 3.1.2)
The second section formulates the argument:
"In this case, neither the essential nature nor the reason exist, or else they do exist because they cannot be defined;
since subservience to another is the reason for being a *śeṣa*, its form is thereby characterized by that."

For now, it is not possible to define the essential nature of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) here. To explain: what is this so-called subsidiarity—is it inseparable concomitance (*avinābhūtatva*), or is it being prompted (*prayojyatva*)?
Or [the definition] is "being enjoined by the end of an injunction.
Not the first [alternative],
because it would entail the undesirable consequence that the six primary sacrifices, which are invariably concomitant, would be mutual auxiliaries to one another.
Not the second [alternative],

because in the case of the statement "he scatters the husks with the cake-pan" (*puroḍāśakapālena tuṣān upavapati*), even though the pan is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) with respect to the scattering of the husks, it lacks the status of being something employed for that purpose (*tatprayojyatva*).
Not the third [alternative].
Because the cutting of the *palāśa* branch, though enjoined by a primary injunction (*vidhi*), lacks the status of being enjoined by a subsequent injunction (*vidhyanta*),
there is no such thing as "subsidiarity" (*śeṣatā*) in its own right,
nor is there any logical reason for it.
"Since no logical reason can be established for the claim that 'the remainder is subject to doubt because it possesses such a nature,' this being the position reached— "
We reply: "The subject under dispute, such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, is a subordinate (*śeṣa*),
because it exists for the sake of another,
like a servant and so forth"— this reason (*hetu*) is well-established.
Even though definitions such as "being inseparable" (*avinābhūtatva*) and so forth may be defective, the definition "that which is for the sake of another" (*parārthaḥ śe�ṣaḥ*) is not defective.
Therefore, the form characterized by that [definition] is its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Furthermore, there is no confusion between the state of being for the sake of another serving as both the reason (*hetu*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because that [reason] is differentiated by a difference in its aspects (*ākāra*):
the aspect that makes [the object] known by employing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped in the example is the *hetu* (logical reason);
the aspect that makes [the object] known through exclusion from others (*itara-vyāvṛtti*) is the *lakṣaṇa* (definition).
Therefore, the cause and the essential nature of subsidiarity (śeṣatā) both exist [in the case of the subordinate].
(Third Section: On the Remaining Objects of Definition;
Sūtras 3–6) Bādari [holds that the purpose of the Veda lies] in substances, qualities, and purificatory acts.
Jaimini [holds that it lies] also in actions, because they are for the sake of the fruit. Jaim_3.1.3–4.
And the fruit [is for the person], because it has the person as its purpose; and the person [is for the ritual action], because he has the ritual action as his purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.5–6)
The third section formulates the inquiry:
Is "subsidiary" (śeṣa) merely substance, quality, and refinement, or is it the fruit, the person, and the action? These two positions are to be adopted according to the difference of opinion.

Bādari states that being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) consists in being helpful to a substance and so forth; Jaimini, however, holds that subordination is the state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), and that this exists in all things.

Substance consists of items such as the wooden sword (*sphyakapāla*) and the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*); quality consists of attributes such as ruddiness (*aruṇimā*); and refinement (*saṃskāra*) consists of actions such as threshing (*avaghāta*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Among these three alone lies the state of being subordinate:
heaven is the fruit, and the person is one who desires it.
The New and Full Moon sacrifices are the ritual action (*karma*).

For the triad beginning with the fruit does not possess the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*); this is because the characteristic of being a subordinate element—namely, the state of being helpful—is absent in the case of the fruit and the others. Such is the opinion of Bādari.
Intending the definition [of *śeṣa*] as "being for the sake of another," Jaimini’s view is that "the fruit and so forth are also *śeṣas*.

Accordingly, three sūtras are recited: "Jaimini [holds that] even ritual acts are [for the sake of another], because they exist for the sake of the fruit; the fruit also [is for the sake of another], because it exists for the sake of the person; and the person also [is for the sake of another], because he exists for the sake of the ritual act.
In that context, [defining *śeṣa* merely as] "being helpful" (*upakāritva*) is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*).
Because even when the master is the primary factor, it is observed that the slave born in the house (garbhadāsa) renders assistance;
therefore, the view of Jaimini alone is the principal established conclusion.
(Regarding the section on the fixed scope of the offerings and other rites in the fourth [chapter], Sūtras 7–10:
"There is a connection of these with their respective purposes" (Jaimini 3.1.7).
"But that which is prescribed should be a property of all, because there is no distinction in its connection and no distinction in its context" (Jaimini 3.1.8).
"Because the purpose is lost, it would not be an action" (Jaimini 3.1.9).
"But the fruit [accrues] together with the effort; since that is the meaning of the word, it would exist in the absence [of the fruit] when there is separation" (Jaimini 3.1.10).
He formulates the fourth section as follows:

The ritual properties (dharma) of rice, clarified butter, and the *sāṃnāyya* offering have been heard [in the scriptures] as either being subject to commingling (*sāṃkarya*) or as being restricted; for if they were to commingle, they would be connected with the unique transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the sacrifice. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.7–8)
Because of the existence of intermediate apūrvas, those [subsidiaries] are directly connected with that [principal act] alone;
this is established by direct statement (śruti), for that is superior to context (prakaraṇa).

The properties of rice-grains include threshing, sprinkling, and so forth; the properties of clarified butter include purifying by straining, inspecting, and so forth; and the properties of the *sāṃnāyya* offering include milking, curdling, and so forth.
All of these [subsidiary acts] are connected with the transcendental potency (*apūrva*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices by way of being both cause and effect;
for there is no intermediate *apūrva* whatsoever,
since once the result is accomplished by a single *apūrva*, there is no basis for postulating another *apūrva*.

When it is argued that ritual duties (dharmas), being performed for the sake of the fruit-apūrva, produce that fruit-apūrva even when performed upon any substance whatsoever—and thus a confusion of application (sāṃkarya) results—we reply: the six sacrifices, such as the Āgneya and others, which exist at different moments and are perishable, are incapable of producing the fruit-apūrva by acting together.
Therefore, one must postulate six intermediate apūrvas produced by the Āgneya and other sacrifices, which are capable of generating that [final] fruit-apūrva.
Among these, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by the sacrifice whose substance is the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is the motivator for the properties of the rice (*vrīhi*),
because of its proximity; however,
the *apūrva* of the fruit is separated from them by that [intermediate *apūrva*].

Thus, for those [substances] characterized by the properties of clarified butter (*ājya*) and those characterized by the properties of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, there is a direct connection only with the intermediate apūrva produced by the sacrifice involving each respective substance.

This being the case, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), being prompted by each respective apūrva, are restricted to the raw materials (*prakṛtidravya*) that serve as the means for achieving each respective apūrva.
Now, it may be objected that the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa is what assigns these purificatory rites.
And since that [removal] is common to all natural substances, the confusion remains exactly as it was.

Now, if it should be argued: "The removal of the husks is possible only in the case of rice-grains; therefore, the *avaghāta* (threshing) applies only to them, and not to the clarified butter (*ājya*) or the *sāṃnāyya*."
"In this way, the pouring out [of the milk] applies only to the clarified butter (ājya), while the milking and so forth apply only to the Sāṃnāyya."—
Certainly.
If it is argued that even though those dharmas with visible purposes are established, those with invisible purposes— such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth— would become confused,
this is not so;

for they are established by the direct scriptural statement of the accusative case in such injunctions as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (vrīhīn prokṣati) and "he gazes at the clarified butter" (ājyam avekṣate).
And direct Vedic statement (śruti) is stronger than context (prakaraṇa);
therefore, the ritual duties (dharmas) are established as restricted [to their respective contexts].
(Regarding the fifth section [of the third chapter], which establishes that the *sphya* and other implements are fixed according to their connection [with specific rites], the sūtra states:
"And a substance, because of its connection with the originative injunction, should be enjoined for that purpose alone. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.11)

The fifth section formulates the following: Is there a commingling of substances such as the wooden sword (*sphyā*) and the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*), or is there a fixed distinction? Since the status of being "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*) applies equally to all of them, there is commingling in this case.
If there were a confusion [of functions], the futility of the statements regarding the *uddhanana* (stirring up) and other acts would result;
for the mention of the weapons is indeed a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, as in the previous case, there is a fixed restriction (*vyavasthā*).

In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "The wooden sword (*sphya*), the potsherds (*kapālāni*), the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle, the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the yoke-pin (*śamyā*), the mortar (*ulūkhalam*), the pestle (*musalam*), the grinding stone (*dṛṣad*), and the lower millstone (*upalā*)—these..."
"Indeed, there are ten sacrificial implements.
By the word *sphya*, a wooden instrument shaped like a sword is meant.

In that regard, although the confusion regarding the preparatory rites such as threshing applied to substances like rice and so forth has been refuted, it is impossible to refute the confusion regarding the substances such as the *sphya* and the *kapāla* in relation to the ritual acts of their respective parts, namely the stirring (*uddhanana*) and the baking of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Since there is no contradiction in any substance whatsoever being called a "sacrificial implement" (*yajñāyudha*) even when it is employed in any action at all—
for the status of being a sacrificial implement does not vanish merely because of a lack of fixed restriction— this being the position reached,

we reply: "He digs with the *sphya*," "He cooks on the potsherds," "He pours out the oblations with the *agnihotrahavaṇī*," "He winnows with the winnowing basket," "He spreads the black antelope skin beneath the mortar."

In the view that there is a confusion [of means], the futility of these sentences— which indicate specific associations— would follow: namely, "He places the lower millstone with the *śamyā*," "He threshes with the mortar and pestle," and "He grinds with the lower and upper millstones."

If it is argued that even under the view of restrictive application (*vyavasthāpakṣa*), the statement regarding the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*)—which conveys only a general relationship—is purposeless, we say: no.
This is because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of matters already established by the statements concerning digging (*uddhanana*) and so forth.
Nor should it be said that, conversely, the statements concerning digging and so forth themselves are merely restatements.
Because excessive redundancy is the least desirable [fault], and the restatement of the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*) is not entirely purposeless;
for it is utilized for the injunction regarding their placement, as in the text: "They collect the sacrificial implements."
Therefore—just like the preparatory rites such as threshing—the substances such as the wooden sword (sphya) and the potsherds (kapāla) are fixed [to specific purposes].
(Regarding the sixth section, concerning the non-confusion of qualities such as "redness" and so forth, the sūtra states:
"When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction because the substance and the quality serve a single function. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.12)

The sixth section formulates the problem: Does the statement "he buys with a red [cow]" apply to the purchase alone as a mixed [qualification], or is the redness mixed with all the substances because it cannot be connected sequentially? MJaiNy_3,1.11 //
Through its connection with the purchase by means of the substance, there is again a syntactic connection with that portion [of the price];
however, the quality [redness] is directly connected to the purchase, while the substance is connected to it by implication when it is proximate.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "One purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow."

In this regard—the word *aruṇā* denotes the quality (*guṇa*) of redness (*aruṇimā*). Even when it is employed with reference to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), it causes the cognition of the quality itself, according to the maxim: "There is no cognition of a qualified object without the apprehension of the qualifier. Furthermore, its linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) is established for the quality alone through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Furthermore, by virtue of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), that quality of redness (*aruṇima-guṇa*) is understood to be a means for the purchase of Soma; however, this is untenable.
Since a formless quality cannot serve as a means for a purchase—just as a garment or a cow cannot—it follows that the instrumental case-ending lacks the power of application (*viniyojakatva*).
Consequently, it must be stated that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is what effects the application here.
Furthermore, the context establishes the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) in all substances, such as the cups (*graha*) and the ladles (*camasa*).
Nor should it be suspected, on this same principle, that the referents of the words *piṅgākṣī* ("tawny-eyed") and *ekahāyanī* ("one-year-old") also apply to all substances;
for those two words denote specific substances.
She whose eyes are tawny in color is a "tawny-eyed cow" (*piṅgākṣī*); likewise, [one] "one-year-old" (*ekahāyanī*). Although these two words denote a single cow, [they are distinct].
Nevertheless, there are two words due to the difference between the two properties that serve as qualifiers.
And these two, functioning simultaneously, enjoin the substance "cow" as qualified by two real properties in its capacity as the means for purchase.
Furthermore, it is not possible to apply one substance to another substance.
However, because the quality of redness is capable of being construed as a qualifier for substances, it is applied to them.
In this regard, the construction of the words is as follows: "aruṇayā" (with the red one) constitutes a separate sentence.

Therein, by means of the direct statement of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), all the substances serving as means within the context are referred to (*anūdyante*), and the quality is enjoined by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*): "Those substances which are the means for the Jyotiṣṭoma..."
"All of those must be made red.
Therefore, when it is argued that the quality is mixed [with the substance], we reply: even though the quality is formless (amūrta),...
Nevertheless, [the word "one-year-old"] delimits the substance "cow," just like [the words] "year" or "eye.
And since that substance is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the quality becomes connected with the purchase by way of that [substance].
This being the case, there will be no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
But surely, even if there is no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is unavoidable,
because it is accepted that a word denoting a quality has as its referent the substance possessing that quality.
Not so.
In this context, the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is expressed by the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) through the word *gusyā* (by devotion).

Since that [status of being a means] is not possible without a substance as its medium, it is postulated—on the basis of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*)—that devotion has the function of delimiting the substance.
If it is argued, "In that case, substances such as the *graha* and *camasa* vessels should also be delimited," we say: no.
Because that substance lacks the status of being a means for purchase, the quality [of the substance] cannot be established as a means for purchase when it is delimited by that [substance].

If it is argued: "In that case, let there be a delimitation by the cloth and so forth, since in the injunctions 'He purchases with cloth' and 'He purchases with goats,' the cloth and others do serve as means for purchase," we say: No, because those [other items] serve as means for different acts of purchase.
For in that case, unlike the optionality of milk, curd, and so forth in the Agnihotra, an option of substances such as cloth is not enjoined by way of a restatement (anuvāda) of the act of purchase;
because the act of purchase alone, being a restatement, is not enjoined elsewhere as it is in the Agnihotra.
Therefore, these are injunctions of distinct acts of purchase qualified by substances such as cloth.
For it is not logical to disregard the substance *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) mentioned within its own sentence and instead effect a delimitation by means of cloth or other items.

Therefore, after the substance and the quality have been directly connected with the act of purchase, they subsequently become connected as mutual delimiters through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).
This being the case, the final meaning established is: "One purchases [the animal] with a one-year-old cow qualified by redness."
Therefore—the quality of ruddiness pertains only to the one-year-old cow, which is the cause of the purchase.

(Section on the Cleansing of the Vessels in the Seventh [Adhikaraṇa]—The Principle of the Singularity of the Vessel; Sūtras 13–15) Sūtra 13: That which is joined with singularity belongs to one [vessel], because of its connection with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Sūtra 14: Or rather, it applies to all [the vessels], because it serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); for a defining characteristic is non-distinct [in its application].
"But when there is an injunction, because it is for the sake of another, it should be understood according to the scriptural text.
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.15). [The author] formulates the seventh section as follows:
Regarding the injunction "he cleanses the cup," is one cup to be purified or all of them?
It is one, because the number of the object to be designated is respected just as it is in the case of the thing to be employed (upādeya).

Because of its predominance, the repetition of its qualities does not require [the action] to be considered as one; otherwise, in prescribing it, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda). Therefore, by mentioning the substance, the purification applies to all.
In some [texts] it is heard: "He purifies the cup with the *daśāpavitra*."
A "fragment of cloth" refers to a piece of ten spans. In that regard—

just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," the singularity residing in the animal, which is the thing to be enjoined (*upādeya*), is intended to be significant, so too the singularity residing in the cup (*graha*), which is the thing to be designated (*uddeśya*), must be intended to be significant.

Furthermore, since the word *graha* denotes a genus (*jāti*), and since the genus is the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), it follows that the genus becomes consecrated by any rite performed upon any substance whatsoever that serves as its substratum;
therefore, one might conclude that "only a single *graha* needs to be purified.

To this we reply: By the accusative case in the word *graham*, the *graha* is understood to be the primary object (*pradhāna*) because it is the intended goal (*uddeśya*) and possesses a purpose (*prayojana*).
The cleansing is a subordinate element (guṇa) with respect to the cup (graha).
According to the principle that "a subordinate element must be repeated for each primary element," as many cups as there are,
all of them are to be cleansed.

Since such a determination has been reached, because there is no desire to know the exact number of things to be purified or grasped, the singular number heard in the subject (uddeśya) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), even though it is explicitly stated.
Now, it might be argued: "This [singular number] does not belong to the subject; rather, two things are being enjoined."
That is not so, because it would result in a split in the sentence:
"One should mix the cups..."
And because there is a distinction between the objects to be enjoined—namely, "that" and "one"—there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
In the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal," however, the animal is subordinate to the sacrifice;
for there is no such principle as "the repetition of the principal [action] for every subordinate element."
Therefore, because the specific quantity [of the object] is what one desires to know, the singularity that is being heard is intended as significant; this constitutes the difference.
Furthermore, a genus (jāti) cannot be the object of a purificatory rite (saṃskārya), because it is immaterial (abhūrtatva).
Therefore, the word *guṇa* (quality) indicates the substance by way of its genus (*jāti*),
and in that context, non-repetition has been stated.
Consequently, all the cups (*grahas*) are to be cleansed.
(Regarding the eighth section, concerning the non-application of purification and other rites to the cup and so forth; Sūtras 16–17:
"Or rather, because it is a purificatory rite, there would be no restriction regarding the subordinate elements.
(Jaimini 3.1.16) "But there is indeed a restriction, because the purpose is connected with the Vedic text, and that [purpose] has the Word as its authority. (Jaimini 3.1.17)
In the eighth section, [the author] formulates [the following]: "And as for the *camasa* cups and so forth, should they be mixed together or not? For them, there is no cleansing."
Because it is possible to disregard even the state of being perceived as a unity.
Non-obstruction is the reason for attention here; indeed, there is no split in the sentence.
However, there is no cleansing of the cups and so forth, because by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), that [cleansing] is assigned specifically to the [soma].

Just as in the word "graham," the singularity that constitutes the meaning of the suffix is not intended to be significant, so too it is possible that the cup-ness (*grahatva*), which is the meaning of the nominal stem, is also not intended to be significant. Consequently, since the word "graha" serves merely to indicate any vessel for Soma, and since the purpose of removing the residue of Soma through wiping is equally possible for the *camasas* (wooden cups) as it is for the *grahas*, the *camasas* and other such vessels must also be cleansed.
This being the position reached, we reply: singularity is not intended to be expressed because it would result in the fault of syntactical split (vākya-bheda);
however, why should the state of being a cup (graha-tva), which is free from such faults, not be intended?
Therefore, even though a purpose exists, there is no cleansing (*saṃmārga*) in the case of the *camasa* cups and so forth due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor can that [purpose] be postulated by depending on the object,
because the object is already provided by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding the *graha* vessels.
Therefore, there is no purification.

(Regarding the nineteenth topic in the ninth chapter, concerning the status of the seventeen-span measurement as a property of the animal sacrifice, the sūtra states: "Because it would otherwise be purposeless, [it applies] to its subsidiaries.
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.18)

The ninth section formulates the problem: "Should the sacrificial post of the Vājapeya be seventeen aratnis in height? Is this measurement an accessory of the substance belonging to the Vājapeya sacrifice, or rather an accessory of the animal?"
Due to its immediate sequence and its context, this [wood] is a constituent part of the ritual in the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice;
it is connected to the action through the *ūrdhvapātra* ladle made of *khadira* wood in the fire.
The limb of the animal is connected to the sacrifice by way of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and the sacrificial post is connected to the sacrifice by way of the animal;
because the Vājapeya is a Soma-sacrifice, there is no sacrificial post without an animal.
(Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Prakāśa 3.1.19) In the section on the Vājapeya, it is heard in scripture: "The sacrificial post of the Vājapeya is seventeen cubits long."
In this regard— the vertical measurement pertaining to the sacrificial post substance, which is expressed by the term "seventeen cubits," is an auxiliary (aṅga) of the vājapeya rite,
because of the proximity between the word "seventeen cubits" and the word "vājapeya.
Furthermore, the context (prakaraṇa) is thus upheld.

If it were impossible for the measurement to apply directly to the ritual action (*karman*), then one might argue that the measurement first connects with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup made of *khadira* wood which stands upright as part of the *vājapeya* sacrifice, and through that medium, it subsequently relates to the ritual action.

To this, we reply: because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is seventeen cubits long," it connects directly with the sacrificial post itself.
Since that sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), its measurement becomes an auxiliary of the animal by means of the post.
Furthermore, since that animal is an auxiliary of the Vājapeya sacrifice, it [the measurement] is an auxiliary of the ritual action by means of the animal.
Even though there is immediate proximity between the words "Vājapeya" and "post," [the relationship is mediated through these intermediate steps].
Nevertheless, since the Vājapeya is a Soma sacrifice, it lacks a direct connection with the sacrificial post (yūpa); therefore, the mediation of the animal (paśu) must be accepted.
This is because the genitive case in the word "vājapeyasya," while denoting a mere relationship, expresses even a mediated relationship.
Because of the usage "the grandson of Devadatta," as for the proximity of the words *saptadaśāratni* and *vājapeya*,
and the fivefold context (*prakaraṇa*), both of these are likewise not contradictory.
Even though it is a part of the animal sacrifice (*paśvaṅga*), it is ultimately accepted as being a part of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Furthermore, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the term *yūpa* (sacrificial post) would have to indicate the *ṣoḍāśi* vessel by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), this fault does not apply.
(Regarding the tenth [section], the adhikaraṇa on the fact that the *abhikramaṇa* and other acts are subsidiary only to the *prayāja*s, Sūtras 19–20:

"But if it were a quality of the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because of the lack of connection with the action. (Jaimini 3.1.19) "However, it should be a single sentence because it is expectant; for it is not completed by the preceding [element]. (Jaimini 3.1.20)
In the tenth section of the third chapter of the *Mīmāṃsājaiminīyasūtranyāyamālāvistara*, he formulates [the following]:
"Regarding the injunction 'He offers while stepping forward,' that [stepping] is connected with the agent throughout the entire [act]."
Or rather, would the entire set of performers belong to the *prayāja* alone?

Because both the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) are actions, they lack a mutual relationship with one another; therefore, it is not so, for they are equal in that regard.
There is no fault [in this], for this meditative concentration (*samāhiti*) is to be brought about through connection with the agent;
therefore, due to its proximity to the *prayāja* offerings, it is connected with that very same agent.
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in proximity to the *prayāja* offerings: "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*).

In that context, regarding this movement around the Āhavanīya fire at the time of the oblation, it is connected with the performer of the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, and not merely with the performer of the Prayāja offerings alone.
If it is argued: "Why? Because *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward), being an action, lacks the status of a factor (*kāraka*) and thus cannot be connected with the action of *prayāja*," [we reply:
"Not so."
Precisely because it is of the nature of an action, it is impossible for it to be connected even with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual action.
Now, if it were argued that "the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) is directly connected with the agent as a factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*),
and through that [agent], it is connected with the entire *darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual"— [we reply:]...
This same solution applies equally to the connection with the *prayāja* offerings;
therefore, by the force of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), it is connected with the agent of the *prayāja*.
START MJaiNy 3.1.23-24:
He sets forth this very section according to the opinion of the Vārttikakāra:
"Or rather, because of its proximity, there is strength [of indication] within the context; therefore..."
In the case of the *kramaṇa* (stepping) studied within the ritual procedure of the *darśa* and other sacrifices, it would be a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that [procedure].

The intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) begins from the injunction "He offers the *samits*" (*samidho yajati*). Because [the *tanūnapāt* mantra] is recited in the midst of that, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it; through that [intermediate context], its status as a subsidiary to the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) is established.
Even in this view, the subject matter and the doubt remain the same.
The only difference lies in the reasons for the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*).

The prima facie view is as follows: because the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is more powerful than the mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*) of the *prayāja* offerings, the act of stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) is included within all the constituent parts belonging to that context.
There exists an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) for the *prayāja* offerings, which begins with the scriptural injunction: "He offers to the *samidhs*."
In the midst of that [context], the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is enjoined.

Since this injunction for the *abhikramaṇa* is observed on both sides by sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the *abhikramaṇa* is subsumed under the *prayāja* offerings alone.
Even according to this view, the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) is not contradicted.
Because [the *prayāja*s] find their place in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) by way of the *prayāja* offerings themselves.

(Regarding the eleventh [topic], the section concerning the status of the *upavīta* as a contextual subsidiary: Sūtra) "But when there is doubt, there would be a split of the sentence due to intervention. (Jaimini 3.1.21)
He formulates the eleventh topic:

"Does the injunction *upavyayate* (he puts on the sacred thread) constitute a subsidiary element of the *sāmidhenī* verses, or is it a subsidiary of the Darśa sacrifice? This is the context; therefore, the former [alternative] applies here. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 3.1.25)
When there is an interruption by the mantras known as *nivit*, which are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the fire-offering (*agni*),
[the *nivit*] is a member of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) because of its mention within the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*).

In the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-prakaraṇa*), within this chapter beginning with "Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ," the *sāmidhenī-brāhmaṇa* is recited in the seventh and eighth anuvākas.
In the ninth [section], there is the Brāhmaṇa for the mantras known as *nivits*, beginning with "O Agni, you are great, O Brāhmaṇa-bhārata.
In the tenth, there are the optional alternatives for the *sāmidhenī* verses.
In the eleventh, however, the *upavīta* (sacred thread) is thus prescribed: "The *nivīta* is for men..."

“The shoulder-yajñopavīta worn over the right shoulder is for the ancestors; the shoulder-yajñopavīta worn over the left shoulder is for the gods; when he wears it over the left shoulder, he thereby creates the very mark of the gods.”

In this regard, if it is argued that the *upavīta* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses because the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* is accepted according to the previous reasoning, we say: no.
This is because the context of the *sāmidhenīs* is interrupted by the *nivid* formulas and the *brāhmaṇa* passage.
Nor should it be said that the interruption does not occur because the *nivid* formulas themselves are read within that context as being accessories to the *sāmidhenīs*.
Because it is understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the *nivid* verses constitute a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the fire-ritual:

having addressed Agni, who is the locus of the oblations, the qualities of Agni are proclaimed by means of the *nivid* sentences beginning with "Great art thou" (*mahān asi*) in order to generate enthusiasm for him.
For this very reason, the etymological explanation is heard thus: "One should cause [him] to be known by means of the *nivid* verses."
"Because they are connected to that [Agni], they possess the nature of being connected.

Now, if it is argued: "By the etymological derivation, 'those Ṛg-verses by which the fire is properly kindled are the Sāmidhenīs,' they too serve the purpose of Agni here through the medium of the flame," let them indeed be so.
It does not follow from this that there is a mutual relationship of principal and subordinate between them.

[Objection: Let the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses be interrupted; could it not be that the *upavīta* is closely connected as a subordinate element to the context of the *nivid* verses? [Reply: No.

If it is argued that because the *nivid* formulas are not heard in the preceding and following sections, there is no *prakaraṇa* (context), and therefore their status as subsidiaries is established by *saṃnidhi* (proximity)— we say no;
for they are separated by the optional *sāmidhenī* verses.
Nor should it be suspected that the *upavīta* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the optional *sāmidhenī* verses;
for the context (*prakaraṇa*) is more powerful than mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*).
Therefore, since the logic of the *prayāja* offerings does not apply here, the *upavīta* is a subordinate element of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by virtue of the primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*).
(Regarding the twelfth section, the Adhikaraṇa on the mutual non-connection of subordinate elements, the Sūtra states:
"And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them], owing to their equality.
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.22)
He formulates the twelfth section: "Now,
regarding the vessels made of *vaikaṅkata* wood and so forth used in the *pavamāna* offerings—
at this point, because of the context (*prakaraṇa*), they are connected to the entire sacrifice, not merely to the *ādhāna*."

That which is purposeless remains among its constituent parts, specifically within the oblations (*havirṣu*). It cannot apply to the entire sacrifice on the basis of a syntactical connection (*vākya*), because of the similarity with the oblations of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*).

In the context of the fire-installation (*ādhāna-prakaraṇa*), a wooden vessel (*dārupātra*) is prescribed for both the purpose of offering (*homārtha*) and the purpose of the sacrifice (*yajñārtha*): "Therefore, a vessel made of *vāraṇa* wood should be used in the sacrificial proceedings, but one should not offer with it."
"An implement for the sacrifice should be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood; one should indeed offer with this.
Here, "implement for the sacrifice" (*yajñāvacara*) means that which is the cause for the performance of the sacrifice.
In this context, the vessels made of *vāraṇa*, *vaikaṅkata*, and other woods first apply to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) by virtue of the contextual connection (*prakaraṇa*).
Since there is no purpose for this vessel in the act of laying the fires (ādhāna), it is restricted to the Pavamāna oblations, which are auxiliary to the laying of the fires;
for the Pavamāna oblations do indeed constitute an auxiliary part of the laying of the fires,
as they are recited within that same context.

In this context, within the section beginning with "One should establish the sacred fire under the Kṛttikās," and in the subsequent recitation beginning with "Prajāpati beheld the truth of speech," these [oblations] are prescribed by the passage starting with "He offers three oblations.

Consequently, just as the measurement of seventeen cubits—being impossible directly in the Vājapeya—is applied to the animal sacrifice which is a subsidiary part of that rite, so too should this [measurement] be understood. This is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
We reply: Just as the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) is prescribed with reference to Agni, so too are the Pavamāna oblations.

This is because the offering of the Pavamāna oblations is enjoined with reference to the Āhavanīya fire, according to the injunction: "In that they offer into the Āhavanīya, by that he [Agni] is pleased and satisfied."

Therefore, there is no mutual relationship of principal and subordinate between the primary oblations prescribed as being consecrated by fire. This being the case, since the *prakaraṇa* (context) lacks the power to enjoin [the *vaikaṅkata* wood] with respect to those specific vessels, the sentence "The sacrificial implement is made of *vaikaṅkata* wood" enjoins it for all sacrifices, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others.
(Regarding the thirteenth section, the *vārtraghnyadhikaraṇa*, the sūtra states: "And because there is no connection of purpose between them [mutually]. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.23)
The thirteenth section formulates the following problem: "The two *vārtraghni* verses belong to the Full Moon sacrifice, while the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses belong to the New Moon sacrifice.
Is this stated as a general subordination to the primary rites, or is it a fixed restriction?
All four mantras have been brought into sequence for the two Ājyabhāga offerings;
since syntactical connection (vākya) is stronger than sequence, these [mantras] are subordinate to the Darśa and other sacrifices.
In the primary sense, there is no single Soma sacrifice; nor [is there a restriction] regarding the locus and so forth, or time.
Because the New Moon (darśa) and other sacrifices would otherwise lack fixed application, their application is established by means of the direct scriptural statement (vākya).
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, it is heard: "The two Vārtraghni verses are recited at the Full Moon."
Regarding the statement, "The two *vṛdhanvatī* verses [are used] on the new moon day," therein—

this pair of *vārtraghnī* verses and this pair of *vṛdhanvatī* verses are recorded in the *Hautraka* section, in the sequence of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, within the section beginning with the mantra "Agni, strike down the Vṛtras. However, by means of the cited Brāhmaṇa passage, the injunction for those [verses] in the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices is understood.
In this regard, since the direct statement (*vākya*) is more powerful [than context], these mantras are auxiliary to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices,
and not auxiliary to the Ājyabhāga offerings— this being the prima facie view, we reply: "Agni shall strike down the Vṛtras"— this first mantra addressed to Agni is the *vārtraghnī*.
"O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous"—this second verse addressed to Soma is the *vārtraghnī* (slayer of Vṛtra).
"Agni by his ancient birth"—this first verse addressed to Agni is the *bṛdhanvatī* (possessing the word *vṛdh*).
"O Soma, we [serve] you with songs"—this second verse addressed to Soma is the *vṛdhanvatī*.

In that regard, since the two primary sacrifices, the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa, contain the Āgneya cake-offering, it may somehow be possible for the two Āgneyī verses to serve as the Puronuvākyās by way of option;
however, this is not possible for the two Saumya offerings,
because there is no deity named Soma [in those specific contexts].
For even in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, Soma alone is not present.
Furthermore, by the two locative endings in "at the full moon" and "at the new moon," the status of [the time] as a locus is understood.
Furthermore, that [designation] is not possible if it denotes a sacrifice, because the sacrifice would then be the primary element;
however, since time is subordinate, its denotation of time is appropriate.
Moreover, this section is recited immediately after the section containing the restatements of the *prayāja* mantras.
And that sequence belongs to the two subsidiary *ājyabhāga* offerings,
not to the primary *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Therefore, the fourfold set of mantras does not constitute an auxiliary element of the primary sacrifices.
Rather, it is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
But surely, this is already established by the very order [of the ritual];
for in that case as well, since the first *ājyabhāga* belongs to Agni, the mantra must also belong to Agni.
The rule that "on the Saumya [day] the second [offering] is Saumya" is obtained through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone.
Certainly;
nevertheless, the pair of *vārtraghna* [verses] is for the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

"The pair beginning with *vṛdhanvatī* [is to be used] on the new moon day"—this rule, which was not previously established, is stated by means of the Brāhmaṇa passage; thus, there is no pointlessness.
(Regarding the fourteenth section, concerning the fact that the washing of the hands and other such acts are subsidiary to the entire context, Sūtras 24–25:
"Proximity is not an injunction [of subsidiarity], because the sentences are complete in themselves.
(Jaimini 3.1.24) "And because the sentences are complete. (Jaimini 3.1.25)
In the section on the fourfold set (caturgaṇa), [the author] formulates [the following]:
"He washes both hands; he spreads a layer of ulapa grass."
The spreading of darbha grass is indeed a subsidiary part [of the rite], as is the purification of the hands in its entirety.
In this case, there would be subsidiarity to that specific [act] due to the sequence consisting of immediate succession;
however, by means of indicative mark (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), there is subsidiarity to the performance of all [the rites].
In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard: "He washes his hands."
Regarding the statement, "He spreads the *ulaparāji*": *ulaparāji* refers to a bundle of grass prepared for spreading upon the altar (*vedi*).

If it is argued that, because the [injunction] for hand-purification and the [injunction] for spreading the *darbha* grass are recited in immediate succession, the former is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the mere spreading of the *darbha* grass by virtue of the authority of sequence (*krama*); [we reply:]...
Not so;
the washing is a purification of the hands.
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the capacity [implied by the statement]: "And when the two hands are purified, they are fit for the performance of all [ritual] acts."
Furthermore, the context (prakaraṇa) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is explicit.

Therefore, because the sequence (krama) is set aside by the more powerful indicators of indicative power (liṅga) and context, the purification of the hands is a subsidiary element (śeṣa) to all [the rites].
This same principle should be understood to apply to the restraint of speech (vāgyama) as well.
And that restraint of speech is heard in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "He makes fists; he restrains his speech.
Immediately after that, this is heard: "He announces the initiated one.
And the manner of the announcement is heard as follows: "This Brāhmaṇa has been initiated," he says three times in a low voice; thus he announces him to the gods.
"Three times loudly he announces him to both gods and men.

In this context, when fickleness of the hands and tongue has been restrained by the clenching of fists and the restraint of speech, the fitness of the one-pointed mind for all ritual acts is the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
By this, the [prescribed] sequence is set aside.
(Regarding the fifteenth [topic], the section on whether the fourfold division and so forth are subsidiary to the Āgneya alone; Sūtras 26–27):

"But the remnant, being connected with a quality, should be understood as common [to all], because there is no mutual connection between them. (Jaimini 3.1.26) "Or rather, there is a restriction because of the connection with the purpose; since the indicative mark is connected with the purpose, the mention of the quality is for the sake of characterization. (Jaimini 3.1.27)
In the fifteenth section (adhikaraṇa), beginning with *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtra* 3.1.34–36, [the author] formulates the following:
"It has been stated that the *āgneya* cake (*puroḍāśa*) is to be divided into four parts."
The division into four parts applies to all remaining [portions], or it pertains solely to the portion dedicated to Agni.
Since the indicative mark [of being dedicated to Agni] is applicable to the Āgneya, it follows that it is a subordinate element to all [the cakes];
therefore, let there be the status of being "Āgneya" for the Agnīṣomīya and the Aindrāgna as well.
The status of being "related to Agni" (āgneyatva) is not primary for those two [the cake and the butter], because they do not depend solely on Agni;
therefore, the division into four parts (caturdhākaraṇa) applies only to one of the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa).
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), it is heard in the scripture: "One divides the cake related to Agni into four parts."

In that regard— if it is argued that because the two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) for Indra-Agni and Agni-Soma are also connected with fire, just like the one for Agni, they are all indicated by the term "āgneya," and therefore the remnant belongs to all three—
this is not so.
For this [suffix] in "āgneyaḥ" is not prescribed merely for a general relationship expressed by a taddhita suffix, but rather for a relationship with a deity;
and Agni alone is not the deity of the two cakes that have two deities.

Therefore, because a single deity serves as an indicator for the entire set of deities, the status of being "dedicated to Agni" (Āgneyatva) does not belong to those two [other cakes] in its primary sense; thus, the fourfold division is restricted to the cake dedicated to Agni in its primary sense alone.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the second quarter of the third chapter.

The status of being subsidiary to the mantras should arise from their capacity to express meaning; therefore, there is a connection with the original [text] because of the eternal association with the purpose. (Jaimini 3.2.1) Because it is a purificatory rite, it would apply even where not specifically enjoined.
(Jaimini 3.2.2)

In the first section of the second chapter, he formulates the following: "Is the *barhis* grass used for the approach to the gods [to be employed] for both the primary and secondary meanings because it possesses their characteristic marks? Or does it enjoin the mantra only for the primary meaning? (MJaiNy 3.2.1).
Because both [the word and its meaning] are the objects of the verbal expression, their application there is appropriate;
however, by virtue of being understood first, the application is restricted to the primary sense.
The mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi) is traditionally recited as a means of manifesting the act of cutting.
In this regard, by the mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the capacity to manifest the act of cutting, this mantra is applied to the action of cutting.
And that which is to be cut—the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—is of two kinds: primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*).
The primary consists of the ten types of *darbha* grass, such as *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and so forth.
But the secondary (gauṇa) [meaning] is another grass similar to that;
for the word *barhis* applies to the boy through a connection with qualities (*guṇayoga*), just as the word *agni* applies to him.

This being the case, since both the primary and the secondary are the meanings of the word, there would follow the application of the mantra to the cutting of both the *darbha* grass and the other grass—this being the position reached (*prāpta*).

We reply: Since the primary sense is understood more quickly, the *liṅga* (indicative power), having fulfilled its purpose by enjoining the mantra for the primary sense, does not wait for the secondary sense due to its slower comprehension.
Therefore, the mantra is restricted to the primary act of cutting alone.
(Second [topic]:

In the section concerning the application of the *aindrī* verse to the *gārhapatya* fire, Sūtras 3–4) / But because of the direct statement, the *aindrī* verse should be used for a purpose other than its literal meaning. Jaimini 3.2.3.

Or rather, the designation may arise from a quality, because the relationship [between the name and its referent] is not based on scriptural authority. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.4) He formulates the third section as follows:
START MJaiNy 3.2.3–4.

"One should assign the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra 'By the Aindrī verse, [enter] the dwelling,'" it is said. Whether the primary Indra or the secondary Indra is intended to be illuminated, let it be the primary one, as in the previous case.
Since the secondary sense (gauṇatā) would otherwise be impossible for one [of the two], and because the mantra itself is merely reiterative (anuvāda),
the mantra is enjoined by direct scriptural statement (śruti) for the worship of Agni due to its secondary application.
In the context of the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), a certain verse addressed to Indra (aindrī), beginning with "The dweller, the assembler," is recited.

Because the latter half of that [verse] is recited as "Indro na tasthau" (Like Indra, he has stood), and the Brāhmaṇa concerning that mantra is handed down thus: "With the verse addressed to Indra, beginning 'niveśanaḥ saṃgamano vasūnām,' one worships the Gārhapatya fire.
By this Brāhmaṇa, the mantra, being enjoined for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire, while illuminating its own meaning, illuminates the primary Indra.
The primary Indra is the lord of heaven, the thousand-eyed one,
because the word "Indra" is established by convention (rūḍhi) in that sense;
the secondary Indra, however, is the Gārhapatya fire.

Because he is similar to the primary Indra—either through the possession of qualities associated with sovereignty or by virtue of being the means for performing sacrifices—the primary Indra is first understood through the mantra according to the previous principle. When he has thus been revealed by the mantra, it is argued that, in order to avoid a contradiction between the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa, either the primary Indra or the location near the Gārhapatya fire must be indicated by the word "Gārhapatya. This being the position reached:

We reply: Since it is necessary that one of the two words "Indra" and "Gārhapatya" be used in a figurative sense, and since the Brāhmaṇa sentence possesses injunctive force, it would be improper to employ figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) within an injunction because its meaning is already established; therefore, the mantra itself, being a restatement (anuvāda) whose meaning is already established, will indicate Vahni by means of the word "Indra."

Therefore, the direct scriptural statement (śruti) in the third case ending in the word "aindryā" enjoins the mantra—which is indeed capable of illuminating the Gārhapatya fire—for the purpose of the worship (upasthāna) of the Gārhapatya fire.
(Third Section: On the Application of the Invocation; Sūtras 4–9) “If it is argued that the invocation is likewise [to be performed],” [we reply:
“No, because it is not an injunction of time, since [the rite] has already been enjoined. (Jaimini 3.2.6)
Because of the absence of qualities; because of the indicative mark; and because there would be a contradiction of the injunction if it were a mere instruction.
START MJaiNy 3.2.5–8.
The third section formulates [the following]:
Having addressed her with the words "O preparer of the oblation, come!", one should call out while threshing three times.
The application [of the mantra] would be to the threshing, or rather, to the invocation or to the act of threshing itself.
The invocation through the mantra is secondary, like that of [the goddess] Aindrī; otherwise, the root *han* would be rendered meaningless.
The number three is obtained through the textual recitation, and the word "invokes" (*hvayateḥ*) is used figuratively.
A triple repetition must be prescribed because there is no rule for its constant occurrence; the time is indicated by the root *han*, and likewise by the root *hvayati* when it has been reached.
In the case of application (*viniyoga*), there would be a split in the sentence; however, by virtue of the indicative power (*liṅga*), it is subordinate to the invocation.

The *aindrī* rule does not apply here because of the absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); thus, by the *barhis* rule, it applies to the primary [meaning]. Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in the scripture: "He invokes [the preparer of the oblation] three times while striking [the mortar], saying, 'O preparer of the oblation, come! (*haviṣkṛdehīti triravaghnannāhvayati*).
She who prepares the oblation for the sake of the gods is the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation).
Having addressed her, the Adhvaryu says, "Come!
Thus, this mantra is explained by the Brāhmaṇa: "'O preparer of the oblation, come! he says; he thereby calls those who are the preparers of the oblation for the gods."
The meaning is that, having uttered this mantra, the Adhvaryu priest calls out while performing the threshing three times.
By this statement, the mantra is enjoined for the purpose of threshing.
[Objection: But it is capable of being used for calling out.
If it is argued that this is not the case regarding threshing, we say no;
for that [word] is indicative of threshing.
Just as, in the previously cited *maitrāvaruṇī* passage, the word "Ucīndra" is used figuratively, so too is it here.
In the same way, the word "come" (*ehi*), being part of the mantra, will be used figuratively with respect to threshing.
Otherwise, since both the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa would be intent upon summoning, the word "threshing" (*avaghnan*) as it is heard in the text would be meaningless.
If it is argued that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in enjoining both the mantra and the number three while referring to the already established act of threshing, we say: no.

Since the number three has already been established, this mantra functions as a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*). In a certain recensional tradition (*śākhā*), this mantra is recorded in the section on mantras (*mantrakāṇḍa*) with a triple repetition.
However, the word "invokes" (*āhvayati*) must be treated figuratively as referring to the act of threshing, just like the word "come" (*ehi*). This being the prima facie position—
We reply: The attainment of the status of a "constant" (nityavat) through triple repetition is not established by mere recitation alone,
because in some schools it is recited twice,
while in others it is recited only once.
Therefore, this [act] is prescribed as if it were permanent;
nor is the word "āvatran" (not cutting) redundant,
because it serves to indicate the time.
If it is argued that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even regarding the injunction of time, we say no; because it is already established.
For the invocation of the assistants during the threshing does not occur at any other time.
Therefore, the time [for the rite] is obtained as a matter of course;
furthermore, since the invocation is also obtained through the very power of the mantra, it need not be enjoined.
For the recitation of the mantra "Come" (ehi) is not possible without an invocation.
The explanation of the mantra has been cited;
therein, the meaning of the sentence results as follows: "At the time of threshing, the invocation that occurs must be repeated three times.
For this very reason, in another Vedic recension (śākhā), the repetition is explicitly enjoined by restating the invocation.
"He calls out three times, for the gods are thrice true.
This being the case, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) even regarding the application of the mantra;
for by its indicative power (liṅga), it is applied to the calling, not to the threshing.
And the principle of the *aindrī* [verse] does not apply here,
because there is no direct hearing (*śruti*) of the instrumental case.

However, by the principle stated in the case of "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," the application of the mantra through its indicative power (*liṅga*) pertains to the primary invocation itself.
But this is not the case when the invocation is used in a figurative sense.
Therefore, this mantra is a supplement to the invocation.

(Regarding the fourth section, concerning the application of mantras that illuminate the carrying of the fire and so forth; Sūtra: Likewise [there is application] in rising and dismissal. Jaimini 3.2.10.
The fourth section formulates the following:
Rising up, one should recite "Agnīd agnīn" and so forth;
likewise, reciting "kṛṇuta vratam," he releases his speech.

Either the two mantras are to be enjoined, or the time [of rising and retiring] is to be enjoined; the two mantras are to be applied to the acts of rising and retiring, for it is not proper to resort to indirect indication (lakṣaṇā) when there is a direct injunction of time.
Because the meaning of the mantra cannot be construed [with the action], an injunction for it is not possible there;
since there is no other way, let there be indication (lakṣaṇā); therefore, the time is enjoined.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they recite: "Rising, he says, 'O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires!'"
Likewise: "He releases his speech with the words, 'Prepare the vow' (*vratam kṛṇuta*).

In this context, the mantra in the form of an injunction for the spreading of the fires (*agniviharaṇa*) and so forth is enjoined by this sentence as a subordinate element to the rising [from silence], after having addressed the *Āgnīdhra*.
Similarly, the mantra "Prepare the vow" is enjoined for the release of speech by the initiated one (*dīkṣita*), who has formed a fist and maintained silence.
Furthermore, in this case, the words *utthāna* (rising) and *vimoka* (unloosing) do not indicate time, as the previously mentioned word *avaghāta* (threshing) does.

This is because, since those two times—like the time of threshing—are not established by the sense of the text, it would be improper to resort to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when they are already established as things to be enjoined.

This being the position reached, we reply: these two mantras are connected with the injunction for the carrying forward of the fire (*agniviharaṇa*) and the injunction for the performance of the vow consisting of drinking milk (*payahpāna*).
But it does not apply to the rising or the release of speech;
therefore, since an application of two things that lack capacity is impossible, time is enjoined by resorting even to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as a last resort.
(Fifth [section]—The section concerning the *sūktavāka* being a subsidiary element of the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastarapraharaṇa*) [the *prastarapraharaṇa-nyāya*]; Sūtras 11–14).
JaiS 3.2.11: And in the case of the *sūktavāka*, it is an injunction of time, because it serves another purpose.
JaiS 3.2.12: Or rather, it is an original instruction (*upadeśa*), for the word "offering verse" (*yājyā*) is not used without cause.
Jaimini 3.2.13: Because of its connection with that [deity], it serves the purpose of the deities along with the gods.
Jaimini 3.2.14: If it is argued that it is a mere disposal (*pratipatti*), then, like the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, it would be a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of both.
START MJaiNy 3.2.12-13
The fifth section formulates the following:

"One should cast the prastara-bundle with the *sūktavāka*. This is a cognition regarding time; or rather, it may be a relationship of principal and subordinate, because [if it were time], there would be no syntactical connection with words such as "he has enjoyed" (*ajupata*). (MJaiNy 3.2.12)
Because the throwing (*prahṛti*) is a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) for the sake of the chosen deity, it is connected to that [deity];
it is to be accomplished by means of the deity, and its status as a subordinate element (*aṅgatā*) is established by the direct hearing of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*).
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recorded in the scripture: "One throws the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka* hymn."
The mantra beginning with "This has become auspicious for heaven and earth" (idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī bhadramabhūt) is the *sūktavāka*.
This is because in that mantra, having addressed Agni, it is traditionally recited: "You are the speaker of the hymn" (*tvaṃ sūktavāgasi*).
The *prastara* is a handful of *darbha* grass.
Its disposal is the throwing [of the *prastara*] into the fire.
In that context, the word "with the *sūktavāka*" indicates the time:
while this mantra is being recited by the *hotṛ*, at the time of its recitation, the *adhvaryu* should throw the *prastara*.
However, this mantra cannot be employed here for the act of striking, because there is no syntactic connection here, as in the case of the previously mentioned *praiṣa* mantras.
In the mantra, it is recited: "Agni has enjoyed this oblation; he has grown strong; he has made [it] greater and more vast," and so forth.
The meaning of that [text] is: "The fire, having grown through the consumption of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), produced an abundance of brilliance during that sacrifice.
And it cannot be connected with the throwing of the grass-bundle (prastara).
This being the position reached, we reply: by the direct statement of the instrumental case in the word "with the Sūktavāka" (sūktavākena), the mantra is enjoined for the act of throwing.
Nor is there an absolute absence of continuity;
for this mantra first causes one to recollect the previously worshipped deities such as Agni,
and the throwing of the grass-bundle (prastara) is the consecration of the desired deity.
Therefore, because the mantra and the act of offering are connected through the medium of the deity, the mantra is employed [in that ritual].
Now, one might object: "Offering" (praharaṇa) is merely an act of casting [the oblation], and not necessarily casting it while designating a specific deity."
If it is argued that this is not so because the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not heard [in the mantra],
and since there would thus be no mention of the deity itself, there could be no connection with it either—
do not say so.
Because of the actual existence of deities:

the fact that the *sūktavāka*, which illuminates deities such as Agni, is an auxiliary to the *praharaṇa* (the act of throwing) is understood through the force of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*).
If Agni and the other deities were present within the context (*prakaraṇa*), [then this would be established].
Then, by means of that manifestation, the visible purpose of the mantra would be attained.
Consequently, through the conceptualization of a deity, the status of the act as a sacrifice (*yāga*)—consisting of an offering preceded by the intent toward that deity—is established.
Therefore, there is indeed a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) by way of the deity.
In the sixth [section], the *viniyoga-sūtras* regarding the *udgātṛ-sūktavāka* according to their respective meanings [are presented]—(15–18).
In the section on application (*yogādhikaraṇa*), concerning the principle of the *sūktavāka*:
"Because of the instruction for the whole, there is mention of all [deities] in both cases. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.15)
Or rather, it is according to the actual meaning, because of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the remaining elements.
(Jaimini 3.2.16) If it is argued that this is due to a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), (Jaimini 3.2.17) [We reply:
Because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), the word "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) applies with respect to both. (Jaimini 3.2.18)
START MJaiNy 3.2.14-15. The sixth section formulates [the following]: Should the entire *sūktavāka* be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *praharaṇa*, or should it be divided?
Therefore, the designation applies to the whole; for that which is divided cannot be a subordinate part [of the whole].
In the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, [the name] should be divided according to the deities;
having set aside the designation by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the name is defined with respect to the specific portion.
In the previously cited mantra, the designation *sūktavāka* refers to the entire mantra.
If it is argued that because the term is used for the entire [sacrifice] by the ritualist (*yājñika*),
therefore everything [in the sacrifice] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the weapon— [we reply: no,
because the name (*samākhyā*) is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

In that very [text] regarding the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*), the mention of its deities is seen in one part: "May Agni and Soma enjoy this oblation. But in another part, there is the mention of the deities of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*): "May Indra and Agni enjoy this oblation," and "May Indra enjoy this oblation."
And [there is the mantra]: "Mahendra has accepted this oblation.
Indra, Agni-Indra, and Mahendra are established in the New Moon sacrifice according to the distinction of persons.
This being so, by the indicative power of the mantra, each deity is established at its respective time as possessing its particular portion.
And the word *sūktavāka* is etymological (*yaugika*) with respect to its constituent parts,
because it is derived from the analysis "he speaks (*vakti*) what is well-spoken (*sūkta*).
Its meaning is that at the time of the sacrifice, he speaks of the deity who has been properly praised by the respective mantra.

For this very reason, it has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa: "When he says, 'May Agni make this oblation palatable,' he indeed says, 'May we satisfy those deities whom we have invoked'; the meaning of "we have satisfied" (arīradhāma) is that "we have gratified them, we have made them pleased."
Therefore, this is applied after being divided.

(Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.19: In the section concerning the fact that the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses of the seven optional sacrifices are subsidiary only to those optional rites—) "On account of indicative power, order, and name, that which is recited is connected with the optional [rites].
The seventh section formulates the problem:
"The optional sacrifices to Indra-Agni and others, as well as their *yājyā* verses, have been mentioned in sequence within two sections;
should they be transferred according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*), or is there a fixed rule?"

The indicative mark (liṅga) is stronger than both the order (krama) and the name (samākhyā); by its force, these [verses] should be transferred even to rites performed without desire (akāmya). What harm is there in applying the *yājyā* verses everywhere?

The application of the *kāṇḍa* (section) is based on its designation; the sequential arrangement of sacrifices requires only the deity. Therefore, the capacity [of the rites] belongs exclusively to those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*).
In that section, the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭayaḥ*) are taught in sequence: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni..."

By the passage beginning with "whose kinsmen have departed" (*yasya sajātā vīyuḥ*), [it is meant that] *sajātāḥ* refers to relatives (*jñātayaḥ*); "have departed" (*vīyuḥ*) means they have gone away or are in disagreement.
In the *Mantrakāṇḍa* beginning with "indrāgnī rocanā," the *yājyānuvākyās* are recited in their respective order.
Therein, it is understood from the designation of the ritualists that "this is the section of optional *yājyānuvākyās*.
For those two—the *Iṣṭikāṇḍa* and the *Mantrakāṇḍa*—an arrangement is made according to sequence, such as: "the *yājyānuvākyās* recited first belong to the first sacrifice," and so forth.

However, since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) pertaining to the mantra contains the characteristics of Indra and Agni, it assigns those two *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses to both the optional and the obligatory *aindrāgna* sacrifice.

Since the indicative mark is more powerful, it follows that they should be applied everywhere—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: here, the order (*krama*) and the name (*samākhyā*) cannot be set aside by the indicative mark.
Because it is that upon which [the ritual] depends;
the manifestation of the mere form of the deities Indra and Agni is the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
However, the relationship of subsidiary and principal between the mantra and the ritual action does not arise from that alone.

Then, once the relationship between the Mantra-section and the Karma-section is understood through the force of the traditional instruction (samākhyā), the general relationship between the mantra and the ritual act is apprehended.
Specifically, however, it is understood from the sequence that "this is the first mantra for this first ritual act.
Now, one might object: "In the sacrifice to Indra and Agni, there is a mantra dedicated to Indra and Agni..."

If it is argued that such a specific detail as "the Vaiśvānara mantra [is used] in the Vaiśvānareṣṭi" is understood through the indicative power (*liṅga*) alone, we say no; for when the indicative power is common to multiple instances, one must rely on the order of sequence (*krama*).
Furthermore, there is also a second sacrifice: "One who has rivals should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni."
In that context, two [verses] dedicated to Indra and Agni are recited.
Furthermore, in the Mantra Section (Mantrakāṇḍa), another pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Indra and Agni is handed down, beginning with “Indrāgnī navatim.
Indeed, it would not be possible to determine [which verses correspond to which rites] there without relying on the order [of the ritual].

Nor should it be argued that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is irrelevant because that [result] is established through sequence alone; for in some cases, the indicative mark itself is the determining factor.

A single *aindrābārhaspatya* sacrifice is prescribed: "If one should desire that a Kṣatriya be born as a warrior and move about slaying enemies, for him he should offer this *aindrābārhaspatya* oblation."
Thus, regarding the birth of a prince, the desire of both the king and his domestic priest is as follows: "May this one be born in the mother's womb unimpeded by any obstacle created by the gods;
and once born, may he move about slaying his enemies."
This sacrifice is for the sake of the prince.

In the section on mantras, within the sequence of that sacrifice, two types of *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses addressed to the deities Indra and Bṛhaspati are recorded. One pair is as follows: "This oblation is for you both in your mouth... and so forth.
"*Asme indrābṛhaspatī*" and so forth constitute another [set].
Although the first pair of these is applied according to the order [of the ritual sequence], the second pair must be applied solely by means of its indicative power (*liṅga*).
Therefore, these *yājyā* verses are restricted to the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) by the combined force of order (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*).
(Regarding the eighth [section], concerning the application of the original mantras in the *agnīdhra-upasthāna*, Sūtras 20–23:

And when there is a governing context (*adhikāra*), the injunction of a mantra applies to those not designated by that [context], because they are taught [therein]. (Jaimini 3.2.20) Or rather, it is designated by that [context], because of both the context and logical consistency. (Jaimini 3.2.21)

And the instruction would be purposeless due to its lack of connection with anything that possesses a result; for [otherwise], everything would be subject to such instruction. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.22–23)
The eighth section formulates the problem:

Regarding the injunction "the Āgnīdhra [shed] with an Āgneyī [verse]," should all verses having Agni as their deity be employed for the rite of worship (upasthāna), or only those that are already present in the context (prakṛta)? 3.2.19.
"Since the word is uttered in a general sense, the presence [of the mantras] should be understood through all of them;
however, let it be accepted that they are restricted to those [mantras] under discussion by the transfer of the injunction to a specific instance.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "One worships the Āgnīdhra altar with an Āgneyī [verse]."
In this regard, if it is argued: "The attendance (*upasthāna*) of the pavilion named *Āgnīdhra* must be performed with some verse from the *Daśatayī* related to Agni;
for when it is stated in general terms that 'a verse whose deity is Agni is an *āgneyī*,' no specific verse is thereby indicated."
Not so;

for it is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself that the *ṛc* verses dedicated to Agni, which are recited within the context of a sacrifice, serve as the means for accomplishing a function prompted by that sacrifice.
When there arises a desire to know the specific nature of that function—namely, "What is this function?"—it is understood that "this [function] consists in the worship of the Āgnīdhra."

Thus, this injunction, by indicating [the application] only to the specific [subsidiaries], achieves brevity (*lāghava*).
