On the other hand, [the alternative view] would entail prolixity (*gaurava*), as it would have to indicate both that non-contextual [subsidiaries] are means for accomplishing the operations employed in the sacrifice, and the specific nature of those operations.
Therefore, the worship is performed with the *āgneyī* verses belonging to the context.

Thus, in the case of the injunctions "with an Aindrī verse [one worships] the Sadas" and "with a Vaiṣṇavī verse [one worships] the Havirdhāna," it should be understood that for the worship of the two pavilions named Sadas and Havirdhāna, one must employ those very Aindrī and Vaiṣṇavī verses that are relevant to the archetype (prakṛta).

(Ninth Adhikaraṇa: On the application of the *bhakṣa*-mantras according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*) at the time of taking [the cup] and so forth; Sūtras 24–25) Jai. 3.2.24: By virtue of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyāna*), the section [of the text] has the purpose of [reciting] the *bhakṣa*-mantra.
Jai. 3.2.25: There is a displacement [of parts of that section] by means of its form (*rūpa*) and specific instruction (*upadeśa*), because the meaning [of those parts] has been separately enjoined.
The ninth section formulates the following:
"Is this entire section beginning with *bhakṣehi* intended for the act of eating?
Or does it remain fixed by being divided according to its application in the acts of taking up [the cup] and so forth? (MJaiNy 3.2.21)
Let that entire [consequence] apply to the eating of unprescribed items such as the grahas;
however, regarding those very items implied by the purpose, it is divided according to their respective characteristics.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the consumption of the remnant of the offered Soma is prescribed. Therefore it is stated in the scripture: "Having pressed [the Soma] and offered it in the Āhavanīya fire, they go back toward the west and consume the Soma in the Sadas. In that consumption, there are four constituent acts: taking hold, looking at, swallowing, and properly digesting.
And the mantra is recited in the section beginning with "abhakṣehi" and so forth;

therein, while the act of consuming (*bhakṣaṇa*) is directly enjoined, the acts of taking up (*grahaṇa*), looking at (*avekṣaṇa*), swallowing (*nigaraṇa*), and properly digesting (*samyagjaraṇa*) are not so enjoined.
Furthermore, a mantra cannot be employed for that which has not been prescribed;
as for the title "The Section on Consuming" (*bhakṣānuvāka*), it refers only to the act of consuming itself.
Therefore, since the entire section is to be employed solely for the purpose of consumption—this being the position reached—[the following is stated].
We reply: Although the acts of taking up [the cup] and so forth are not explicitly enjoined, they are implied by the sense of the matter, because consumption is impossible without them.
Therefore, the recitation (anuvāka) should be applied to those acts by dividing it according to its indicative marks (liṅga).

In this context, the passage beginning with "Come, eat" (*abhakṣehi*) and ending with "I shall accomplish you with the arms of the Aśvins" (*aśvinostvā bāhubhyāṃ sādhayāsam*) reveals the act of taking [the cup],
as it shows both the summoning with "Come" and the grasping with "I shall take you with my two arms."

The portion, "O divine Soma, may I, who have good eyesight, look upon you, the one who watches over men," reveals the act of looking; for it expresses: "May I, possessing beautiful vision, gaze upon you who are renowned among human beings. The section beginning with "Impel my limbs" and ending with "May [the food] not pass below my navel" reveals the act of proper digestion.
This is because that [digestion] is understood through the satisfaction of the body and the prohibition against passing [the food] down the lower part;
digestion is not implied by the sense [of the word], since the act of eating is accomplished even without it—so says Śabara. No.
Because eating is meaningful only up until the point of digestion;
nor is there an absence of human effort during digestion,
since proper sitting and so forth are for the purpose of digestion.

The passage beginning with "mandrābhibhūtiḥ" and ending with "bhakṣayāmi" reveals the act of consumption. Therefore, setting aside the name (samākhyā) by means of the indicative mark (liṅga), the application (viniyoga) must be established. // MJaiNyC_3,2.21-22 //
(Regarding the tenth [section], the adhikaraṇa on the single-mantra nature of "mandrābhibhūtiḥ" and so forth, there is the sūtra:
"Because it denotes a quality, 'mandra' and so forth should constitute a single mantra, since those two are connected to a single purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.26)
The tenth section formulates the problem:
Should the two mantras, "mandrā" and "vasumadve," be divided between the act of satiating and the act of eating,
or should they both be used entirely in the eating that is conjoined with the act of satiation?
"Let there not be a division based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*); for there is no satisfaction from anything other than eating.
Since the indicative mark is impossible [in the case of the tongue], let everything [the mantra] belong to the act of eating, on the basis of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).

The portion beginning with "joyful and overcoming" (*mandrābhibhūtiḥ*) and ending with "may she, enjoying the Soma, be satisfied" (*juṣāṇā somasya tṛpyatu*) reveals the satisfaction of the tongue—which is joyful, which overcomes distaste, and which partakes of the Soma.
If it is argued that the portion beginning with "of the group of Vasumadgaṇa" and ending with "I eat" (bhakṣayāmi) is indicative of the act of eating,
and that its application is determined by dividing it according to its indicative power (liṅga) as in the previous case—
that is not so.

Indeed, satisfaction is not produced by any activity other than eating; rather, it is brought about by the act of eating itself. This being so, in what other activity could the portion that manifests satisfaction be employed?
Therefore, since application by means of *liṅga* (indicative power) is impossible, the portion of the *bhakṣaṇa*-sentence that reveals satisfaction (*tṛpti*) will serve as its supplement (*śeṣa*).
And this portion is indeed applicable there,
because it generates enthusiasm in the person by revealing the act of eating accompanied by satisfaction.
Therefore, the entire [mantra] beginning with "mandra" is employed for the act of consuming.
(Regarding the eleventh [section], the section on the application of mantras beginning with "indrapītasya," Sūtras 27–28:

JaiMi 3.2.27: Because of the specification of a particular indicative mark (*liṅga*), those offerings not dedicated to Indra (*anaindra*) are without mantras, even when the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) is the same.
JaiMi 3.2.28: Or rather, they should have mantras according to their respective deities; for it shows that they have that [Indra] as their archetype (*prakṛti*).
Starting with *Mīmāṃsājātinī* 3.2.25–27,
the eleventh section (*adhikaraṇa*) formulates the following problem:
Is the portion of the consumption mantra (*makṣamantra*), "of that drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*), intended here for the Soma belonging to Indra?
"Only in another case, because it is expressed by conventional usage; everywhere else, it is according to the literal sense."
Because of its capacity, the consumption by others is indeed [performed] silently like that of Indra;
or rather, there is modification (ūha) regarding the others, because although the ritual action is one, there is modification due to the difference in the portions consumed.
Because the Soma is drunk by Indra at this libation (savana),
the mantra should be recited without modification for all those present at the libation.
[MJaiNy 3.2.27] — In the *bhakṣa-mantra*, a certain portion is heard in the form "of that which has been drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*).
In this context, the meaning is: "I consume the remnant of the Soma purified by Indra.

This being so, since this mantra is capable of functioning only for the consumption of the remnant of the offering made to Indra, it is employed only there, and not for the consumption of the remnants of the offerings made to Mitra-Varuṇa and others.
Therefore, one prima facie view is that its consumption must be performed without a mantra;
for even if the phrase "drunk by Indra" lacks the necessary capacity [for modification], there will be capacity once the modification has been made into "drunk by Mitra and Varuṇa."

If it is argued: "Since the Āgneya sacrifice is the archetype (prakṛti), the mantra belonging to it—namely 'agnaye juṣṭam'—is modified in the ectype (vikṛti), the Saurya oblation, into 'sūryāya juṣṭam'; however, in this case, because the ritual action is one and the same, there is no modification," we say: No.
Since it is possible to perform an *ūha* (modification) even when there is a difference in the substance consumed, as in the case of a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*),
this is the second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). In the phrase "of that drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is to be understood.
For if it were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of its final syllable being udātta by the rule *asamāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.123);
however, this word is traditionally recited as having its initial syllable udātta.
However, a word denoting Indra (*indrapratipādika*) is inherently acute-accented on its first syllable.

This being the case, by the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam* (Pāṇini 6.2.1), which prescribes that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound the preceding member retains its original accent, the entire compound likewise becomes acute-accented on its first syllable. Since the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the soma-drinking in which [sacrificial session] was drunk by Indra," when it refers to the *savana* (pressing), the term *aindrabhakṣaṇa* [is formed].

Since it is impossible to restrict [the mantra] with the word "thus" (eva), the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that this mantra should be employed without modification (anūha) in all instances of eating.

(Section 12: On the Consumption of the Re-offered Soma; Sūtras 29–31) In the case of those [cups] that have been re-offered, there is a designation for all [the priests], because they possess two distinct portions. Jaimini 3.2.29.
Or rather, because of the removal [of the previous portion], there is no designation for the former [priest]. Jaimini 3.2.30.
"Or, because of the mention [of the number], there would be a removal [of the original].
Jaimini 3.2.31. He formulates the twelfth section as follows:
In the case of modification (ūha), that which is to be modified is considered within the fivefold logic:
when Indra has been offered, and then the remnant of that [offering] remains in the cups held by the Hotrakas.
When the Soma has been drawn out and offered to the gods, it is then consumed;
at that time, Indra is neither to be characterized nor not to be characterized, because there remains no purpose for another [deity].
It is indeed brought forward and connected, but it was not previously connected with other deities;
therefore, for the sake of establishing Indra, this [mantra] must be characterized along with the others. [Commentary:
Regarding the second prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) in the form of a modification (ūha) presented in the preceding section—
In connection with that, the subject matter is considered through five logical arguments (*nyāya*) by way of a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*).
The Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, and others are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), known as the *hotrakas*.
And they possess sacrificial cups (*camasa*).
The *camasa* cups are vessels containing the essence of Soma.
With these, one must offer oblations during both the *vaṣaṭ* and the *anuvaṣaṭ* calls.
Since the *camasa*s belong to Indra, Indra is the first to be offered to upon the *hotṛ*'s *vaṣaṭ* call.
Immediately thereafter, having again poured out another portion of Soma into the goblet containing the remnants of the previous offering, the Hotrakas offer it to other deities at the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
Therein, the Maitrāvaruṇa sacrifices to Mitra and Varuṇa with the mantra, "We invoke Mitra...
The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin sacrifices to Indra with the mantra, "O Indra, we [invoke] you, the bull..."
One worships the Maruts with the mantra, "potā 'maruto yasya hi kṣaye.
Having offered thus, Soma is subsequently consumed.
In that consumption, the mantra "mitrāvaruṇapītasya" is to be modified accordingly.
At that time, in the formula "of that which has been drunk by Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa," Indra should not be mentioned together with Mitra and Varuṇa.
Why?
Because when the remnant of Indra is again poured out and intended for Mitra, Varuṇa, and others along with him, that remnant lacks any connection with Indra.
If it is argued that only the subsequently drawn [cup] has a different purpose, while the previous one does not, we say no;
because at the time of drawing, there is no intention [on the part of the priest] that "this [cup] is for the sake of Mitra and Varuṇa, etc."
At the time of offering, however, it is offered together with the remnants of the previous [offering] to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others.
Therefore, since there is an absence of connection with Indra, Indra need not be indicated by secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)—this being the prima facie view, we reply:
let there be no such formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Nevertheless, the act of drawing out [the soma] is intended solely for the sake of the sacrifices to Mitra-Varuṇa and the others;
it is not possible for that [soma] to have the status of being a remnant from the previously performed sacrifice to Indra.

Therefore, since the drawn-out portion is a remnant connected to Mitra-Varuṇa and the others, yet remains connected to Indra as well, when drinking both portions, Indra must also be invoked (upalakṣaṇīya) along with Mitra-Varuṇa and the rest.
(Thirteenth Section: On the Non-indication of Indra and Others in the Consumption of the Pātnīvata Cup;
Sūtras 32–33) But in the case of the Pātnīvata [cup], it is as before. (Jaimini 3.2.32) Or rather, because of its being taken up, it should be excluded. (Jaimini 3.2.33)
In the thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa), [the author] formulates [the following]:
"The remnant of the two deities [belongs] to the vessel of the Ādityas, which is designated as the Āgrayaṇa."
Then, when the drawing of the Pātnīvata cup has taken place, [the remnant] reaches the vessel.
Regarding the consumption of that [remnant], are the deities of the two [cakes] to be indicated along with the Pātnīvata deity?
Or not? According to the previous principle, let there be an indication.
The Pātnīvata cup does not exist apart from the Āgrayaṇa;
there is no expectation regarding the previous deities, for it is the one accompanied by the wives (patnīvān) alone that is indicated.
The cups dedicated to two deities, such as those for Indra and Vāyu, [are distinct].
Of those, the remainder goes to the Āditya vessel; from that vessel again, it goes to the Āgrayaṇa vessel. From that Āgrayaṇa vessel, the Pātnīvata draught is drawn.

In the consumption of that *pātnīvata* cup, Indra-Vāyu and the others are to be mentioned as secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇīya*). This being the position reached—just as in the preceding section Indra was mentioned together with Mitra-Varuṇa and the rest—it is argued: [The siddhāntin replies: No, because it is a different deity. In the case of the *pātnīvata*, the mention of Indra-Vāyu and the others is not required. Why? Because it is a different deity. Just as in the case of the *vaiśvadeva* offering, where the mention of Viśve-devas is not required for the *pātnīvata* because it is a distinct deity, so too here. Furthermore, the mention of Indra-Vāyu and the others would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), since they are not connected with the act of giving. Therefore, only Agni Patnīvat is to be mentioned. Thus it is concluded.
We reply: Since the text states, "He draws the Pātnīvata cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel with the Upāṃśu vessel," the Āgrayaṇa vessel is heard to be the source (apādāna).
Thus, when the Soma juice has issued forth from it and its connection to that vessel has ceased, the drawing for the deity Patnīvat occurs subsequently.
This being the case, there is no requirement for the entirely distinct Pātnīvata portion to relate to the previous deities.

Furthermore, when the Soma is brought back and mixed with the remnant of Indra’s portion, the connection of Indra does not depart from that mixture, just as it does not depart for the Maitrāvaruṇa and others; thus there is a disparity [between the two cases]. Therefore, in the consumption of the Pātnīvata cup, Indra, Vāyu, and the others are not to be mentioned as indicators (upalakṣaṇīya).
(Regarding the fourteenth section on the non-noticing of Tvaṣṭṛ during the consumption of the remnants of the Pātnīvata offering, Sūtras 34–35:
"One should notice Tvaṣṭṛ," [says the opponent].
"But it should not be so, because of inequality" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.34–35).
In the fourteenth section (adhikaraṇa) of the third chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra (3.2.34–35), [the author] formulates the following:
Is Tvaṣṭṛ indicated by that cup together with Patnīvat, or not?
Because of the statement "drink together with Tvaṣṭṛ," he too is indicated by virtue of his divinity.

Tvaṣṭṛ’s presence would consist merely in association, not in being a drinker, because there is no word for it and because there is no injunction [for him]. Therefore, as a deity, he is not indicated [in the mantra].
In that very *pātnīvata* cup, Tvaṣṭṛ should also be indicated along with Pātnīvata in the mantra for consuming the remnant.
Why?
Because Tvaṣṭṛ also has that as his deity;
and this is understood from the oblation-mantra.

In this mantra, "O Agni, accompanied by the wives (patnīvat), in harmony with the god Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma, Svāhā!", one addresses Agni as "accompanied by the wives" using a protracted vowel at the end;
since it states "drink together with the god Tvaṣṭṛ," Tvaṣṭṛ possesses the status of a deity in that [rite] just like Patnīvat, by virtue of being a drinker.
Then, having reached the position that the phrase "of that drunk by Patnīvat Tvaṣṭṛ" (*patnīvattvaṣṭṛpītasya*) is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*),
we reply: at the time of drinking, only the co-presence of Tvaṣṭṛ is understood by the word *sajūḥ*, but not his status as a drinker.

For the unenlightened Tvaṣṭṛ, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "drink. Nor does one possess the status of a drinker merely by being in the company of a drinker— as in the expression, "The she-ass carries the load together with her ten sons."
In this case, since the sons are not seen to be the ones who carry out [the rite],
let the mantra be set aside; but if it is argued that Tvaṣṭṛ’s status as the deity follows from the force of the injunction, we say no.
In the case of the injunction, "He takes the Pātnīvata from the Āgrayaṇa," Tvaṣṭṛ is not perceived;
therefore, because he is not a deity [in that context], Tvaṣṭṛ is not to be indicated as a secondary qualifier.
(Regarding the fifteenth section on the non-indication of the thirty [deities] in the consumption of the remains of the *pātnīvata* offering, the sūtra states:
"And the thirty [are not indicated], because they exist for the sake of another. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.36)
He formulates the fifteenth section:

"The thirty-three gods accompanied by their wives—'gladden them,' [it is said]. Are these indicated or not? Because of the explicit mention in the *yājyā*, they are indicated as deities. (MJaiNy_3.2.36)
"One fire has been gratified by the sacrificer, while the others have been gratified by the [offering] fire;

therefore, since Agni alone possesses the status of a deity, there is no indicative mark for the others."—In the *yājyā* verse of that very *pātnīvata* cup, having addressed Agni, [the text says]: "O Agni, gratify the thirty-three gods who bear the name *pātnīvata*."

Thus it is stated: "O Patnīvān, bring the thirty-three gods according to their respective shares (anuṣvadham) and cause them to rejoice. *Anuṣvadham* means according to their respective portions. Here, because they are to be made to rejoice by the Soma juice being offered, those thirty-three possess the status of deities.
If it is argued that you too must be understood as the objects of consumption [by Agni], we say no;

for only Agni, who is to be exhilarated by the sacrificer, possesses the status of deity here. As for the thirty-three gods, they are exhilarated by means of Agni; therefore, they do not have the status of deity in this context.
Therefore, it is not an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
(Regarding the sixteenth section on the non-noticing of the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* at the time of consumption, the sūtra states:
"And the *vaṣaṭkāra* is as before. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.37) START MJaiNy 3,2.38-39
The sixteenth section formulates the following:

Is the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*—declared in the formula "of Soma, of Agni"—to be indicated [as the recipient], or not? It should be indicated because it is a deity; however, it is distinct from the thirty [deities mentioned previously]. (MJaiNy 3.2.38)

The fire existing in the archetype (prakṛti) is characterized by its not being the object of a specific injunction; Indra, however, is characterized as the object of an injunction. Therefore, the same applies in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti). [Thus:
"O Agni, accept the Soma."
Thus it is heard in the scripture: "He performs the after-offering. In that context, the deity for the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is Agni, as established by the wording of the mantra.
And it is not the case that Agni lacks the status of a deity, as might be argued for the thirty-three [gods].
If it is argued that fire (*agni*) is to be indicated because the mantra addresses fire by designating it as the drinker of Soma, we say no;
for it has not been indicated in the context.
The *aindraśvamasa* is the archetype;
the others are of the nature of modifications (*vikṛti*).
For it is thus: the Soma for Indra is both drawn and measured.
Therefore, Soma exists only in those offerings dedicated to Indra;
in those not dedicated to Indra, there is no Soma at all. Thus, all the ritual properties of Soma apply only to the Indra-offerings; those not dedicated to Indra are devoid of such properties.

The desire for the *dharmatā* (the nature of the ritual) by the *codaka* (the extended injunction) indicates that they possess the same properties; thus, there is a state of being a modification (*vikṛti*).

The fact that the *soma* being taken up and measured belongs to Indra is understood from the taking-up mantra, "For Indra accompanied by the Vasus, thee," and so forth. In the consumption of that *indra-camasa*, which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*), the deity Agni of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is not indicated.
Why?
Because there is no reference to him in the act of grasping;
Indra, however, is indicated because he is the object of reference.
Thus, even in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), it is logical that the deities who are the objects of the injunction alone should be indicated.
Therefore, Agni is not to be indicated.

(Seventeenth [topic]: Concerning the consumption without mantras by those not belonging to Indra, in the form of a *kṛtvācintā*; Sūtra: "But there is a prohibition of the meters because they apply to all. (Jaimini 3.2.38)

Starting with *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya* 3.2.40–41, [the author] formulates the seventeenth section (*adhikaraṇa*), setting aside the position that there are no mantras, and proceeding with three further hypothetical investigations (*kṛtvācintā*).
Is there modification (ūha) or not? It exists here, because it is possible in this modified form.

Because the injunction "with the Soma-cup" is common to all offerings, there is no modification (ūha) even in the case of no change; therefore, there is no consumption of the cup dedicated to Indra without the mantra.

Setting aside the first prima facie view—that "in the case of [soma] not belonging to Indra, the consumption is without a mantra"—which was formulated in the preceding section following the aforementioned *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical) considerations, three further *kṛtvācintā*s are now stated: If it be argued that there is no modification (*ūha*) because, as in the previously mentioned manner, modification is impossible since those [offerings] not belonging to Indra do not constitute a *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice), we say:
No; for it is impossible for those not belonging to Indra to be *vikṛtis*.
Soma, as mentioned in the originative injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," is a constituent of the ritual action itself, and not a constituent of any particular offering.
That very same Soma is repeated in all the offerings; thus, all [the offerings] are equally primary.

Therefore, since there can be no relationship of archetype (prakṛti) and modification (vikṛti) between those offerings dedicated to Indra and those not dedicated to Indra, there is no *ūha* (modification of the mantra) here.
Let the mantra beginning with "For Indra, thee, accompanied by the Vasus" be understood as referring to Indra on account of its indicative mark (*liṅga*);
however, this much does not establish a relationship of archetype and modification.

Therefore, because the mantra mentioned has Indra as its subject matter by virtue of its indicative mark (*liṅga*), the consumption [of the soma] in rites not dedicated to Indra is to be performed without that mantra.
(Regarding the eighteenth [topic], the section concerning the mantra-less nature of the consumption of the *aindrāgna* [offering], Sūtras 39–40:
"But in the case of the *aindrāgna*, [the mantra] should apply because of the presence of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Or rather, it applies to one [deity] alone, as in the case of the division from another deity. (Jaimini 3.2.39–40)
Starting with *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtravṛtti* 3.2.42–43,
the eighteenth section (*adhikaraṇa*) is formulated as follows:
Should the consumption of the [soma] dedicated to Indra-Agni and others be accompanied by mantras or without mantras?
In the offering to Indra-Agni, because it is possible for [the Soma] to have been drunk by one other than Indra, that [offering] is accompanied by its respective mantra.
Drinking is not appropriate for that which is bodiless; however, giving is applicable to what is mixed.
But this mantra is not fit for what is mixed; therefore, this [act] is without a mantra.
Regarding this consumption of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣaṇa*) prescribed by the injunction, "One takes the cup for Indra and Agni" (*aindrāgnaṃ gṛhṇāti*):

If it is argued that the consumption [of Soma] must be accompanied by the mantra because of the application [of the text] through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) itself— namely, "the Soma drunk by Indra and Agni is also drunk by Indra"—
it is not so; for,
according to the principle of the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) to be stated in the ninth chapter, it is impossible for the bodiless Indra to drink.
If, on the other hand, the word *pati* were intended to signify "giving," then the meaning of the mantra would be "the Soma has been given to Indra.
Yet, in this case, the sacrificer did not give it directed toward Indra.
However, since [the offering] is intended for Indra and Agni,
the gift (dāna) concerns a mixed object,
whereas the mantra does not concern a mixed object; therefore, the consumption is to be performed without a mantra.

(Regarding the section on the application of mantras beginning with "In the nineteenth [chapter], 'of the agāyatracchandas,'" Sūtras 41–43: And the metre is like the deity. Jaimini 3.2.41. Or rather, it applies to all, because of the absence of any single metre. Jaimini 3.2.42.
According to Aitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all [the priests], because [the Adhvaryu] is purified by his devotion; for he indeed possesses the authority over the *savana*s.
[The author] formulates the nineteenth section: Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.43–46.
Even in the case of a gift to Indra, whether it is joined with the Gāyatrī meter alone or joined with other meters as well,
the first [meter] would prevail in the mantra, because it is so stated.

A Bahuvrīhi compound is equal [in application] to two [words], but never to a single word; however, for a plurality of words, it is only the Aindra [method]. This deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*) has been stated.
The statement "the mention of Indra’s drinking is for the purpose of the *savana*" is called the "unveiling" (*udghaṭana*);
by this, the recitation of the mantra remains as it stands in all offerings (*pradāna*).
In that very same *bhakṣa-mantra*, it is heard: "of that which has been drunk by Indra and possesses the *gāyatrī* metre."

If it is argued that, because the mantra phrase "that which has the *gāyatra* meter alone" expresses a compound, the consumption mantra applies only to the Soma for Indra when it is joined with a single meter—
this is not so;
for the same logic applies even when it is joined with many meters, as the *bahuvrīhi* compound remains identical.
By discarding the particle *eva*, the analysis "that which has the Gāyatrī metre" becomes possible;
however, there is no Soma sacrifice anywhere that consists of a single metre alone.
Therefore, in a Soma sacrifice consisting of various metres, this mantra applies only to the offering to Indra, and not elsewhere.
Thus, having done so, the three types of "inconceivability" (kṛtvācintā) are completed;
however, the disclosure of the two-fold inconceivability was already demonstrated by the proponent (siddhāntin) previously.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the third quarter of the third chapter. (First section: The determination that loudness and other such qualities are properties of the Veda; Sūtras 1–8).
The entitlement [to perform the rite] would belong to one born [of such parents], because of the Vedic revelation (Jaimini 3.3.1);
or rather, it belongs to the Veda itself, because of the observation of the general rule (Jaimini 3.3.2);
and also because of the indicative mark (liṅga) (Jaimini 3.3.3).

And because of the instruction on the dharma, there is indeed no connection with the physical substance [of the Veda] (Jaimini 3.3.4). And it is called the "knowledge of the three Vedas" because one who knows that [dharma] is so designated (Jaimini 3.3.5).
If it is argued that [the order of recitation] follows the sequence of individual instances according to the literal text (Jaimini 3.3.6).
Because it applies to everything;
[Jaimini 3.3.7] because of its connection with the Veda, it is not set aside by the context; [Jaimini 3.3.8] START MJaiNy 3.3.1-3.
In the first section of the third chapter, he formulates the following problem:
"Should the Sāman chants be recited loudly and the Yajus formulas silently?
These rules pertain either to the mantras or to the Vedas, since the properties reside in the mantras. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā 3.3.1)
In the injunctions, the words "Ṛk" and so forth are stated to denote the mantras;
furthermore, there is the Vedic statement at the beginning [of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā], "The Ṛgveda was produced from Agni. (MJaiNy 3.3.2)

Because no contradiction has yet arisen, and because [the general rule] is withdrawn by virtue of that [specific rule], when there is a leading [of the specific rule] by means of the sentence, the properties [of loudness, etc. pertain to the Veda.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "The Ṛgveda is recited loudly."
"Inaudibly with the *yajus*, loudly with the *sāman*. In that injunction,
because the words *ṛk* and so forth— which denote mantras— are employed, the properties of the mantras, such as loudness and so on, [are thereby established].
If it be argued that, such being the case, even those Ṛg-verses produced in the Yajurveda and employed by the Adhvaryu priest must be recited loudly—
this is not so; for,
following the stronger initial statement (upakrama) since no contradiction has yet arisen, the concluding portion (upasaṃhāra) must be interpreted in accordance with it.
For at the beginning, the word "Veda" is heard: "The three Vedas were created: from Agni the Ṛgveda, from Vāyu the Yajurveda..."
"From the Āditya [comes] the Sāmaveda.

Therefore, in accordance with the Vedas mentioned in the introductory portion (upakrama), since the words "Ṛk" and so forth occurring in the injunctive statement (vidhyuddeśa) must also refer to the Vedas, even the Ṛks produced from the Yajurveda are to be recited in a low voice (upāṃśu).
Now, it may be objected that the introductory portion is weak here because it is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda).

If it is argued that the concluding statement (upasaṃhāra) is more powerful because it pertains to the injunction (vidhyuddeśa), we say: certainly so; for the strength belongs to the injunction once its own nature has been established.
But here, first of all, there is an introductory operation that gives rise to the cognition;

at that time, because it has not yet attained its own nature, it possesses no subverting power. However, subsequently, for the sake of the unity of the sentence, it will attain its own nature precisely without contradicting that [cognition].
Thus, this application of the sentence is determined by the force of the unity of purpose between the opening and the conclusion.

(Regarding the second section on the low-voiced chanting (*upāṃśutā*) at the primary consecration, the sūtra states: "When there is a conflict between a subordinate and a principal [element], the connection with the Veda belongs to the principal, because [the subordinate] exists for its sake. (Jaimini 3.3.9)
The second section formulates the problem:

Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) situated in the Yajurveda, what is the case for the Sāman that is its subsidiary—is it to be chanted loudly (*uccaiḥ*) or in a low voice (*upāṃśu*)? It is to be chanted loudly, because it is understood more quickly [in that manner]. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 3.3.4)

In this case, the application [of the rule] arising from the originative injunction is more powerful, since the primary element must be followed by its subsidiary; therefore, the low-voiced recitation (upāṃśutva) applies to the singing.
In this case, either the establishment (*ādhāna*) is primary and the singing (*gāna*) is subordinate, or rather,
the application (*viniyoga*) is primary and the origin (*utpatti*) is subordinate here.
[In the *ādhāna*, the Vāmadevya and other Sāmans are prescribed as subordinate elements.]

In this regard, if it is argued: "Although these are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) belonging to the Yajurveda, nevertheless, because they originate in the Sāmaveda, and because origination is the cause for immediate cognition, they should be sung according to the rules of the Sāmaveda"—we say: no.
This is because the application (*viniyoga*) is more powerful;
and that application is heard in the Yajurveda: "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya [Sāman].
For it is logical that the primary element should follow the subordinate one.
If it is asked, "What is the quality (guṇa), and what is the primary element (mukhya)?"—
in this case, because it is the principal factor (aṅgin), the laying of the fires (ādhāna) is the primary element, while the singing of the Sāman is the quality as a subordinate factor (aṅga).

Just as the mantras forming part of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), such as "Dharma is the head," are recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), so too the Sāmans should be sung in a low voice in accordance with that consecration.
Alternatively, the application (*viniyoga*) is primary because it is the injunction that prompts the performance.
Because the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is not of that nature, it is a subordinate element (*guṇa*).
Therefore, in this case, the [hymns] are to be sung in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), in accordance with the Veda that effects their application (*viniyoga*).

(Regarding the third section on the Yajurvedic character of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the sūtra states: "By virtue of the greater number [of characteristics], there is the scriptural authority for both. Jaimini 3.3.10.
The third section formulates the problem:

The Jyotiṣṭoma exists in both the Yajurveda and the Sāmaveda; in that case, should it be performed with loudness or with low voice? There is no determination because of the absence of a specific cause.
When the substance and the deity are already established by the Yajurveda, the injunction for that [sacrifice] resides there;
because the determination of the accent depends on that, the performance should be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
The sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" is recited in both Vedas.

If it is argued: "In that case, since there is no discerning cause to determine which is an injunction (*vidhi*) and which is a restatement for the purpose of prescribing a quality (*guṇavidhānānuvāda*), there would be no definitive conclusion that 'the dharma of this Veda is to be performed'"; [we reply: No.

Since the substance *soma* and the deities such as Indra and Vāyu are understood from the *Yajurveda*, and because many auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are heard [prescribed] therein, the injunction belongs to that [Veda] alone; thus, there is the practice of whispering (*upāṃśu*).
(Regarding the eleventh sūtra in the section on the applicative power of context within the fourth chapter:
"That which is not connected [by direct statement or other means] is [applied] by virtue of context, because there is a requirement for the manner of performance. Jaimini 3.3.11.
He formulates the fourth section:

"The *prayāja* and other such rites are not subsidiaries of the sacrifice, nor is there subsidiariness [of the sacrifice to them]; because the *prakaraṇa* (context) is not authoritative, or because the two sentences are already satisfied by their own requirements. (MJaiNy_3.3.9)
The prayāja and other such rites have a requirement for a result, and the sacrifice has a requirement for the manner of performance (kathaṃbhāva).

Therefore, their mention in the context (prakaraṇa) establishes the relationship of principal and subordinate between them. [Note: Those means of application—namely, direct assertion (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and syntactical connection (vākya)—which were stated in the preceding two and a half quarters [of the commentary] as the factors that effect application, [are now discussed].

We do not observe any means of knowledge called "context" (*prakaraṇa*) that is distinct from those [other means]. Indeed, no portion of the Veda is ever handed down that is not already encompassed by words, their capacities, and their syntactic relations.
If it is argued that "context" is a collection of sentences that has attained the status of a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatā*), we say no.
Because there is no state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) after the two sentences have already existed;
for indeed, there is no mutual expectancy between these two sentences— "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "He sacrifices to the Samidhs"—
by which a unity of sentence could be postulated.

Therefore, when it is argued that the *prayāja* offerings and so forth do not constitute subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), we reply: the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are causes for a result,
because they consist of human activity, like service and the like.
The New- and Full-Moon sacrifices are assisted by the accessories, because they are instruments, like the eye assisted by a lamp.

That being the case, when there arises the expectancy—"What is the fruit of the *prayāja* and other such rites, or rather, what is their service to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices?"—there occurs *prakaraṇa*, which consists in the formation of a single syntactical unit with the completed sentences.
And by means of that, the status of the *prayāja* and others as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) is understood. (MJaiNyC 3.1.9–10)
(Regarding the fifth section [adhikaraṇa] on the application of *krama* [order], there is the following sūtra:
"And *krama* [is a means of application] because of the commonality of location. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.12)
The fifth section formulates the following:
Is the mantra "dabdhir nāma" an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice or not?
It is not an auxiliary, because it is common [to other rites] and there is a lack of evidence from indicative marks (*liṅga*) or other means of proof. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-naya 3.3.11)
In this context, the sequential recitation of mantras and ritual acts is observed;
since sequence is an authoritative means [of determining subsidiarity] like syntactic structure (prakriyā), subsidiarity follows from their respective order.

The sequence [of application] arises from being in the same location, from the order of recitation, and from the meaning; from recitation, it is "according to number" (yathāsaṃkhyam), and from proximity, it is "according to number," as has been illustrated.
The mantra "śundhadhvam" (be purified) is considered to be an auxiliary to the *sāṃnāyya* vessels because of their proximity (*saṃnidhi*).
However, the ritual properties (*dharma*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice would belong to the *agnīṣomīya* animal due to the proximity of purpose (*arthasādeśya*).
In the *Yājamāna* section of the *Mantrakāṇḍa* for the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, a certain mantra is recited: "Thou art unerring; may I become unerring."
"I shall strike this one"—
neither a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) nor a syntactical connection (*vākya*) exists regarding this mantra's status as an auxiliary to the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice;
for in the *Brāhmaṇa*, no application (*viniyoga*) is recorded, but rather only an explanation of its meaning.
"By this very weapon (dabdhi), the gods indeed overcame the Asuras;
by that same [weapon] he overcomes his rival," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
*Dabdhi* is a weapon made of metal.
Since the capacity to ward off the undesirable (*aniṣṭanivārakatva*) is present in both the *āgneya* and *agnīṣomīya* offerings as well, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is common to all three;
furthermore, the context (*prakaraṇa*) for these three is one and the same.
Therefore, in the absence of any specific evidence to the contrary, this mantra is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *upāṃśuyāja*—this being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

We reply: In the *Ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa*, the rites for Agni, the Upāṃśuyāja, and Agnīṣomīya are prescribed in their respective order; and in the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa*, the mantras pertaining to them are likewise prescribed in that same order: "By the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food," and "Thou art a piercer; may I be unpierced; may I pierce so-and-so."
"By this sacrifice to Agni and Soma, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra.

In that case, just as *prakaraṇa* (context), which is constituted by the connection of two sentences, is a separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), why should *krama* (order), which is constituted by the connection of two *prakaraṇas*, not likewise be a valid means of knowledge?
Nor does it fall within the context (*prakaraṇa*) [of the Upāṃśuyāja],
because two contexts cannot form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), just as two sentences cannot.
Therefore, by the authority of sequence (*krama-pramāṇa*), the mantra situated in the middle is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Upāṃśuyāja situated in the middle.
"Succession is the state of occupying the same location"—this is the essential nature of succession.
And that is of two kinds: produced by recitation (*pāṭhakṛta*) and produced by meaning (*arthakṛta*).
Among these, that produced by recitation is also of two kinds: according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*).
Of these two, an example of the indicative power (*dabdhimantra*) of the first is as follows:
the mantra “*śundhadhvaṃ daivyāya karmaṇe*” (Be purified for the divine rite) appears to be common to all things that require purification.

In this context, since the vessels for the *sāṃnāyya* offering—such as the *kumbhī*, the branch, and the *pavitra*—appear in the immediately following mantras beginning with “*mātariśvanaḥ*,” the word “*śundhadhvam*” [is understood] through proximity (*saṃnidhi*) to refer to the sprinkling of those specific vessels.
Thus the mantra is applied.
Due to the proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*), the characteristics of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) constitute a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
In this way, the threefold nature of order (*krama*) is to be understood.
(Regarding the sixth section on the application of name as a means of injunction, the sūtra states:
"And name is likewise [an authority], because it has that as its purpose. Jaimini 3.3.13.
The sixth section formulates [the following]:

There is a conjunction of the three priests with the duties prescribed in the three Vedas, whether by way of non-restriction or restriction; it is a restriction, because there is no other determination. (MJaiNy 3.3.15)
The designation (*samākhyāna*) such as "hautra" (pertaining to the *hotṛ* priest) is itself an indicator of restriction;
it is uncontradicted like other [designations], and therefore it is the factor that effects application (*viniyojaka*) in this case.
Dharmas such as the recitation of the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses are prescribed in the *Ṛgveda*.

If it is argued that the milking, the cooling, and so forth belong to the Yajurveda, while the Ājya-stotra, the Pṛṣṭha-stotra, and so forth belong to the Sāmaveda, and that because no restrictive rule can be established stating "these are the duties of this [specific Veda] alone," any duty may be performed by any officiating priest (ṛtvij) according to their own will— [The response follows: ... [as per the source text].
Not so;
by the designations "pertaining to the Hotṛ," "pertaining to the Adhvaryu," and "pertaining to the Udgātṛ," a restriction is understood.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any sublater of the designation (*samākhyāna*).

Therefore, since the two causes of invalidity—namely, non-comprehensiveness and being sublated—are absent, the ritual duties (*dharma*) are established by means of the designation, which possesses authority just like the pentad beginning with direct statement (*śruti*), such as indicative mark (*liṅga*).
(MJaiNyC 3.1.15–16, in the section on the relative strength of each preceding among direct statement and the others [Sūtras 7–12])

In the case of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose. Jaimini 3.3.14. [The seventh [section] concerns the superiority of direct statement.]
The author formulates the discussion:
"By the *aindrī* [verse], let Agni be worshipped"— is there an option between Indra and Agni,
or a combination, or is Indra alone identical with Agni?
There is an option based on direct statement and indicative mark; there is a combination through the figurative repetition of a quality.
Direct statement follows the capacity [of the word]; here, by virtue of the indicative mark, Indra alone [is intended].
Direct assertion (*śruti*) is said to be more powerful; indicative mark (*liṅga*) is that which leads to inference through its expressive power.

When there is a cognition characterized by the absence of expectancy, the application rests solely upon direct assertion. In this regard, it is heard in scripture: "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī [verse]."
"O Indra, you are never a destroyer; you never fail the donor"—this is a Rigvedic verse addressed to Indra, because it reveals Indra therein:
"O Indra, you are never at any time a slayer."
Rather, the meaning is: "You are pleased with the sacrificer who has offered the oblation.
In that regard, from the *liṅga*—which consists in the capacity to manifest Indra—it is understood that the mantra is a means for an action directed toward Indra.
For if this mantra were not a means for an action in which Indra is the primary object, [it would lack such indicative power].
In that case, the manifestation of Indra by means of this mantra would be purposeless.
Therefore, the application by *liṅga* (indicative power) consists in producing the cognition: "Indra is the primary object with respect to the action performed by means of this mantra.

When there arises a desire to know the specific nature of "that action," the conclusion is reached regarding the action of *upasthāna* (standing near/worshiping) by means of the sentence consisting of two non-contradictory words: "He stands near [Indra] with the *aindrī* [mantra]."
That being the case, the meaning results in: "One should worship Indra with the Aindra mantra.
Likewise, by the direct scriptural statement (śruti) consisting of the word "gārhapatyam" ending in the accusative case, the primacy of the Gārhapatya fire is understood;
and that [primacy] is not possible without some action in which it serves as a subordinate factor (guṇabhūta) and something is performed as the instrument (karaṇa).
Therefore, the application by direct scriptural statement (*śrutiviniyoga*) consists in producing the cognition that "certain [subsidiaries] are primary with respect to such-and-such an action.
Through the two words "with the *aindrī* [verse], he worships," there comes about the determination of a specific mantra and a specific action.
This being so, the meaning becomes: "He worships the *gārhapatya* fire with the *aindra* mantra."

Thus, when there is a conflict between direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga), since both possess equal authority, there is an option (vikalpa) between them— like the case of rice (vrīhi) and barley (yava)— this is the first prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). Alternatively, since Indra and the Gārhapatya fire are equally primary and the act of worship (upasthāna) is subordinate, according to the principle that "the subordinate is repeated for each primary," there is a combination (samuccaya) of the direct statement and the indicative mark through the repetition of the worship— this is the second prima facie view.
The scriptural injunction (*śruti*), while enjoining, enjoins only by conforming to the inherent capacity of the thing (*vastusāmarthya*).
Otherwise, one might as well enjoin that "one should sprinkle with fire" or "one should burn with water.

Therefore, because the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger due to its being the basis upon which the injunction depends, Indra alone is to be invoked by the mantra—this is the third prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It has already been demonstrated in the example of "niveśanaḥ" that, although the *aindra* mantra lacks the primary capacity (*mukhyavṛtti*) with respect to the *gārhapatya* fire, it does possess the capacity through secondary function (*gauṇavṛtti*).
This being the case, since there is no obstruction caused by a lack of capacity, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) enjoins [the mantra] swiftly and without hindrance,
whereas the indicative power (*liṅga*) is delayed.
At the outset, the words of the mantra convey their own respective meanings;
thereafter, the capacity of the mantra is determined;
subsequently, by virtue of that capacity, the verbal testimony (śruti) expressive of its status as a means (sādhana) and its status as the primary element is inferred.

And that direct Vedic statement (śruti) enjoins [the mantra] with the words, "One should worship Indra with the mantra. This being so, since the two operations of determining the capacity (sāmarthya) and postulating a further scriptural injunction— which intervene between the direct expression of its own meaning and the injunction— do not exist when there is a direct Vedic statement, the indicative power (liṅga) is sublated by it due to its superior strength.
Nor should it be suspected that "how could the indicative power (*liṅga*) be sublated when it has not yet attained its own nature at the time of the application by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)?
For here, sublation consists precisely in the prevention of its future attainment.
Since a mantra already applied by a direct statement has no further expectation for application, how could the indicative power ever attain [the status of] an applicator?
Therefore, the mantra is enjoined for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire by direct scriptural statement (pratyakṣaśruti).
START MJaiNy 3.3.20-22: The section concerning the eighth [point] (the superiority of *liṅga* over the beginning of a sentence) is formulated as follows:
The phrase "syonaṃ te" constitutes the first half, and "tasmin sīda" the second;
this [mantra] is established as being divided into two halves, each corresponding to the respective seat (sada) and the place of sitting (sādana).
If there were syntactic unity due to that word, the first [indication] would prevail over direct statement;
however, because indication is more closely connected, it establishes itself by subverting the sentence-meaning.
This is an illustration [of a case] where there is sublation by the [injunction of the] sentence, but not by the sense-perception [of the object];
because after the sublation, it would be purposeless, resulting in the consequence of invalidity.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; I fashion it well with a stream of ghee."
"Sit upon this nectar, O cloud of rice, and take firm root there with a well-disposed mind.
"O sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa),
I provide a fitting place for you."
And I shall prepare that place so that it is well-suited for being served with a stream of clarified butter. O essence of rice, sit down with a concentrated mind in that excellent place.
The meaning is: "Be firm therein.

In this context, by the word *tatra*—that is, by the pronoun *tasmim* (in that)—which refers to what has been previously mentioned, the preceding and following halves of the verse form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*). Consequently, since there would be no division into two separate mantras, this entire mantra would constitute an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for the act of establishing the [fire] in its place.
The Vedic injunction that assigns the mantra should be construed as follows: "By means of this entire mantra, the placement [of the vessel] is to be performed.
Likewise, it should also be construed as: "By means of the entire mantra, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is to be set down."

Since the status of the mantra as an auxiliary to the installation (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) is also indicated by that same scriptural statement—just as its status as an auxiliary to the seating (*sadana*) is—it follows that this mantra will be subject to either option (*vikalpa*) or combination (*samuccaya*) with the acts of seating and installation according to one's own preference. To this we reply: since this constitutes a single sentence formed by the mutual syntactic connection of the preceding and following halves, [it cannot be split].
Therefore, without assuming the capacity of the latter half of the verse to perform the act of preparing the seat, one cannot apply the entire mantra to that preparation;
likewise, without assuming the capacity of the former half to perform the act of placing [the oblation], it has no power in that regard.
Consequently, because it is separated by the mediation of the assumption of indicative power (*liṅga*), the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is more remote from direct assertion (*śruti*).
However, the two types of indicative marks (*liṅga*) are directly perceived.
This being the case, because the sentence is sublated by the indicative mark, the two meanings are established for both.
Now, [one might object]: "By means of the *aindrī* [verse], [one worships] the *gārhapatya* [fire]."

If it is argued: "In this case as well, since the sentence—consisting of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of two words—is perceived to be the factor that assigns application (*viniyojaka*), let that very example be cited to illustrate the conflict between indicative power (*liṅga*) and sentence (*vākya*)," we say: No. For in that case, once the sentence is sublated by indicative power, each individual word lacks the capacity to convey meaning; consequently, even the application established by direct assertion (*śruti*) would not be accomplished, and the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the cited example would follow. But here, even though the larger sentence (*mahāvākya*) is sublated, the meaning of the two subordinate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) is still perceived, and thus the application based on indicative power is established. Therefore, this alone is the appropriate example. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāya-mālā-vistara 3.1.20–22)

The section (adhikaraṇa) beginning with *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtra* 3.3.23–24— [which establishes that] the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*) and the other [criteria]— is formulated as follows:

From the statement, "May Agni and Soma enjoy this oblation," it follows that the phrase beginning with "this [oblation]" and so forth would either apply as a supplement to all [the deities] or not at all. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.3.23)

One might think that [the sentence] prevails over the context; let it not be so, for the sentence is separated from the context by three [intervening factors], whereas it is separated from the syntactical connection (vākya) by only two; therefore, it is stronger than the context.
In the *sūktavāka*, it is heard: "May Agni and Soma have enjoyed this oblation; may they have caused it to increase; may they have achieved great and further glory."
"May Indra and Agni enjoy this oblation; may they cause it to increase; they have accomplished a greater greatness."

In this regard, it was determined in the preceding section (Pūrva-pāda) that words denoting deities, such as "Agni-Soma" and the like, should be employed at the time of the Full Moon sacrifice and others by dividing them according to the respective deities.

As for the remaining collection of words, such as "this oblation" (*idaṃ haviḥ*) and so forth— even those occurring within the Agni-Soma mantra— they should be recited on the New Moon day after omitting the word "Agni-Soma."

In this way, even the mantra pertaining to Indra and Agni should be recited on the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) with the omission of the words "Indra and Agni. If that were so, the placement of these mantra portions within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—which indicates their status as subsidiaries to the entire sacrifice—would be respected. This being the position reached, we reply: because there is no scriptural hearing (*aśravaṇa*) of the connection of the words "Indra and Agni" with the remainder of the mantra dedicated to Agni-Soma.
By means of the context (*prakaraṇa*), in the first instance, a sentence (*vākya*) consisting of that syntactic connection must be inferred.
By that sentence, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the capacity to reveal Indra and the others is inferred.

And that indicative mark infers a third-person scriptural statement (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) which serves as the application (*viniyojikā*), stating: "By this portion of the mantra, an action directed toward Indra and Agni is to be performed."
Consequently, between *prakaraṇa* (context) and *viniyoga* (application), there is an intervention of three [means of proof].

However, the *vākya* (syntactical connection), which consists of the coordination of the words "Agni" and "Soma," being directly heard, is intervened upon by only *liṅga* (indicative power) and *śruti* (direct assertion).
Therefore, since *prakaraṇa* is sublated by *vākya*, its subsidiary element remains fixed in that very place.
Now, the section concerning the superior force of order (krama) over position (sthāna) within the tenth chapter is formulated as follows: [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.3.25–26].
In the Rājasūya sacrifice, regarding those elements such as the gambling (devana) and so forth that occur in the rite called the Abhiṣecanīya:
they are either subsidiary to that [specific rite] alone, or they are for the sake of the entire [Rājasūya], because they are in proximity to it.

Because the inquiry into the nature of the Rājasūya continues, it applies as a supplement to all [the constituent rites]. Since the requirement for the consecration (abhiṣecanīya) must be supplied, its context (prakriyā) is more powerful than that. In the Rājasūya, there are many principal elements consisting of animal sacrifices, iṣṭis, and Soma sacrifices.
In that context, there is a certain Soma sacrifice called the Abhiṣecanīya.
In proximity to it, gambling and other such activities are heard [in the scripture]: "He plays with dice;
he defeats a member of the royal caste."
"He causes the Śaunaḥśepa [story] to be recited.
It conquers, it wins.
The narrative concerning Śunaḥśepa, as handed down in the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*, is the Śaunaḥśepa.
If it is argued that, due to the force of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), gambling and the other acts are subsidiary parts of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice,
this is not so.

Since the expectancy regarding the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) of the *rājasūya* persists, gambling and the others, being enjoined while that expectancy remains, are subsidiary to the *rājasūya* by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Furthermore, since the Rājasūya consists of many sacrifices, it serves as the subsidiary context for all the sacrifices within it. Moreover, there is no expectancy on the part of the Abhiṣecanīya regarding the gambling and other such acts;
for its expectancy is satisfied by the archetypal (prakṛta) subsidiaries themselves, which are extended to it by virtue of its being a modification (vikṛti) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

If it is argued that expectancy is raised by the force of the proximate injunction (*saṃnihita-vidhi*), then for that very reason, the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*)—consisting of that expectancy—is first postulated; and through that medium, by the subsequent construction of syntactical connection (*vākya*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and direct statement (*śruti*), the proximity is rendered remote.
However, the great context (*mahā-prakaraṇa*) consisting of the expectancy of the Rājasūya, being already established, is brought into closer proximity by a single degree of strength.
Therefore, because the context (prakaraṇa) sets aside the proximity (saṃnidhi), the gambling and other acts are subsidiary to the entire sacrifice.
START MJaiNy 3.3.27-28: He formulates the section [dealing with] the superiority (of *krama* over *samākhyā*)— namely, that *ekādaśinī*— as follows:
The mantra "śundhadhvam" (be purified) is a subsidiary element used for the purification of the sacrificial cake vessels;
or rather, let it be used for the purification of the Sāṃnāyya vessels by virtue of its name.

In the case of the term *pauroḍāśikam*, whether by means of the verbal root or the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [the connection] is to be inferred due to the absence of explicit mention of proximity; and because it is already established, the latter [method] prevails according to the sequence.

The mantra "Be purified for the divine rite" (*śudhadhvaṃ daivyāya karmaṇe*), being recited in the section titled *pauroḍāśikam* as designated by the ritualists, [belongs] to the mortar, the *juhū*-ladle, and other implements mentioned in the *puroḍāśa* section by virtue of that designation (*samākhyā*).
If it is argued that [the term] "puroḍāśa" is a subordinate element (aṅga) in the act of purification,
it is not so;
for in the designation "pertaining to the puroḍāśa" (*pauroḍāśika*), the base word (*prakṛti*) denotes the *puroḍāśa* cake alone.
And the word "kāṇḍa" is a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita-pratyaya).
Moreover, by this much alone, the proximity of the mantra to all the vessels for the entire sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) does not become directly perceived;
rather, it is inferred through presumptive reasoning (arthāpatti).
If there were no proximity of what is connected [to it], then the section of the text that sets forth the mantras would not have the designation *pauroḍāśika* (pertaining to the cake-offering).
For indeed, mantras such as "iṣe tvā," which do not have fire (*agni*) in close proximity, do not receive the designation of the *Āgneya-kāṇḍa* (the section on Agni).

However, this designation applies to the mantras that are in close proximity, such as "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ" and so forth. Therefore, having postulated proximity by means of the designation of the *kāṇḍa*, and having— on the grounds that such proximity would otherwise be inexplicable— postulated the entire context (*prakaraṇa*) of the vessels in the form of mutual expectancy, and having thereby postulated the sentence (*vākya*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and the direct assertion (*śruti*), one acts through that *śruti*.
The designation (*viniyoga*) is more remote than the name (*samākhyā*).
However, the proximity of the mantra to the purification of the *sāṃnāyya* vessels is directly perceived.

Furthermore, the location for the *sāṃnāyya* vessels is stated to be the interval between the preparation of the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) and the pouring out of the handfuls of grain (*muṣṭinirvāpa*).
If the mantra is recited in an intermediate section between the two Anuvākas concerning the fuel (idhma) and the sacrificial grass (barhis) and the act of pouring out (nirvāpa),
then, by virtue of that direct proximity (pratyakṣasaṃnidhi), proximity (saṃnidhi) is brought closer than the four [other means of proof] beginning with context (prakaraṇa).
Therefore, setting aside both order (krama) and name (samākhyā), this final position— that "the mantra is a remnant for the purification of the Sāṃnāyya vessels"— must be accepted.
START MJaiNy 3.3.29-30:
He formulates the section concerning the twelve [factors] (the fitness for sublation):
Refutation is neither logical nor appropriate; it is not applicable to either what has been reached or what has not been reached.
For that which is unestablished yet clung to by the intellect—that indeed must be subject to refutation.

In this case, however, there is a sublation (bādha) of that which has been established by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to the tenth [book]; whereas here, because it is established through error, there is no sublation of what has not been attained.
Since that which has been attained exists as an active operation, its prevention is impossible.
If it is argued that for that which has not been apprehended, there can be no subsistence as an object of sublation,
and therefore sublation is not logical— do not say so.
For that which has not been made an object of the intellect can be prevented;
nor has this [wrong path] proceeded to its ultimate extent,
because it lacks a culmination in the form of the fruit of actual practice.
Nor is it absolutely non-arisen,
because the cognition of that [object] has arisen.
Therefore, neither of the two aforementioned faults applies.
In the tenth [book], it is "sublation of what has been reached" (*prāptabādha*), because an object understood through the authority of an injunction (*codaka*) is sublated.

Here, however, it is "sublation of what has not been reached" (*aprāptabādha*), because [the object] is understood through successive fallacious authorities (*pramāṇābhāsa*) that contradict each preceding authority.
In the thirteenth [section], concerning the point that the twelve-fold *upasads* constitute a subsidiary part of the *Ahīna* sacrifice (*Ahīnanyāya*), the two sūtras state:
JaiSū 3.3.15: "Or rather, the *Ahīna* is [merely] figurative because of the context.
JaiSū 3.3.16: "But because of the lack of connection with the primary [meaning], it should therefore be extracted [from the context]."
The thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"Indeed, there are only three [pressings] in the *sāhnāhīna* sacrifice; therefore, there are twelve in the *ahīna*."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the number twelve applies either to the [sacrifices] themselves or to the group of days.
Let it be that, according to the context, the first [alternative] is accepted; for there is no contradiction with the state of being non-deficient (*ahīnamatva*).
Since he is not deficient in anything due to his being the archetype (*prakṛti*), let him be considered here as such.
The term *ahīna* is conventionally established as distinct from *sāha*; this [distinction] occurs in the context of the *ahargaṇa* (multi-day sacrifice).
By virtue of the explicit mention (*śruti*) of "twelve," let the number twelve be withdrawn from the *prakriyā* (the Jyotiṣṭoma procedure).
In the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "There are three *upasads* for the *sāha*, and twelve for the *ahīna*."
Because it is to be accomplished in a single day, the Jyotiṣṭoma is "of a day" (sāhna).
The Upasad oblations are those to be performed after the day of initiation and before the day of the Soma-pressing.
Their number of twelve is established as belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa).
Furthermore, the term *ahīna* (non-deficient) applies to that very [Jyotiṣṭoma];

for since the Jyotiṣṭoma, as the archetype (*prakṛti*) of all Soma sacrifices, contains the instruction of all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), there is no deficiency in it even when compared to modified forms (*vikṛti*) that lack such instructions. Therefore, the conclusion reached is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the number twelve and the number three. This being the position:

We reply: A multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) consisting of two or three nights and so forth, which takes the form of repeated Soma sacrifices, is the term *ahīna* used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*). If it were derived etymologically (*yaugika*), however, by analyzing the compound as "not deficient" (*na hīnaḥ*), it would have an acute accent on the first syllable, like the word *ayajña*.
However, it is recorded in the Vedic tradition with the accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*).
Furthermore, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is a cause for immediate cognition because it is independent of etymological analysis (*vigraha*).
Therefore, this name *ahīna*, which is distinct from the word *sāhna* denoting the Jyotiṣṭoma, designates a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) that is distinct from the Jyotiṣṭoma.
In that group of days (*ahargaṇa*), the number twelve mentioned therein is to be applied by virtue of the direct scriptural statement (*ṣaṣṭhīśruti*).
For the sake of establishing that, this [number] must be removed from the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth.

(Fourteenth Section: On the Superiority of the Pratipad in the Kulāya and Other Sacrifices; Sūtras 17–19) Jaimini 3.3.17: Or rather, it is connected with duality and plurality because of the injunction regarding that [sacrifice].
Jaimini 3.3.18: If it is argued that this is due to the purpose served by the alternative [Pratipad].
"Not from the original [text], because of the connection with a single [element].
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.19). He formulates the fourteenth section as follows:

In the two [verses] beginning with "yuvam hi," one should employ this introductory formula (*pratipad*) for two performers or for many; it may be used in the Jyotiṣṭoma or in a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*).
If one [agent] lacks the capacity, then by two or even by many [agents],
because the Jyotiṣṭoma is to be performed, that [capacity] must exist here in the archetype itself.

The plurality of sacrificers is directly heard in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*); having been displaced from the model sacrifice, it should be applied to the *kulāya* and other such rites by means of the *pratipad*.
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard: "Since you two are the lords of heaven"—one should employ this as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers.
The word *pratipad* denotes the verse to be recited at the commencement of a hymn, such as "These drops have been poured forth"— which is prescribed for sacrifices involving many sacrificers.
And that cited *pratipad*, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), finds its place in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Nor is it impossible for there to be two or many sacrificers (*yajamāna*) in that case;

for when a single sacrificer is unable to perform the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) due to a lack of materials and so forth, and since its abandonment is impossible, it must necessarily be performed by two or more people.

This being the position reached, we reply: the duality of sacrificers is directly prescribed (*āmnāta*) in the sacrifice named *Kulāya*: "The king and the domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice with this."
The plurality of sacrificers is prescribed in the *sattras*: "Twenty-four at most should perform the *sattra*.

Therefore, by means of the two scriptural texts containing the words "two" and "many," the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside, and the aforementioned method of disposal must be transferred to the *kulāya* and other such rites.
Furthermore, even in cases of incapacity, a pair or plurality of sacrificers is possible.
Because one who has been accepted as a substitute by someone unable [to perform the rite] lacks the status of being the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
It will be stated that "there is no substitute for the sacrificer.
If another person were to proceed on his own initiative, he would then be performing only his own ritual application (*prayoga*).
One should provide assistance to one who is incapable.

Therefore, since the singularity of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) as it is heard in the text cannot be abandoned—because, like time and other factors, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that is not something to be prescribed for performance (*anupādeya*)—duality or plurality of the sacrificer are not possible in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. (MJaiNyC_3.1.34–36; Section Fifteen: The Sub-section on the Non-Transfer of the Tail [Jāghanī])
And the tail [is part of the offering] because it is a single portion; JaiS 3.3.20. Or rather, it is a primary injunction because it is something not previously established; JaiS 3.3.21.
If it is argued that it is merely a single portion; JaiS 3.3.22.
Not so, because the natural state is not established by the scripture. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.23).
[The author] formulates the fifteenth section as follows:

They cause the wives to perform the *saṃyājana* with the tail (*jāghanī*); this applies to the animal sacrifice as well as to the New Moon and other sacrifices. That [use] is appropriate for the animal sacrifice because of the presence of the tail there.
This part called the tail (jāghanī) indeed belongs to the Darśa and other sacrifices;
it must not be displaced [to another time], nor is it to be further consecrated, because it is a means of accomplishment as indicated by the instrumental case.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "They perform the *saṃyājana* with the tail (*jāghanī*).
The *jāghanī* is the tail of the animal.
Here, the word *patnī* is a partial name for the ritual consisting of four oblations.
For this very reason, it is heard in scripture: "Five *prayājas* are offered; four *patnīsaṃyājas*.

In that context, since the wives of the gods (*devapatnyaḥ*) are the deities (*devatā*) of the third oblation, the term *patnīsaṃyāja*—which is the name of the ritual action—is applied by way of them.
In this regard, the *patnīsaṃyāja* consecration is prescribed with reference to the tail (*jāghanī*).
Now, the tail is an integral part of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), but not of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Therefore, since it must be displaced from the context (*prakaraṇa*) and applied to the animal sacrifice—this being the prima facie view—[the following is stated]:
We reply: by the word *jāghanī*, the tail of the animal (*paśu*) is denoted.
And that [tail] can be procured through purchase and other means even in the absence of an animal sacrifice in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Furthermore, it is not the case here that the tail existing on the animal is to be consecrated by the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Because it is understood as a means by means of the third [case-ending],
there is therefore no displacement from the context.
(Regarding the sixteenth section [Adhikaraṇa] on the placement of *saṃtardana* within the sacrificial session, Sūtras 24–31:

*Santardana* (the act of binding together) should belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*), like the purchase [of Soma], because there is no loss of purpose. (Jaimini 3.3.24) Or rather, it should be displaced [to the ectype], because of the mention of a specific [feature]. (Jaimini 3.3.25)

Or rather, [the distinction] is based on the agent, because he is the cause of that [distinction]. (Jaimini 3.3.26) Or rather, it should be based on the sacrifice, because the explanatory passages (arthavāda) are thus rendered consistent. (Jaimini 3.3.27) And the terminuses (saṃsthā) are like the agents, because there is no difference in their purpose for supporting [the sacrifice]. (Jaimini 3.3.28)
Because the purpose exists in the Ukthya and other [sacrifices] (Jaimini 3.3.29).
If it is argued that praise is useless because there is no distinction [between them] (Jaimini 3.3.30), [the reply is:
it may be so, because of their non-permanence (Jaimini 3.3.31).
START MJaiNy 3.3.39-40: The sixteenth section formulates [the following problem]:
Should the [sacrificial post] be split in a long *soma* sacrifice—[is this] in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)?
When "O long-lived Soma" is uttered, however, the piercing [of the skin] remains as in the archetype (prakṛti).

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is stronger than the genitive case, there is a displacement [of the quality] to the *ukthya* sacrifice and others characterized by length, due to its sublation elsewhere.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "In a long Soma sacrifice, one should join [the vessels] together for the sake of support."
The *dīrghasoma* is a specific type of *soma* sacrifice.
In that sacrifice, the *saṃtardana*—the firm joining together—of the two pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*) upon which the pressing and the support for the *soma* are placed must be performed.
*Saṃtardana* is a tight fastening so that there may be no looseness resulting from mutual separation.
This [instruction] enters into the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) by virtue of the force of the context;

nor is there any impossibility of a "long Soma" (*dīrghasoma*) therein, because the word "long" (*dīrgha*) can be understood as qualifying the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), as in the expression "the long Soma of [the sacrificer]. This being the position reached—
