We reply: it will be stated in the *Niṣādasthapati* section that "the *karmadhāraya* compound is stronger than the *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) compound.
This being the case, length is a property of the *soma*, not of the sacrificer.
[Objection: "But even so, the *soma* that constitutes the archetype (*prakṛti*) is indeed longer in comparison to the *iṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). [Reply: No;
for once that [length] is understood by the word *soma* itself, the word *dīrgha* (long) would be redundant.
Indeed, there is no *soma* whatsoever that is short in comparison to the *iṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice.
For the purpose of excluding that from which the word "long" (*dīrgha*) would otherwise be applied— namely,
the short vowel which is the original form (*prakṛtirūpa*)— this word "long" is employed to exclude it.
In the modified forms (*vikṛti*) such as the *ukthya* sacrifice and others, there is "length" due to the addition of extra cups (*graha*).
In the case of the *dvirātra* and other sacrifices, there is lengthening through repetition;
therefore, by means of the direct statement (*vākya*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside, and its application is in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
However, as for the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the sublation of the word "long" (*dīrgha*) has already been stated previously.

Furthermore, the prohibition of *saṃtardana* (joining together) is directly heard in scripture: "The two pressing-skins (*adhiṣavaṇe*) are indeed the jaws of the sacrifice; one does not join them together, for the jaws are not joined.
Therefore, there is no application [of this rule] to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
(Seventeenth Section: The Prohibition of the Pravargya Rite;
Sūtras 32–33) That which is associated with a number [of performers] should belong to the sacrifice because of the context.
(Jaimini 3.3.32) Or rather, it is occasional (naimittika), because of its connection with the performer, since the indicative mark (liṅga) has that as its cause. (Jaimini 3.3.33)
START MJaiNy 3.3.41–41: The seventeenth section (adhikaraṇa) formulates [the following]:
"Should one not perform the *pravargya* rite in the first sacrifice, or should it be performed when that [sacrifice] has been undertaken?"
The prohibition is appropriate in the context of a sacrifice, for its status as a non-sacrifice has already been stated.
Because of the statement "one prepares [the Pravargya] prior to the Upasads," there is an injunction regarding the sacrifice;
therefore, that prohibition applies only in some cases, due to its being the first instance in the initial performance.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, with reference to the rite called Pravargya, it is heard in scripture: "One should not perform the Pravargya at the first sacrifice."
If it is argued that "this prohibition is to be understood as applying to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice in general, and not to its first performance;
for why?
because its status as the first sacrifice is declared by the statement, 'The Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the first of sacrifices,'" we say: do not speak thus.

Because the Pravargya rite is enjoined for the sacrifice by the sentence, "He performs the Pravargya before the Upasads," there is no lack of determination despite the equal force of the injunction and the prohibition;
for, by the word "first" in the prohibitory sentence, it is determined that the prohibition pertains to the performance [of the rite].
Words such as "first," "second," and so forth, are primary in reference to the repetition of an action; they are applied figuratively to things by virtue of their connection to that action.
Because it is to be studied first, the [first] section is called the "First Section" (*prathama-kāṇḍa*).
The second section (kāṇḍa) follows because it is to be studied immediately after that.
Likewise, a son is called "first" because he was born first,
and "second" because he was born immediately after him.

That being the case, when there is a specific repetition of the performance of the ritual action, the word "first" (prathama) is used in its primary sense; however, by virtue of referring to that repetition, it is used figuratively for the sacrifice. Even in your own view, the word "sacrifice" (yajña) is primary when applied to the rite itself.
If it is argued that [the term] would be figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) in its application, we say:
certainly. Nevertheless, rather than assuming figurativeness for a word whose opposition has not yet arisen, it is better to assume it for the subsequent member of the compound.
Therefore, there is a prohibition of the *pravargya* rite in the first performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Now, one might object: since the *agniṣṭoma*—which constitutes the first of the seven forms (*saṃsthā*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—is that very form, this prohibition must apply specifically to it.
And a rule is heard in that regard: "In the Agniṣṭoma, he chooses [the priests].
If this is so, then let there be a systematic arrangement of injunctions and prohibitions according to the difference in the qualified persons (adhikārin).
For it is heard thus: "But one who is learned in the Vedas may, at his will..."

"One should avoid that [first performance]. Therefore, this prohibition applies specifically to the first performance of the Agniṣṭoma when it is performed by someone other than one who has completed the study of the Vedas (anūcāna).

(Aṣṭādaśa Adhikaraṇa: On the application of the grinding of the Pūṣan-oblation in the modified sacrifice; Sūtra: The grinding of the Pūṣan-oblation should be understood as applying to the modified sacrifice, because it is not enjoined in the archetype. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.34)
He formulates the eighteenth topic:
"The portion for Pūṣan is ground" (prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ pūṣā)—does this apply to the archetype (prakṛti) or the ectype (vikṛti)?
It is logical that it applies to the archetype, precisely because of its context within the section on the iṣṭi sacrifice. (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.3.43)

"Or, like the *saṃtardana* and other [rules], because Pūṣan is not present in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the restatement of what is already established is for the purpose of intending something additional.
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard: "Therefore, Pūṣan has a portion of ground [grain], for he is toothless."
In this regard, it is established— like the *saṃtardana* (piercing), the *pratipad* (opening verse), and so forth— that Pūṣan, being toothless, has flour (*piṣṭa*) as his portion. Nevertheless,
the subsequent section is introduced here to state a specific distinction concerning that very same subject matter.
(Nineteenth [adhikaraṇa]: On the placement of the grinding of the *pauṣṇa* [offering] specifically in the *caru*; Sūtras 35–38. Jaimini 3.3.35:

That [grinding] is for all [offerings], because there is no distinction. Jaimini 3.3.36: Or rather, it applies to the *caru*, because it is stated for that purpose; it would not apply to the *puroḍāśa* due to a contradiction of purpose, nor to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).
If it is argued that [the term applies] even to the act of moving, [we reply]:
No, because it is a name for the act of cooking. Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.37–38.
The nineteenth section formulates the following:

Is the grinding performed on the cooked rice (caru), the animal victim (paśu), and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), or only on the cooked rice? Since no specific distinction is observed, this [grinding] is prescribed for all of them. (MJaiNy 3.3.45)

Because it has already been obtained [in the case of the cake], there is no grinding in the *puroḍāśa* due to the destruction of the shape of the heart and other parts; nor is there grinding in the animal sacrifice. By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), grinding applies only to the *caru*.
Thus, the *caru* is prescribed by the injunction: "One should subsequently offer a *caru* to Pūṣan."
"One desiring food should sacrifice a dark-colored animal to Pūṣan"—this is the injunction regarding the animal.
"Having sacrificed the animal, he offers a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)"—this is obtained for the animal sacrifice to Pūṣan by means of the *codaka* (archetypal extension).
In that context, according to the principle that "the sacrificial cake has the same deity as the animal," Pūṣan is the deity of the sacrificial cake.
In this regard, taking the previously mentioned grinding as the subject, the doubts, prima facie arguments, and final conclusions being stated are clearly evident.
(Regarding the twentieth section [Adhikaraṇa], concerning the placement of the *pauṣṇapeṣaṇa* [the grinding for Pūṣan] in an offering to a single deity; Sūtras 39–46:
Because of the connection with one [deity] in a single [offering], Jaimini 3.3.39.
And because of the contradiction of ritual properties (*dharma*), Jaimini 3.3.40.
Or rather, it should apply when there is a companion [deity], because the deity is the determining factor (Jaimini 3.3.41);
and because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) (Jaimini 3.3.42).

Due to the explicit scriptural statement, there is grinding of all [grains] with respect to that [deity], since the scripture prescribes it; however, in the case of the *vicāra* [mixture], there is no grinding because the purpose is absent (Jaimini 3.3.43).

In one case, because it is the nature of the object, [the offering] for Indra and Agni would not belong to both, since it is not enjoined as such. (Jaimini 3.3.44) The state of ending in "ad" is merely a reason. (Jaimini 3.3.45) The scriptural statement is paramount. (Jaimini 3.3.46)
The twenty-first section (viṃśādhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
Should one grind [the grain] even for an offering to two deities, or only for an offering to Pūṣan alone?
Even in the case of the offering to two deities, that [ground] belongs to Pūṣan as well, because he is a participant in the grinding.
The deity should not cause the grinding to be rendered fruitless;
because the mention of a "portion" (bhāga) occurs in the context of the sacrifice's essence, that [grinding] does not pertain to another sacrifice.
In the Rājasūya, it is heard: "He offers a caru-oblation to Soma-Pūṣan."

Regarding the injunction, "A pap (caru) for Indra and Pūṣan," one might argue that even though the pap is for two deities, since Pūṣan is a recipient of the ground flour, the grinding must be performed for the sake of Pūṣan. To this, it must be replied: Is the deity the motivator for the grinding?
Or is it the sacrifice?
Not the first;
for without the sacrifice, the deity alone lacks the capacity to produce the fruit, and thus cannot necessitate the act of grinding.
If the grinding is the motivator for the Pūṣan sacrifice, then that grinding cannot apply to another, two-deity sacrifice.
If it is argued that "in the statement ‘Pūṣan has the ground portion as his share,’ no sacrifice is mentioned," this is not so.
Because the sacrifice must be inferred due to the otherwise inexplicability of the word "portion" (bhāga),
for the status of being a deity cannot be established without the recipient of the flour-substance;
and once the status of deity is established, the sacrifice is inferred through the attainment of both the substance and the deity.
Therefore, since the act of grinding is prompted by a sacrifice to a single deity, there is no grinding in a sacrifice to two deities.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the third chapter.
(In the first section, concerning the fact that the *nivīta* is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there are nine sūtras.)
"‘The nivīta [is] a duty for humans, because the word has that as its primary meaning' (Jaimini 3.4.1);
'Or rather, it is a descriptive reference (apadeśa), because the fact of the matter already exists' (Jaimini 3.4.2);
'But it must be an injunction (vidhi), because it conveys something not previously known' (Jaimini 3.4.3)."
It would be a duty of action (karmadharma),
because it is a supplementary part of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa). That which is connected within that context [is the duty], because there is no contradiction.
Or rather, [the mention of the other] is equal [to the mention of the primary], because it is enumerated as such; for the other is for the sake of that.
(Jaimini 3.4.7) Or it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because of the context. (Jaimini 3.4.8) And because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction. (Jaimini 3.4.9)
In the first section of the fourth quarter, [the author] formulates the argument: "But *nivīta* is for humans; it is an injunction, not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)."
Because it is something not previously established, it is enjoined either by virtue of the context, or as pertaining to the person, or to the sacrifice.
The *nivīta* is established as pertaining to mortals because it is generally seen among them;
its status as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) follows from its syntactical unity with the injunction regarding the *upavīta*.
In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "The *nivīta* is for men."
"The cord worn over the right shoulder belongs to the ancestors;
the cord worn over the left shoulder belongs to the gods. He wears it over the left shoulder; thus he assumes the characteristic mark of the gods."
In this regard, since the *nivīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread has not been established by any other authority previously, its status as something to be enjoined must be accepted.
Furthermore, that *nivīta* is enjoined for the sake of human beings (*manuṣyāṇām*) by means of the genitive case; this is one prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Under this position, the connection with human beings is twofold: either a connection with every individual person, like the wearing of gold ornaments, or [a connection with a specific class].
This is one interpretation.

Another interpretation is that since the *upavīta* and *prācīnāvīta* are observed even in independent rites for the gods (*daivika*) and ancestors (*paitṛka*) when they are not part of a formal sacrifice (*kratupraveśa*), by association with those, the *nivīta* applies to independent rites concerning humans, such as those for teachers, guests, and so forth.
The second prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that, by the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is a duty pertaining to the sacrifice (*yagadharma*), like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
In this view, the mention of "human" (*manuṣya*) is a restatement of the connection with the agent.

Another alternative position arises: since there is no contradiction between the direct statement of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīśruti*) and the context, it is a duty pertaining to humans who are connected to the ritual (*kratu*), by relying on both [the word and the context].
And that [duty] is of two kinds: one type is that which is a duty of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), like the red turban and so forth;
the other is that action which, within the sacrifice itself, has humans as its primary agents, such as the giving of the *anvāhārya* rice-offering and so on.
"Furthermore, if that were its nature, the association with the *upavīta* would also be upheld"—this is the view of another.
Since, in every respect, the *nivīta* is not a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), this being the position reached, we reply:
the *nivīta* and so forth perceived here refer to clothing (*vāsas*).
But it does not concern the threefold cord (*trivṛtsūtra*),

because it is similar to the statement, "having placed the skin or the garment over the right shoulder" (*ajinaṃ vāso vā dakṣiṇata upavīya*); furthermore, for the sake of convenience, the *nivīta* position would naturally apply to the garment.
In the case of the *cīnā* and *upavīta* [garments], one or the other garment would necessarily fall down on one side;
therefore, since this is already established by necessity, the scriptural mention of the genitive case in the word "amanuṣyāṇām" (of non-humans) is not injunctive.
Nor can there be an injunction based on the context [of the sacrifice] as a subordinate element (*kratvaṅga*) of the ritual.

Because it would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda). First, the wearing of the sacred thread (upavīta) is enjoined; otherwise, the praise [contained in the statement] "it makes that very mark of a non-god" would be rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, regarding that rule for the *upavīta*, since it is possible for the *nivīta* and *prācīnāvīta* to form a single syntactical unit as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), it is improper to treat them as separate injunctions.

The *nivīta* is a praise by way of contrast, implying: "The *nivīta* and *prācīnāvīta* are unsuitable for divine rites because they relate respectively to humans and ancestors, whereas the *upavīta* is suitable."
Therefore, it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
(Regarding the second [topic], the section on whether the *upavīta* is an auxiliary of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, Sūtras 10–11):

The *upavīta* should be a duty for all [rituals] because of the observation of an indicative mark; or rather, it is not so, because of the context, since that [mark] is observed [only there]. Jaimini 3.4.10–11.

The second section (adhikaraṇa) begins with Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.4.3–4, formulating the inquiry: "Is the act of wearing the sacred thread (*upavyayate*) for all purposes, or is it for the sake of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*)?"
In the Agnihotra, the act should be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, as indicated by the indicative mark [of the scriptural text].

If it is argued that, because of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the mention of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) as an established fact in the Agnihotra rite in the passage "for one wearing the sacrificial thread milks for the gods"—establishes that the *upavīta* is for the purpose of all rites; we say no. For this [mention] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to praise the milking of one whose Agnihotra fire has been extinguished. (Jaimini Nyāyamālāvistara 3.4.4)
Because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) can be explained otherwise:
on that day, the *agnihotra* for the deceased is offered by another person.

In that context, having prescribed "he should milk [the cow] wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*)," the passage beginning with "wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*)" is restated as a eulogy for that injunction.

Therefore, since there is no possibility of sublation by a fallacious indicative mark (*liṅgābhāsa*), the *upavīta* is an auxiliary to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
(Regarding the third section, on the injunction of the sacred thread:
Sūtra) Or it may be an injunction, because it is something not previously established. Jaimini 3.4.12.
The third section formulates [the following]:

"In the case of *upavyāna*, is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) or an injunction (*vidhi*)? The first [alternative] holds because it is already established in the Smṛti. This is not so; rather, because it is something previously unknown (*apūrva*), it is enjoined in the ritual context by means of the *leṭ* suffix. (MJaiNy_3.4.5)

If it is argued that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established by the Smṛti rule, "One should always carry water and always wear the sacrificial thread" (*nityodakī nityayajñopavītī*), [the reply is:
Not so.

Even though it may be established as serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it is not established as serving the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); therefore, by means of the fifth mood (*pañcamalakāra*), it is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Candrikā 3.1.5)
(Regarding the section on the restatement of wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder and having its tip pointing north in the fourth [chapter], Sūtras 13–14:
"And the state of being turned upward [is not a new injunction] because it is something already established;
or rather, it is a restatement, as there is an observation of indicative marks. Jaimini 3.4.13–14.
The fourth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*) [is for] the gods; facing eastward (*puraudañcaḥ*)—are these two injunctions?"
Or rather, because it is not obtained from elsewhere, this discourse prescribes a previously unknown matter.

The discussion arises from the two occurrences of the word *hi*. From the perspective of the Smṛti, the two [rules] regarding the grass-pointing-southward (*dakṣiṇāgra*) and the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) have been established; this is a praise of them.

Regarding the Agnihotra for the deceased, it is heard in scripture: "One should cause the milking while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), for one causes the milking for the gods while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*)."

"Those darbha grass blades which were pointing eastward, one should spread them with their tips pointing southward. In that regard, at the milking for the Agnihotra of the deceased, the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta).
Just as the state of having the tips pointing southward is prescribed for the spreading of darbha grass,

so too, prior to death while one is still living, the sacrificial cord (upavīta) must be prescribed as an auxiliary to the milking in the Agnihotra, and the state of having the tips pointing northward must be prescribed as an auxiliary to the spreading of darbha grass.

If it is argued that the syntactical formulation is "one wearing the sacrificial thread should milk [the cow] for the sake of the gods" and "those *darbha* grasses which were used before death should be directed northward," and that since neither of these two is established from any other source, an injunction for a previously unknown matter (*apūrvārtha*) must be prescribed; [we reply: no.
Not so;
for in both cases, the status of restatement (*anuvāda*) is perceived through the use of the word *hi* and the word *yat*,
and there is indeed the prior attainment (*prāpti*) of those two.

By the Smṛti rule, "the tips should face north," the state of having the tips directed northward—which is applicable to all rites for the gods—is restated (anūdyate) in order to praise the prescribed state of having the tips directed southward.

Similarly, in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, by the injunction "he wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder" (*upavyayate*), the divine mode of wearing the thread (*upavīta*) is restated in order to praise the prescribed *prācīnāvīta* mode.
Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). MJaiNyC_3,1.67 //

(Fifth section: The rule regarding the kindling of the fire; Sūtra 15) But there is indeed an injunction for the maintaining [of the fire], because it is something not previously established. Jaimini 3.4.15.
He formulates the fifth section:

"Because he holds [it] above for the sake of the gods"—this is a commendation (saṃstava). Or rather, it is an injunction; the first [clause] is a praise, as before, of the holding prescribed in the rite for the ancestors (pitrya).
The holding [of the fuel-stick] upward is obtained from the text itself, not from any other source;
for it is by the abandonment of the literal word that a new meaning is enjoined.
Regarding the Agnihotra performed after death, it is heard in scripture: "One should run after [the fire], holding the fuel-stick below."

Regarding the statement, "For he holds it above the gods," here it is prescribed that when one recites the mantra while holding the ancestral oblation (*pitrya havis*) in the hand, one should hold the fuel-stick (*samidh*) beneath the handle of the offering-ladle (*sruc*).
If it is argued that this very point is praised by the subsequent supporting argument,
since the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in the preceding section—
let it not be so.

In the case of a divine oblation (*daivika havir*), since the placing of the fuel-stick (*samid-dhāraṇa*) upon the handle of the ladle (*sruc-daṇḍa*) must be enjoined as something not previously established, the word *hi*—which would otherwise indicate that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*)—is to be disregarded due to its impossibility [in this context]. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāya-mālā-vistara 3.1.8–9)
(Regarding the sixth section [Adhikaraṇa], concerning the fact that the division of directions is an explanatory statement [arthavāda]—the sūtra:
"And the division of directions is like that, because the connection [of the directions] has a purpose as its cause. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.16)

The sixth section formulates the problem: "Men divided the western direction"—is this an injunction, or is it a statement here intended as a praise of a past event (purākalpa), which thus implies an injunction? MJaiNy_3,4.10 //

Because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction [regarding] the statement concerning the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall, this description of the directions is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), just like the *nivīta* [description] regarding the *upavīta*.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "He makes the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall."
The gods, humans, and [ancestors] divided the quarters: the gods [took] the east,
the ancestors the south,
and humans the west.
"The Rudras [are] in the north; in that he makes the sacrificial shed (prācīnavaṃśa) face eastward, the sacrificer thereby approaches the world of the gods.
In this regard, since gods and others lack qualification for ritual action (karman), there can be no suspicion of an injunction (vidhi) concerning them.
"The men should divide [the space] toward the west"—this would be the injunction.
Why?
Because it is being praised by means of an explanatory passage (arthavāda) in the form of a past event (purākalpa).
The Purākalpa is the statement that [the practice] was performed by the ancestors (*pūrvapuruṣa*).
This is expressed by the word "they divided" (*vyabhajanta*), which denotes a past fact (*bhūtārtha*).
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this is an injunction (*vidhi*).
That particular pavilion whose bamboo rafters point toward the east is called *prācīnavaṃśa*.

Since it is understood to form a single syntactical unit with the injunction [regarding the direction], it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). In the case of the evening *Āpti* sacrifice and others, the western direction would otherwise be obtained. // MJaiNyC_3,4.10-11 //

(Sūtra on the section concerning the restatement of [the sacrificial post] split at the knot, full, smeared with ghee, and burnt, in the seventh [chapter]: "And [the sacrificial post] split at the knot, full, smeared with ghee, and burnt is likewise [a restatement]. (Jaimini 3.4.17)
He formulates the seventh section:
By the statement "cut at the knot," the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is understood to include its roots;
by the statement "clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is for the gods, whey (*mastu*) is for the ancestors," fresh butter (*navanīta*) is indicated.
By the statement, "That which is burnt belongs to him," [the text] praises the state of being cooked for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
The preceding and following positions (*pakṣa*) are to be applied here as in the case of the *nivīta* [injunction].
In the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard: "That which is torn apart by the teeth belongs to the gods."
"That which is between [the roots] belongs to humans;
that which is with its root belongs to the ancestors;
the sacrificial grass (barhis) is provided with its root for the sake of distinction."
*Paruḥ* means a joint; *ditam* means cut or divided.
Likewise, in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, regarding the anointing for initiation, it is heard in scripture: "Clarified butter is for the gods."
The whey belongs to the ancestors, the cooked curd belongs to human beings; indeed,
that which is fresh butter (navanīta) belongs to all the deities.
"Whoever anoints [himself] with fresh butter (navanīta) gratifies all the deities.
*Mastu* is the whey produced from curd;
it is fresh butter that has been cooked until slightly melted so as to be applied to the head, or buttermilk (*takra*).

Regarding the baking of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: “That which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti; that which is uncooked belongs to Rudra; that which is properly cooked belongs to the gods.”
"Therefore, it should be cooked without being burnt; [only] then does it attain the state of being fit for the deity. "Burnt" means overcooked; "uncooked" means undercooked.

In that context— since the cutting of the grass together with its roots, the use of fresh butter for anointing, and the cooking of the sacrificial cake as prescribed are the matters enjoined— all that remains is merely laudatory.
This is simply an elaboration of the discussion concerning the *nivīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread.
In the same way, this should also be understood in the case of the statement, "That which is full belongs to humans.

And that refers to the churning performed during the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices in the *Mahāpitṛyajña*, specifically in the rite where, according to the injunction "one prepares a stirred drink (*mantha*) in the milk of a cow that has recently calved (*abhivānyā*) for the *Agniṣvātta* ancestors," one adds flour to the milk of a cow that has lost her calf and is designated by the term *abhivānyā*.
It is heard: "That which is full is above humans;
half belongs to the gods, and half to the ancestors."
"He stirs half [the milk],
for it is the portion of the ancestors.
In this context, since the stirring must be performed upon a quantity of milk measured by half— the lower portion of the vessel— it is that "half" which is prescribed.
And that [act] is praised by means of the passage beginning with "Full" (pūrṇa).
(Regarding the eighth [topic], the section on the prohibition of speaking untruth as being a duty pertaining to the sacrifice—sūtras:

"That which is not an action connected with the sacrifice would be a constant restatement because of its connection. (Jaimini 3.4.18) "Or rather, it is an injunction because of a different connection. (Jaimini 3.4.19)
The eighteenth section (adhikaraṇa) [of the third chapter] formulates [the following]:
"One should not speak untruth"—is this a Vedic injunction or a duty for men? It is the latter, as it is a restatement.
Or [the injunction] applies to a person who has performed the sacrifice, or to one who is pure after the sacrifice, or rather, the rule pertains to the sacrifice itself.
Because speaking untruths serves human ends, there is a prohibition of that kind;
it is a restatement (anuvāda) of Smṛti rules regarding human and Vedic rites, due to the absence of a scriptural injunction (śruti) for their procedure.
In the case of an injunction (*ākhyāta*), there is no non-mention of the person; it applies only to the sacrifice, just like the *prayāja* offerings.
Since the rule of speaking the truth is distinct from other connections, it is therefore an injunction regarding the sacrifice.
In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, it is heard in the scripture: "One should not speak untruth."
In this regard, this prohibition is enjoined as a property of the person.
Why?
Because since its counter-positive, namely false speech, is a property of the person, its negation must likewise be enjoined as a property of the person alone.
The verb "should speak" (*vadet*) denotes the agent,
because the agent is understood through that verb.
Since the person (*puruṣa*) is expressed by the verbal suffix, it is logical that the act of speaking— the meaning of the verbal root— is a property of the person.
For grammarians proclaim: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, yet between the two, the suffix is predominant.
Since speaking is a property of the person (puruṣadharma), it is logical that its prohibition is also a property of the person.
Otherwise, if they had different objects of application, there would be no sublation [of the Smṛti rule by the Śruti].
Therefore, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the verb, which denotes the person, sublates the context (*prakaraṇa*), and this prohibition is enjoined as having the person as its purpose.
If it is argued that "the Smṛti prohibition already exists," [the response follows].
In that case, let this scriptural statement be its source.
Therefore, "it is for the purpose of man"—this is one prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Alternatively, to avoid contradicting both the heard verbal form (ākhyāta-śruti) and the context (prakaraṇa), let it be a duty for the person engaged in the sacrifice (kratuyukta-puruṣadharma).
For this statement is not the source of the Smṛti,
because their subject matters are different;
and the Smṛti prohibits untruthfulness for a person from the time of initiation until death.
Since it falls within that [category], the Smṛti prohibition is indeed applicable even in the case of a sacrifice (*kratu*).
Therefore, this prohibition, though serving both purposes, is not enjoined;
rather, it is merely restated (*anūdyate*). This is the second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is denoted by the verbal suffix;
however, the agent is understood through implication as being invariably concomitant with it.

Therefore, in the absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), [the element in question] enters into the sacrifice itself as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), like the *prayāja* offerings, solely on the basis of context (*prakaraṇa*).
And even there, it is not being enjoined;
rather, since the universal prohibition already applies to the sacrifice as well, it is merely restated—this is the third prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
"One should speak only the truth," [so it is said].

This connection, which is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), is distinct from that connection for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) consisting of the Smṛti rule "one should not speak untruth.
Therefore, because it has not been previously established, it is enjoined.
In the event of a transgression of this [rule], there is only a deficiency of the sacrifice (kratu),
but no sin (pratyavāya) for the person;
therefore, in this case, the expiation (prāyaścitta) pertains to the sacrifice.
However, when there is a transgression of the rules pertaining to human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), the fault belongs to the person alone and does not constitute a deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratu*).
In that case, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed by the Smṛti; this is the distinction. (MJaiNyC 3.4.14–16)
(Regarding the ninth section on the placement of the *jañjabhyamāna* duties within the context, Sūtras 20–22:
Sūtra 20: The person [is subordinate] like the *ahīna* sacrifice, because he exists for the sake of that [sacrifice].
Sūtra 21: Or rather, due to the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that which is connected to it, just like a material substance (*dravya*).
It would be set aside because of the designation. (Jaimini 3.4.22). He formulates the ninth section as follows:

The recitation of the mantra while yawning is a duty of the person or of the sacrifice; by virtue of the direct statement, it is the former, but by the context, let it be the latter, as there is no contradiction. In the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard: "Breath indeed is skill (*dakṣa*). [The question arises: Is this [recitation] a duty of the person or of the sacrifice?

By the force of the direct statement (*vākya*), it is the former; however, by the context (*prakriyā*), let it be the latter, since there is no contradiction. In the section on the Darśapūrṇamāsa, it is stated: "Prāṇa is indeed skill. [The doubt is: Does this mantra-recitation belong to the human agent or to the ritual act? Based on the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the first [option] holds; yet, based on the ritual context (*prakriyā*), let the second be accepted, as it is not contradictory.
The apāna is the will (kratu). Therefore, while being born, one should say: "In me, skill and will!"—thus he places both the prāṇa and the apāna within himself.
A man with his mouth wide open due to the distortion of his limbs and gnashing his teeth—
by his speech, the recitation of a mantra is understood;
and direct statement (vākya) is stronger than context (prakaraṇa).
If it is argued that, for this reason, [the act of *jañjabhyamāna*] is a duty pertaining solely to the person,

it is not so; because even within the sacrificial ritual (*kratu*), since a person who is "sneezing" can exist, and there being no conflict between the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), both establish that it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the person engaged in the sacrifice.

(Regarding the tenth section [on the topic that acts such as threatening others serve the purpose of man], the sūtra states: "And in the case of the Śaṃyu [rite], because of the surrender of everything. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.23)
The tenth section formulates the problem: "One should not threaten a Brahmin"—is this for the sake of the sacrifice or for the sake of the person?
Because it is in proximity to the fruitful sacrifice, it is for the sake of the sacrifice, like the preceding mantra. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Bindu 3.4.18)
The avoidance of suffering is appropriately the result of a prohibition;
since this prohibition serves a human purpose, it should be extracted from its context.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "Whoever should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, him one should cause to suffer for a hundred years."

"Therefore, one should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa. If it is argued that— just as in the preceding section the recitation of a mantra, though itself devoid of a fruit, is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the fruitful sacrifice,
so too here the prohibition against insulting a Brāhmaṇa is an auxiliary to the sacrifice— it is not so.
Because of the disparity.
For in the former case, the maintenance of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths within the self cannot be the fruit of reciting the mantra,
since that [maintenance] is already established beforehand.

In this case, however, having introduced the torment lasting for a hundred years as the consequence of threatening someone with a weapon, it is appropriate that the avoidance of that torment constitutes the result of the prohibition against such threatening.
Therefore, since the prohibition serves solely the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha), its removal from the context is justified.
(Regarding the eleventh section, concerning the prohibition of conversation with a woman in her courses, Sūtras 24–25:
Because there is no prior exclusion for a woman in her courses;
and because of the prohibition regarding food. Jaimini 3.4.24–25.
MJaiNy 3.4.20: The eleventh section (adhikaraṇa) formulates [the following]:
"One should not converse with a woman in her courses," as in the previous case.

The human purpose [of the prohibition] would apply to some sacrifice, because there is no possibility of its application [to ordinary life]. If it is argued that, since it is heard in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—"One who has menstrual flow shall not converse"—this prohibition is therefore a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice due to that context; [we reply: no.
Not so;
for that would entail the negation of something that was not even proposed as a possibility. [The rule applies to] one on whose day of the vow his wife becomes menstruating...
"Having excluded her, one should sacrifice"—by this [injunction] for the removal of the menstruating woman from the ritual, there is no possibility of conversation with her during the sacrifice.
Therefore, because it serves solely the purpose of the person, this [injunction] is displaced from its context (prakaraṇa).

(Section on the Human Nature of Holding Gold and Other Such Acts in the Twelfth [Book], Sūtras 26–30) "But when not in a specific context, it is a human duty because of its distinction from that [context]. (Jaimini 3.4.26) "But because it does not have a substance as its object, it must be a subsidiary act. (Jaimini 3.4.27)
Because of the connection with the Veda (Jaimini 3.4.28);
and because of the connection with the substance (Jaimini 3.4.29).
Or rather, there should be a connection for this [act] with the fruit, like the connection [of other acts]; therefore, it is a ritual act, according to Ātiśāyana (Jaimini 3.4.30).
In the twenty-first to twenty-third sūtras of the third chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra, the twelfth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"Gold should be worn because it possesses a [specific] color; wearing it would be an auxiliary part of the sacrifice."
Or rather, in this case, it is either the refinement of gold, or the color, or the human purpose.
Because it is Vedic, that [initiation] is an auxiliary to the ritual action through the Smṛti;
however, since the caste is primary, let it be a subordinate factor (guṇa) for the sake of the simplicity of the injunction.
Since it is heard as not being connected to a specific context (*anārabhyaśruta*), the Smṛti rule regarding the sacrifice is not fixed;
therefore, its purpose must be for the person, and heaven—or something else—must be postulated as the result, as in the case of the *Rātri-satra*.
It is heard as not being connected to a specific context: "Therefore, gold should be worn."
"He himself becomes fair-complexioned, while his rival becomes ill-favored.

In this regard, one position is that since the wearing of gold endowed with a beautiful color constitutes a Vedic ritual act, it serves as a reminder of the sacrifice; therefore, the wearing is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
The second position is that even though it is an auxiliary part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), it is not a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*);
rather, the gold belonging to the performer is consecrated by the act of wearing.
This is because, in the word *bhāryam*, the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*), and thus the gold—as the objective factor—is understood to be primary.

The third position is that, because it would be cumbersome to enjoin the wearing [of gold] as qualified by its color, one should instead refer back to the gold already associated with wearing and enjoin only the excellence of its color.

(Fifth [section] – In the section concerning the twice-eating of the remnant in the *aindravāyava* cup, the sūtra:
"But in the case of the *aindravāyava*, because of the specific scriptural statement, there should be eating for each ritual act. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.18)
The fifth section formulates the following:
Should there be a single consumption of the remnant of the Aindravāyava cup, or multiple?
Since it would follow from the previous reasoning that there is a single consumption, there shall be a double consumption because of a specific scriptural injunction. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Prakāśa 3.5.8)

If it is argued that in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding this Aindravāyava cup, since the Soma to be consecrated is a single entity, the ritual action involving the remnant (śeṣakārya) should be performed only once—
this is not so;
for "one partakes of the Aindravāyava twice."
Because of the scriptural statement, "For he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call twice for this [offering]," there is a double consumption.

(Regarding the sixth section on the consumption of the remnants in the Soma sacrifice, sūtras 19–21: In the case of the Soma, there is no consumption because there is no scriptural injunction. (Jaimini 3.5.19) Or rather, there should be [consumption], because of the observation of another purpose. (Jaimini 3.5.20)
"But the words [of the mantra] are to be used according to the instruction, because they are not previously established [by other means]. (Jaimini 3.5.21).
The sixth section formulates [the following]:
In some [Soma sacrifices], there is no eating of the remnant, or rather, it is not to be eaten because of the cup-offering;
since only a small portion is mentioned, a remnant exists, and its eating follows from the force of the unprecedented statement.
— In the Soma sacrifices, there is no eating of the remnant.

If it is argued that because the injunction "one offers the cups" (*yadgrahāñjuhoti*) prescribes an oblation from the entire cup, there can be no remnant— just as there is none in the case of the *kumbhīs*—
it is not so;
for a remnant is established by the specific statement, "one offers a small amount" (*alpaṃ juhoti*).
That consumption [of the Soma], however, is understood from scriptural statements that establish an unprecedented (apūrva) purpose.
Statements such as "They consume the Āśvina," "They consume the Aindravāyava twice," and "They consume in the assembly" establish an unprecedented purpose.
Therefore, because of the injunction for consumption, there is consumption of the Somas.
(Regarding the seventh section on the consumption of the remnants of the *camasa* vessels, the sūtra states:
"In the case of the *camasa* vessels, [the priests consume the remnant] because of the designation, since the connection [of the name] is based upon that. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.22)
The seventh section formulates the following problem: Regarding the phrase "Does the Hotṛ’s cup go forward?", is there no consumption [of the Soma], or is there consumption?
There is no consumption because it is not explicitly stated; however, that [consumption] must occur by virtue of the designation "the Hotṛ’s cup. (MJaiNy_3.5.10)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward; let the Brahman’s go forward; let the Udgātṛs’ go forward."

"If it is argued that there is no consumption [of the soma] in those cases because of the absence of an explicit statement— namely, 'Let [the portions] of the sacrificer go forth' and 'Let [those] of the members of the assembly go forth'— "
Not so;
for when the word *camasa* occurs in the traditional designation (*samākhyā*), the act of drinking is understood,
since its etymology is "that particular vessel in which Soma is drunk (*camyate*) or consumed."
Therefore, there is such eating of it.

(Eighth [section]: Regarding the consumption by the Udgātṛs together with the Subrahmaṇya; Sūtras 23–26) Jaimini 3.5.23: Only one [should consume] from the cup of the Udgātṛ, because of the connection with the Vedic text.
Jaimini 3.5.24: Or rather, all [should consume], because of the connection with all [the priests].
Or rather, it belongs to those who perform the praise, because of their connection with that [act] and because of the abundance of scriptural tradition.

(Jaimini 3.5.25) But all [the priests] should participate because of their connection with the Veda; on account of this reason, it would apply to only one part [of the rite]. (Jaimini 3.5.26) START MJaiNy 3,5.11-13
The eighth section formulates the problem: "Of the Udgātṛs"— does one Udgātṛ consume [the soma],
or do all of them, or rather all the Sāman-singers mentioned by the Subrahmaṇya?
Or rather, all of them today are associated with him as Udgātṛs according to the Vedic text;
because of their plurality, they are connected through the act of singing, while the third [alternative] is set aside by conventional usage.

In the case of the *yoga* [of the word], by virtue of its conventional designation (*samākhyā*), the final [option] is what is intended here according to the maxim of the "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍinnyāya*); the third [option], on the other hand, is mentioned in the Vārttika because of the absence of staying in the assembly (*sadas*). In the previously cited sentence, "of the *udgātṛ*s," there is the consumption (*bhakṣa*) by only one.

One prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the nominal stem *udgātṛ* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) to denote the specific Sāman-chant portion designated by the word *udgītha*, [the term "udgātṛ" refers only to the Udgātṛ priest].

A second view is that since plurality (*bahutva*) expressed in the word "of the Udgātṛs" (*udgātṝṇām*) cannot possibly reside in a single individual, all sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), indicated by the term "Udgātṛ," should consume [the remnant].
This is because at the time of performance, the Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, and Pratihartṛ chant the respective portions consisting of the *udgītha*, *prastāva*, and *pratihāra*.
The third position is that, according to the etymological derivation (yoga) from the phrase "they sing with elevation" (*udutkarṣeṇa gāyanti*), the three *udgātṛ*s should consume [the soma];
however, by the maxim that "conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) sets aside etymological meaning," there is only one *udgātṛ*.
And for the sake of accounting for the plural number [in the text], those closely associated with him are indicated by implication.
Furthermore, proximity exists for the Subrahmaṇya priest just as it does for the Prastotṛ and Pratihartr priests;
for since he is a student of the Sāmaveda, the designation "Audgātra" (belonging to the Udgātṛ) applies to his own duty as well, namely the invocation known as the Subrahmaṇyā.
Therefore, the final position—that "the four Sāman-singers, including the Subrahmaṇya, should consume [the Soma]"—is the one favored by the author of the Bhāṣya.

The author of the Vārttika, however, accepted the third position—that because the *sadas* is the place for consuming [the Soma] and the Subrahmaṇya priest does not enter the *sadas*, the remaining Sāman-singers consume it without him—stating in the ninth book, in the section concerning the consumption of Soma by the Grāvastut (Sūtras 27–30):
"There is no consumption for the Grāvastut, because it is not so prescribed. (Jaimini 3.5.27).
Or rather, [the offering] belongs to the *hāriyojana* cup because of its connection with all [priests];
or it belongs to the *camasins* because of their proximity;
but since [the rule] applies to all, the mention of the *camasa* cups is for that purpose.
Now, the author formulates the ninth section (adhikaraṇa) [of the third chapter]:
"Should the consumption of the Hāriyojana cup belong to the Camasins alone?"
Or rather, it belongs to all of them, because it is the first among them due to its proximity to the preceding statement.
"All [of them] indeed consume [the soma]," according to the statement regarding the *hāriyojana* cup;
thus, even for the *prāvastut*, there is consumption, as being a *camasin* (one who possesses a cup) is not the cause [for consumption].
The cup taken with the mantra "Thou art the tawny one, the yoker of the tawny ones" is the *hāriyojana*.
The Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the others are *camasin* (holders of the *camasa* cups).
However, among the four *hotṛ*s, he who is the fourth, named Grāvastut, is not a *camasin*.
In that case, the consumption of the *hāriyojana* cup belongs to the *camasins* alone.

Why? Because in the preceding sentence—"As for the other cups, the *camasins* consume them according to their respective cups; but of this *hāriyojana* cup, everyone indeed desires [to drink]"—the word "everyone" (*sarve*) in the subsequent sentence must refer to those very same *camasins*, since they are the ones present in the context of the prior statement.
Therefore, since it might be argued that there is no consumption [of the Soma] for the Grāvastut priest there, we reply:

By means of the word *atha* and the particle *eva*, any suspicion that the rule applies only to the *camasins* is set aside; and because it is impossible to restrict the universal consumption prescribed by the sentence through mere proximity, the Grāvastut also has a share in the consumption.
Therefore, being a *camasin* is not the cause for consuming [the Soma].

(Regarding the tenth section [of the third chapter], which establishes that the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* is the cause for consuming [the soma]: "And one should consume [the soma] because of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.31)

The tenth section formulates the problem: Is the first [portion] for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer a rule regarding priority alone, or rather does it apply to the consumption associated with that [first portion], which is occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance? (MJaiNy 3.5.16)

"It is not so, because the prior [application] does not obtain; for a compound cannot exist [in that way]. Therefore, there is an injunction for a qualified [act]; thus, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is also a cause. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 3.5.17) The scripture is heard as follows: "The first draught belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*."

If it is argued: "The Hotṛ is the one who pronounces the *vaṣaṭ* call; his consumption [of the portion] is already established by conventional designation (*samākhyā*), but its priority is not established; therefore, that [priority] alone is what is enjoined here."
Not so;

since "first-eating" (*prathamabhakṣaḥ*) is a compound word, it is unfit to be analyzed by separating it as "that which is an eating, that is first," and therefore, what is enjoined here is the act of eating qualified by priority.
In that act of eating, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is the cause.
(Regarding the eleventh section [of the third chapter], the topic concerning whether the oblation and the pressing are also causes for consumption, the sūtra states:
"And by means of the oblation and the pressing. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.32)
The eleventh section formulates the problem:

Are the name, the word, and the *vaṣaṭ* call alone the causes for consuming [the Soma], or are the pressing and the oblation also included? Regarding this, let the first view be maintained according to the direction already stated.
"Having pressed [the Soma] in the Havirdhāna shed and having offered it, one should consume it in the Sadas";
because this is heard in the scripture, both of these are causes for consumption, just like the others.
In the case of the formula "May the Hotṛ’s cup go forward," the designation (samākhyā) is the cause for consumption.

If it is argued that, because the statement regarding the *hāriyojana* cup says, "The first draught belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*," and thus the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance [is mentioned], there are therefore only three causes for the drinking; [we reply:]...
Not so;

for it is heard in scripture: "Having pressed [the soma] with stones in the two *havirdhāna* sheds, having offered it in the *āhavanīya*, and having gone westward, they consume the portions in the *sadas*.
The pressing takes place in the circle west of the *uttaravedi* and east of the *sadas*.
The oblation is performed on the *uttaravedi* altar;
the consumption [of the remnant] takes place in the *sadas* hall.

In this context, since the pressing and the oblation are already established by other scriptural injunctions and are thus not themselves to be enjoined here, they are restated as the causal conditions (*nimitta*) for the injunction of the consumption.
Therefore, like the name and so forth, these two also possess the status of being causes for consumption.
(Regarding the twelve [sūtras] on the consumption of Soma from the cups by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer and others, Jaimini-sūtras 3.5.33–35:
"Because of the direct instruction regarding the cups, there is no [consumption] from the remnant in the case of the cups.

(Jaimini-sūtra 3.5.33) "Or rather, it should be so because of the existence of a cause; there is no specific designation for the cups, since that [instruction] refers to the agent. (Jaimini-sūtra 3.5.34)
"And because another [act] is seen in the *camasa* cup. (Jaimini 3.5.35).
He formulates the twelfth section as follows:
Regarding the collection of causes, is there an option, an exclusion, or a combination?
Because they are equal, let there be an option; let those that have scope be set aside by the designation.
Nor indeed is the scriptural injunction to be set aside here regarding the consumption [of the Soma] in its various divisions;
since an option between established alternatives is not logical, a combination (*samuccaya*) must therefore be accepted. "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward... [etc.]

In the case of the text "pra brahmaṇaḥ," the designation (*samākhyā*) is the cause for the consumption among those desiring to consume. In the case of "the first consumption belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is the cause for the Hotṛ’s consumption. In the case of "having pressed with the stones in the *havirdhāna* shed and having offered in the *āhavanīya* fire, they consume in the *sadas*," the oblation accompanied by the pressing is the cause for the Adhvaryu’s consumption.
In that regard, the conjunction of the *camasa* and the *vaṣaṭkāra* falls upon the *hotṛ*,
while the conjunction of the *camasa* and the pressing (*abhiṣava*) falls upon the *adhvaryu*.
Since the two reasons possess equal force, there being an option (*vikalpa*), the consumption is performed based on either one of these causes— this is the first position.

The second position is that because the [reasons for] the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and so forth have scope in the case of cups other than the *camasa*, they sublate the designation (*samākhyā*) of "cup-drinker" (*camasin*), which has no such scope; consequently, even the occasional consumption based on the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and so forth does not exist among the *camasins*. [To this, the reply is:
because the sentence beginning with "of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer" is more powerful, its sublation by the designation is not tenable.
If it is argued that this [second means] is also powerful because there is no room for the other,

then, since two distinct means of knowledge have prescribed separate methods of consumption, their combination (samuccaya) must be accepted, rather than an option (vikalpa) as in the case of rice and barley.
In that case, because the visible purpose of preparing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is singular,
whereas here the eating is for the sake of a restricted unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); and that unseen merit is of two kinds, according to the scriptural injunction.
Therefore, there is a combination [of both].

(Thirteenth Section: On the Hotṛ’s First Consumption; Sūtras 36–39) In a single vessel, the Adhvaryu should consume first according to the sequence. (Jaimini 3.5.36) Or rather, the Hotṛ [should consume first] because of the wording of the mantra. (Jaimini 3.5.37)
And because of the scriptural statement;
and because of the sequence of the causes. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.38–39)

He formulates the thirteenth section: Should the Adhvaryu eat from the same vessel as the others who have already drunk? No; because the vessel remains in his hand, he must be the first to consume it. (MJaiNy 3.5.22)
"Protect us as you have protected us before"—by this mantra, priority is established;
for the statement of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer is not overridden by logic.

In a certain case, the consumption [of the soma] by many from a single vessel is prescribed. Regarding that, if it is argued: "The Adhvaryu should consume first, because of his proximity to the vessel."
Not so;
for by means of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is understood that the Hotṛ is the first to consume.

In the mantra, "Like a Hotṛ, as the first, protect us," the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having addressed the Adhvaryu, thus pray: "Just as the Hotṛ, having consumed [the Soma] before us, protected us by the offering of the remainder..."
"In the same way, you too should drink.
This is an indicative mark (liṅga) regarding the Hotṛ's first consumption.
And the scriptural statement (vākya) is thus handed down: "The first consumption belongs to the one who utters the vaṣaṭ-call."
In this case, priority is established because of a specific injunction;
nor can this statement be set aside by mere logic in the form of proximity to the vessel.
Therefore—the Hotṛ should consume first.
(Regarding the fourteenth section, concerning the fact that eating is preceded by permission, the sūtra states: "Eating is permitted because of a specific scriptural statement. (Jaimini 3.5.40)
He formulates the fourteenth topic:
"In this case, the consumption [of Soma] is neither preceded by permission nor followed by it, because of parsimony;
the first [view] is rejected because of the statement that it should not be drunk by one who has not been invited. (MJaiNy 3.5.24)

If it is argued that, because both the permission (*anujñā*) and the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) are to be performed, out of consideration for the weight of the ritual requirements, only the consumption is intended here— this is not so;
for by the scriptural injunction, "Therefore, Soma is not to be drunk by one who has not been invited," the necessity of obtaining permission is established.

(Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.41): In the fifteenth section concerning the request for permission by means of Vedic speech, the sūtra states: "One should request permission with the words 'Thou art invited; invite [me],' because of the indicative mark."
He formulates the fifteenth topic:
Is the permission (anujñā) by means of worldly speech or Vedic speech, whichever may be?
Since there is no distinction [in the rule], it must be Vedic because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of the *upahvāna* mantra. ②—MJaiNy_3,5.25—②
The mantra "Upahūta upahvayasva" (Invoked, do thou invite) enjoins the granting of permission by means of its indicative power (*liṅga*);
therefore, that permission is expressed through Vedic utterance.
(Regarding the sixteenth section, concerning the response by means of a Vedic statement, the sūtra states:
In that case, the response follows from the sense of the matter. Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.42.
The sixth section formulates the following:
"Upahvayasva" and "Upahūta"—this entire formula should apply to both [the acts] of requesting permission and granting permission; or else, it is divided [between them]. (MJaiNy 3.5.26)
If there were no division [of the mantra], and thus the entire [mantra] were [to be used] without distinction, then [the sacrificer] would invoke [the gods] by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*);
likewise, the other [priest] would grant permission when [the sacrificer] has requested permission.

In the mantra "Upahūta upahūyasva" (Invoked, may you be invoked), although the portion ending in the second person singular is recited later, it is capable of effecting the initial request for permission because of its equality with the preceding part.
However, although it is recited first in the nominative singular case, because it is identical to what follows, it is capable of functioning in the subsequent permission;
therefore, it is applied by being distinguished through its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
(Seventeenth [topic]: The section concerning the authorization for those using a single vessel—) Sūtra:
"Because of the commonality of those who use a single vessel. Jaimini 3.5.43.
The seventeenth section formulates the following:
Should the invitation (*upahvāna*) be for all [the priests] without exception, or only for those who share a single vessel?
The first [position] would hold because it is based on an unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*); the latter [position] follows from the superiority of a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭa*). (MJaiNy 3.5.28)
If it is argued that the purpose of seeking permission is invisible (adṛṣṭa) and that this is the same even when using separate bowls, we say no; for a visible purpose does indeed exist.
When a common object is involved, an offense occurs if there is some excess of one's own portion;
therefore, the request for permission to avoid such deficiency or excess applies only to those who share a single vessel.

(Chapter 18: Section on the Existence of the Eater for the Sacrificer Himself; Sūtras 44–45) The eating [of the portion] is removed by the removal of the *yājyā* verse, just like the *pravara*. (Jaimini 3.5.44) Or rather, it belongs to the sacrificer himself, because of the arrival of the cause [for his eating]. (Jaimini 3.5.45)
Because it has already commenced, there is no cessation for the *pravara*; thus concludes the eighteenth section (Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.46).
[The author] formulates the eighteenth section as follows:
When the Hotṛ’s *yājyā* is removed, is there a removal of the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the consumption [of the portion], or rather a mere disappearance? There is no "removal," because they are distinct.
The sacrificer himself must perform the sacrifice; there is no substitution for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
Since the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance follows the *yājyā* verse, the eating [of the oblation] likewise departs together with it.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the sacrifices known as the *ṛtuyāja*, it is traditionally taught: "The *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer; he gives the direction: 'O Hotṛ, recite this *yājyā*!'"

"Or, sitting down himself, he performs the sacrifice. Thus, the *yājyā* verses recited in the *hautra* section are obtained for the Hotṛ by virtue of their designation (*samākhyā*). Among those, a certain *yājyā* is removed from the Hotṛ and prescribed for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Then the sacrificer, according to his own wish, either directs the Hotṛ or recites the *yājyā* himself;
however, in the case of not reciting it, the *yājyā* is removed from the Hotṛ.
However, the *vaṣaṭ*-call and the consumption [of the portion] are not excluded;
for those two are not included within the *yājyā* [verse].
Therefore, when it is established that "the Hotṛ utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call and consumes [the portion],"—
We reply: Since we accept the position that "having sat down himself, he performs the sacrifice," the sacrificer must perform the sacrifice himself.
And that sacrifice is not possible without the *vaṣaṭ* call, because it is prescribed thus: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā*."
If it is argued that "let the sacrificer recite the *yājyā* verse, and let the *hotṛ* priest utter the *vaṣaṭ* call," it is not so.
Because the injunction "he offers without breathing" establishes that the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭ*-call belong to a single agent by prohibiting breath between them,

the *vaṣaṭ*-call passes from the Hotṛ to the sacrificer along with the *yājyā*. Upon its departure, the right to consume [the soma], which is caused by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, also departs from the Hotṛ and settles upon the sacrificer.

(Section on the Fruit-Cup being a Modification of the Sacrifice, Sūtras 47–51) The fruit-cup is an occasional modification of the consumption [of the soma], because of its connection with the scriptural statement.
(Jaimini 3.5.47) Or rather, it is a modification of the sacrifice, because the consecratory rite is for the sake of that [sacrifice]. (Jaimini 3.5.48)
Because of the *homa* [offering];
because of the equality of time with the *camasa* cups;
and because of the observation of an indicative mark.

The nineteenth section (adhikaraṇa) [of the third chapter] is formulated as follows: "The flour of the nyagrodha tree is [substituted] for Soma in the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. (MJaiNy 3.5.31–33).
One may perform the modification for the mere act of eating, or likewise even in the Soma sacrifice.
Having begun with the statement "he should offer for consumption" (bhakṣaṃ yacchet) with the intention of making it an object of consumption,
the modification therefore applies only to the act of consuming.
Because it is heard in scripture that "he should sacrifice with the cup called *phalaka*," there is a modification in the sacrifice;
for the preparation of the portion for consumption is for the purpose of the sacrifice.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "If he should cause a Rājanya or a Vaiśya to sacrifice..."
"If he should wish to partake of Soma, one should fetch fruits from a Nyagrodha tree, grind them, mix them with curd, strain them, and give that to him as his portion,
not the Soma."
*Stibhinyaḥ* means buds.
If it is argued that— since the opening and closing [of the flowers] pertain to the act of eating— the Soma is merely modified by being ground into flour during the entire process of eating—
this is not so.
It is heard in the scripture: "When they offer other cups, then, having taken [a portion] from this [cup] with a young blade of darbha grass, he offers it.
In that context, having accepted the sacrifice as being performed with the aforementioned flour in the form of the fruit-cup (phalacamasa), the quality of the young blade of grass is enjoined.
Furthermore, eating is indeed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of a desired substance,
and that [consecration] is untenable without a sacrifice.
Therefore, there must be a modification (*vikāra*) even regarding the sacrifice.
(Regarding the twentieth section on the Brahmins' approach to the cups of the Kṣatriyas, Sūtras 52–53:
Because of the commonality among those who approach; or rather, because of the equality of the words with "Brahman. Jaimini 3.5.52–53.
In the Rājasūya sacrifice, in one instance, there is a cup for the performer [to drink] from, [filled] by ten people. This constitutes the twenty-third topic (adhikaraṇa).

The author of the Mīmāṃsājaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara formulates the [next] section as follows: "In the Rājasūya, in a certain case, there is a cup for the performer [to drink] from, [filled] by ten people."
In that case, are the Kṣatriyas the ones who eat, or are the Brāhmaṇas the eaters?

O Brahmins, because of the mention of "one hundred and ten" through the counting of the first [cup] as being won by one, and because of the statement "they move toward the cups," it is understood that the royal vessel also belongs to the Brahmins.
In the Rājasūya sacrifice, in the ritual known as the Daśapeya, it is heard in scripture: "Ten persons each move toward a single cup."
In that context, as for the cup belonging to the Kṣatriya sacrificer,
it is to be consumed by those ten Kṣatriyas alone.
Why?

Regarding the word "ten," because the number appears as a single genus (*jāti*), it is as follows: since the *Daśapeya* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the entire collection of archetypal properties (*dharmajāta*) is extended to it by the rule of transfer (*codaka*). And in the archetype, there is no consumption of the sacrificer’s cup (*yajamānacamasa*) by individuals of different castes (*bhinnajāti*).
In this case as well, the same [conclusion] follows:
if "ten" is prescribed here as a specific qualification, then let only the original number of eatings be set aside.
But there is no single caste-hood [among them].

Therefore, when it is argued that "the Kṣatriya sacrificer should consume [the Soma] together with nine other Kṣatriyas," we reply: among the ten persons who approach for the purpose of consuming the cups (camasa) as obtained from the archetype (prakṛti), there are ten.

By means of the distributive repetition "ten," the number ten is prescribed for each cup; having then referred to the number one hundred as established by the sense of the context, the Brāhmaṇa status of all those to be numbered is enjoined in the statement: "Now, a hundred Brāhmaṇas drink."
That being the case, since there is no cup-consumption even for the Kṣatriya sacrificer,
how could other Kṣatriyas consume it?
Therefore, only Brāhmaṇas are the consumers.
Thus ends the fifth pāda of the third adhyāya in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* composed by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the sixth pāda of the third adhyāya.
(In the first [section], concerning the rule that the use of *khadira* wood and so forth in the *sruva* ladles and other implements applies to the archetype, there are sūtras 1–8.)

It serves all purposes, because there is no specific context [restricting it]; or rather, it belongs to the archetype (prakṛti), because it is not mentioned [separately] there; but that [archetypal application] is excluded when there is a direct scriptural injunction.
If it is argued that [the injunction is established] because of its being seen [in the text], [we reply]:
No, because the purpose of the injunction is one and the same. If it is argued that [it is established] because of its origination [as a distinct act], [we reply]: No.

Not so, because of their equality. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.7) But because of the completeness of the purpose of the injunction, and because the primary [meaning] is contradicted, the meaning of the archetype [applies]. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.8) START MJaiNy 3,6.1-2

The first section of the sixth chapter formulates the following problem: Is the injunction "he whose [ladle] is made of *parṇa*-wood" applicable to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), or does it apply to the archetype alone?
It applies to both because of the identical scriptural statement.
The injunction regarding the *parṇa* (palāśa) wood, which depends on the *juhū* ladle, applies only to the archetype (*prakṛti*);
since both [the ladle and the wood] are obtained for the ectype (*vikṛti*) through the extended application (*codaka*), what purpose would there be for an injunction here in the ectype?
An independent statement is heard: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood..."
"He does not hear an evil report.

In this context, based on the *juhū* ladle—which possesses an inseparable connection with the sacrifice—the *parṇa* tree, which is its material cause, is enjoined by the sentence: "That which is a *juhū* is made of *parṇa* wood.
And such a sentence applies equally to both the primary (*prakṛti*) and the modified (*vikṛti*) sacrifices.

Since the *juhū* ladle exists as the substratum in both cases, it follows that this injunction applies to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*). To this, we reply: does this injunction take effect in the modification prior to the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), or after it?
Not the first,
because the juhū, which serves as the substratum, cannot exist without the extended application of the rule (codaka).
In the second case, however, even the quality of being made of parṇa wood is extended by the rule along with the juhū itself.
Furthermore, because an injunction would otherwise be purposeless, this injunction applies to the base material alone.
Thus, the example "for whom the *sruva* ladle is made of *svādu-kāṣṭha* wood" should be cited.

(Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.9: In the section concerning the application of the number seventeen for the *sāmidhenī* verses to the modified sacrifice in the second [topic], the sūtra states: "But because of the specific context, it would be contradictory in the modified sacrifice."
The second section formulates the problem:
Are the seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses for the archetype (*prakṛti*) or for the ectype (*vikṛti*)?
As in the previous case, they belong to the archetype; this [number] is an alternative to the fifteen [verses].

The number seventeen (sāptadaśya) should apply to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti) it is set aside by the force of the ritual procedure (prakriyā), since the expectancy [of the archetype] has been satisfied by the number fifteen (pāñcadaśya). Regarding this, it is heard in a detached injunction (anārabhyādhīta): "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses."

The verses beginning with "pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ," which are for the purpose of kindling the fire, are the *sāmidhenīs*. Their number as seventeen is established by the previous section as belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
If there were an injunction in the archetype stating, "He recites fifteen *sāmidhenīs*," [then the rule would apply].

If it is argued that, in that case, the numbers fifteen and seventeen would have to be treated as optional alternatives, we reply: the number seventeen applies only to the modified sacrifices (vikṛti).
This is because the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti), already constrained by the number fifteen, lacks any further requirement for a numerical specification regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses.

Nor should it be suspected that there is no conflict between the two statements regarding fifteen-foldness (*pāñcadaśya*) and seventeen-foldness (*sāptadaśya*), on the grounds that they possess equal strength;
for in the case of fifteen-foldness, there is the additional support of the *prakaraṇa* (context).
Therefore, seventeen-foldness remains established in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the Mitravindā and the Adhvarakalpa.
And the previous reasoning does not apply here;
for since there is no application of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) regarding the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*), there is no fault in its being prescribed again.
(Regarding the third section, concerning the application of the contingent seventeen-foldness to the archetype, the sūtra states:
But the contingent [element] belongs to the archetype; it is a modification of that, because of a specific connection. Jaimini 3.6.10.
The third section formulates the problem:
"Is the number seventeen for the Vaiśya in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) or in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti)?
If it were as in the previous case, [one might say] no, because of the restriction resulting from the statement of a contingent rule (naimittika) regarding the obligatory (nitya)."
The author of the Bhāṣya cited the rule, "One who desires [cattle] should lead with a milking vessel," and let that also stand, since the underlying logic is the same here.

If it is argued that the seventeen-fold nature prescribed for a Vaiśya by the injunction, "One should recite seventeen for a Vaiśya," belongs to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) according to the previous principle—[we reply: no.
Not so;
for by this occasional statement, the constant fifteen-fold nature inherent in the archetype must be restricted to the scope of those other than Vaiśyas.
The constant [rule] is weaker because it is general in form and because it possesses a wider scope.
However, the occasional (naimittika) rule is stronger due to its specific form and lack of scope for alternative application.
Therefore, the number seventeen (sāptadaśya), occasioned by the Vaiśya, remains established in the archetype (prakṛti).
On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya cited another example: "One should carry water with a wooden cup (camasa); [but] with a milk-pail (godohana) for one who desires cattle."

In this regard, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that because the *camasa* (wooden cup) is already established by its inherent nature (*prakṛti*), the *godohana* (milk-pail) applies only to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the *godohana* applies to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) itself; for the *godohana*, which is occasioned by a specific desire, must restrict the scope of the permanent (*nitya*) *camasa*, which pertains to those without such desires. Thus, the *godohana* is subsumed within the model sacrifice.
(Fourth [topic]: In the section concerning the fact that the *ādhāna* (fire-laying) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *pavamāneṣṭi*s, Sūtras 11–13.

The fire-laying is for the sake of the *iṣṭi*s, because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.11) Or rather, it is not so, because those [iṣṭi*s] have that [fire-laying] as their purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.12)
