"And because of the observation of an indicative mark" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.13). [The author] formulates the fourth section as follows:
The establishment (ādhāna) of the fires may or may not be an auxiliary to the Pavamāna and other sacrifices;
because the fires are subsidiary to the sacrifice, the establishment is an auxiliary to it by way of those fires.
Since there is no injunction that does not have a specific purpose, no subsidiary rite can be established for its own sake;
rather, because they are intended for the fire, the *iṣṭi* is for the sake of the fires, and those fires are those pertaining to the *agnihotra*.
This is recorded in the tradition: "One should offer a cake on eighteen potsherds to Agni Pavamāna..."
"To Agni Pāvaka,
to Agni Śuci," and also: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires."
In this regard, the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) should be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *pavamāna* and other offerings (*iṣṭis*).
Why?

Because, since the fires such as the *āhavanīya*, which are obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*) in the *pavamāna* and other offerings that are modifications (*vikṛtis*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), serve as auxiliaries to those offerings, the establishment of the fires—which consists of their consecration—must also be an auxiliary to them by way of the fires themselves.
If it is argued that this is because [the fire-installation] is unavoidable,
do not say so; for this installation is not recited within the context (prakaraṇa) of any specific sacrifice.
However— since this is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*),
it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to anything;

rather, like the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), because the *iṣṭis* also serve the purpose of consecrating the fire, there is no suspicion of a mutual relationship of principal and auxiliary (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

If it is argued: "Surely, since the Pavamāna offerings lack the status of being subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) [of the Agnyādheya], their purpose would otherwise be futile; therefore, it is logical that they are subsidiary to it by way of the fires (*agni*)," we reply: No.
This is because it is understood from various specific scriptural injunctions (*vākya*) that the consecrated fires are employed in subsequent sacrifices such as the Agnihotra and others.
Therefore, the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not a subsidiary part [of those other rites]. (Mīmāṃsā-Jaiminīya-Nyāya-Mālā-Vistara 3.6.7–8)
(Fifth [section], concerning the topic that the establishment of the sacred fires serves all purposes; Sūtras 14–15):
"It is for the sake of its own archetype, just like other *anārabhyavāda* passages" (Jaimini 3.6.14).
"Or rather, it serves all purposes, because the establishment of the fires has its own specific time" (Jaimini 3.6.15).
Starting with *Mīmāṃsājaiṇī* 3.6.9–10, he formulates the fifth section:
"Is the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*), or is it joined with fire alone?"
This [result] resides in its original state like a leaf, by means of the channel of the consecrated fire.
If it were merely a worldly form, its application in the ritual would be fruitless;
therefore, let the independence of the *parṇa* wood [as a material] apply to the scriptural [acts], such as the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth.

Just as the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood, though taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*) through the mediation of the *juhū* ladle.

If it is argued that, in the same way, the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), which consists of the consecration of the fire-channel (*agni-pranāḍī*), is included in the archetype (*prakṛti*),
this is not so;
for there is a disparity.
For the form of the *juhū* ladle is twofold: worldly (*laukika*) and scriptural (*śāstrīya*).
That which is perceived as being one cubit in length, having a wide mouth, and possessing a hollowed-out surface, and so forth, is the worldly form;
however, the form characterized by its connection to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) is the scriptural form.
For those two, there is no quality of being "unprecedented" (apūrvīyatva) without entry into the ritual (*kratu*).
In that case, if [the injunction] were to terminate merely in a worldly form, then the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood would be fruitless.
For that form can be easily accomplished even by means of other wood;
whereas the *parṇa* [leaf] has entered into the ritual for the sake of being something not previously existing.
However, for the Āhavanīya fire and the others, there is only one scripturally prescribed form.
And that [fire] is produced only by means of the formal installation (*ādhāna*), not otherwise.
Therefore, since the installation is capable of producing the Vedic forms such as the *āhavanīya* fire even without entering into the ritual (*kratu*), it is connected with the *Agnihotra*.
This being the case, because of the difference from the *parṇa*-leaf rule, it does not enter into the archetype (*prakṛti*) but, having produced the fires, remains independent like the ritual itself.

Therefore, just as gold, rice, and so forth are produced by worldly means, let the Āhavanīya and other fires—produced by the act of *ādhāna* and being independent in themselves—be subsequently assigned to sacrifices by means of scriptural injunctions.
(Regarding the sixth section on the performance of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis in a fire that has not been consecrated, Sūtras 16–17:
"For those [iṣṭis], the fire should come from the archetype, just like the *prayāja* offerings. (Jaimini 3.6.16)
"Or rather, they [the mantras] do not [apply], because they have that as their purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.17). He formulates the sixth section as follows:
When the fire has been consecrated by the Pavamāneṣṭi, the subsequent sacrifices (iṣṭis) are not to be performed with that very same fire;
rather, they should be performed in a fire consecrated by those [Pavamāneṣṭis], in accordance with the requirements of the extended injunction (codaka).
The challenger is not able to establish that [the Pavamāna-iṣṭis] in the Pavamāna-iṣṭi,

because the iṣṭis are neither subsidiary parts nor are they established, since the sacrifice would be performed upon a fire that has not been consecrated. The Āhavanīya and other fires are consecrated by means of the Pavamāna and other iṣṭis.
The Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other sacrifices proceed in fires that have been consecrated by refinement (*saṃskṛta*).
This being the case— the disputed Pavamāna-iṣṭis must be performed in a fire refined by those very iṣṭis,
because they are iṣṭis.
It is like other sacrifices;
the injunction also functions in this way,
and thus it becomes supported.
When the fire has been consecrated by these *iṣṭi*s, [the view is that] the primary rite (*prakṛti*) should be performed— this being the position reached—
we reply: although the *pavamāneṣṭi* is a modified rite (*vikṛti*),
nevertheless the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is not capable of transferring another *pavamāneṣṭi* into this *pavamāneṣṭi*.

Because, like the *prayāja* offerings and others, the *pavamāneṣṭi* lacks the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, if one were to accept another *pavamāneṣṭi* for the sake of accomplishing the consecrated fire (*saṃskṛtāgni*) for this *pavamāneṣṭi*, then for that [second] one as well, the same would apply; thus, in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the sacrifice itself could not be accomplished.
Therefore, the *pavamāneṣṭis* must be performed in a fire that has not been consecrated by those [other] sacrifices. (MJaiNyC 3.6.11–12)
(Seventh [section]: On the topic that the *upākaraṇa* and other rites belong to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, Sūtras 18–27.

The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice applies equally to all [three], because there is no distinction in the context. (Jaimini 3.6.18) And because of its position, it belongs to the first [sacrifice]. (Jaimini 3.6.19)

"But for some, the prior mention there is for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa). If it is argued that, therefore, it is an injunction of time for what has been displaced [from its original context], we say no, because it is a partial statement. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.20–22)

If it is argued that [the order] is determined by the purpose (*artha*), [we reply]: No, because that would contradict the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Rather, it is due to the position (*sthāna*); for the preceding preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is intended for that very purpose.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) [Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.26];
or rather, it is not an injunction, because it serves the purpose of a subordinate element (guṇa) [Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.27].
The seventh section formulates the problem:
In the case of the Agniṣomīya, Savanīya, and Anubandhya animals, are these primary rites—the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) and so forth—common to all, or not? 3.6.13.

Because they are recited within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, these animal-ritual details are common [to all its parts]; yet, since the Soma sacrifice does not involve the seizing of an animal, those details would be purposeless [if applied there]. (MJaiNy 3.6.14)
The fact that those [details] possess the characteristics of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is established by their position;
they are obtained for the other two animals through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
— The Agniṣomīya.
The Savanīya,
the Anūbandhya, and [the Āgneya]— these three animals are recited in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
And the animal rites, such as the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) and *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), are prescribed therein.
The touching of the animal with the two verses beginning with "Born from Prajāpati" and "This animal" constitutes the *upākaraṇa*.
Circumambulating [the animal] three times to the right with a blaze of *darbha* grass is the *paryagnikaraṇa*.
These very dharmas are prescribed as common to all three animals, because they are equally recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma for all three.
Now, one might object: "The Jyotiṣṭoma itself will take up these dharmas that are recited in its own context."
If it is argued that [the animals] are not [sacrificial victims], we say no;
for that [rite] is a Soma sacrifice,
and the Soma indeed requires ritual acts such as pressing and so forth.
But this does not apply to the acts of erecting the sacrificial post, tying the animal, slaughtering it, and so forth.

Therefore, when it is argued that—since these acts are purposeless with respect to the whole (the sacrifice)—they enter into the parts and thus apply without distinction to all three types of animals—we reply:
there is a distinction here characterized by proximity.
These ritual rules are prescribed for the day called Aupavasathya, which precedes the day named Sautya, following the construction of the Dhiṣṇya altars.

That same location applies to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice as well. However, the Savanīya is mentioned on the Sautya day itself: "Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted cord, he dedicates the Agneya Savanīya animal."

The *anubandhya* (the animal to be bound at the end) is prescribed at the conclusion of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). Therefore, by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), those ritual details (*dharma*) are connected to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice;
however, they are extended to both the *savanīya* and the *anubandhya* sacrifices through the force of the general rule (*codaka*).
(Regarding the eighth section, concerning the fact that the acts such as fetching the branch are properties common to both milkings, Sūtras 28–29:
Because of the difference in time between the two milkings, the boiled milk (*śṛta*) would be unconnected [to the specific milking]. Jaimini 3.6.28.
Or rather, because of the division of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the scriptural injunction regarding the time applies only to that which is connected [to the specific milking]. Jaimini 3.6.29.
The eighteenth section (adhikaraṇa) of the Mīmāṃsājaiminīyasūtravṛtti (MJaiNy) 3.6.16–17 formulates [the following]:
"The ritual acts such as cutting the branch are established as duties (dharma) pertaining to the milking in the evening."
And whether they exist in the morning or in the evening, they remain in their respective places as before.
The objection regarding futility does not exist here as it did previously;
therefore, by virtue of the stronger context (*prakaraṇa*), those [subsidiary elements] apply even to the morning milking (*prātardoha*).
—In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice: the cutting of the *palāśa* branch...
With that branch, the driving away of the calves and other such *dohada* rites are prescribed;
and two milkings are known to exist: one milking on the night of the new moon.
If it is argued that on the first lunar day (pratipad), there is another milking in the morning,
and that by the same principle as before, those properties heard first are restricted to the initial evening milking—
this is not so.
Because of the difference [in context].
For in the previous case, regarding the Soma sacrifice, the context was obstructed by the pointlessness [of the injunction] due to the non-connection with ritual details such as immolation;
here, however, there is no obstruction by pointlessness.
Therefore, since the context (prakaraṇa) sets aside the specific location (sthāna), those properties should be understood as applying to both milkings.

(Regarding the ninth section on the fact that the rites beginning with the placing [of the cups] belong to the nature of all three pressings, the sūtra states: "In the same manner, there is the scriptural injunction for the cups in another pressing.
Jaimini 3.6.30.
The ninth section formulates the following:
"The duties pertaining to the cups (graha), such as the placing [of the vessels], belong to the morning pressing alone;
or rather, they belong to all three pressings because their place is fixed. The first view is as before; the latter is the correct one."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are the Aindravāyava and other cups at the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana),
the Marutvatīya and others at the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana),
and the Āditya and others at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana).

In that context, the ritual acts such as the placing and the wiping are prescribed in proximity to the morning-pressing cups (*prātaḥsavanīya-graha*): "The other cups are placed on the smeared [spot],
but the *dhruva* cup is not smeared," and "He wipes the cup with the fringed filter (*daśāpavitra*)."
For the planets other than Dhruva, one should place them there after first spreading a layer of earth beneath;
however, for Dhruva, it is not so.
In the preceding section, the acts such as bringing the grass-bundle were taught as being subsidiary to the two principal substances, curd and milk.

If it is argued: "And since that curd cannot be accomplished without the evening milking of the previous day, the cow is milked in the evening solely for the sake of accomplishing that [curd]; however, because the evening milking has its own unique characteristics, there is no recitation of [those] characteristics together with [the morning ones] in a single location, and thus their position is not fixed. But here, their position is indeed fixed; therefore, those characteristics belong to the morning pressing alone."
Not so;

for it is understood from the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that the acts of seating and so forth are properties of the cups (*graha*), while from the context (*prakaraṇa*) they are understood to be properties of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

Even though a specific location for it has been determined, that is set aside by the force of the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), and thus the acts of placing and so forth are established as occurring at all three pressings (*savana*).

(Regarding the tenth section [Adhikaraṇa], which establishes that the threefold nature of the rope and other such qualities are properties common to all animals, the Sūtra states: "And the rope [is for all], because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini 3.6.31).
He formulates the tenth section as follows:
The acts such as the girding with the rope (*raśanā*) and so forth are performed either in one place alone or everywhere.
These belong specifically to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice; the latter view is established by sequence, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and other criteria.

In the proximity of the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, certain ritual properties are prescribed, such as the encircling of the sacrificial post with a rope, the threefold nature of that rope, and its being made of darbha grass; thus it is stated: "He encircles [the post]."
"The cord is indeed strength," "It has three strands," and "It is made of darbha grass."

In this regard, if it is argued that this girdle and those items such as the wrappings and so forth should all belong to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice alone, on account of proximity (saṃnidhi) and the intermediate context (avāntaraprakaraṇa);
Not so;
for its existence is understood even in the case of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice through an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The indicative mark is the statement, "Having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-wound [rope], he dedicates the *āgneya* *savanīya* animal," which is an explanatory reference (*anuvāda*) to the tripling and the encircling as already established.
Furthermore, by virtue of the instrumental case-ending and the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*) is a property of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),
not a property of the animal (*paśu*);
and the sacrificial post is common (*tantra*) to the three animals.
Thus it will be stated.
Therefore, these properties should apply to all sacrificial animals.
(Eleventh [Adhikaraṇa], Sūtras 32–34: On the fact that even the Aṃśu and Adābhya vessels possess ritual properties such as being set down, etc.
Sūtra 32: That which is enjoined at a distance is not connected with the others because of its proximity [to the primary act].
Sūtra 33: Or rather, it is connected, because the subsidiary is for the sake of that [primary], and because the subsidiary is caused by that [primary].
One should determine [the rule] from the specific instruction. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.34).
The eleventh section (adhikaraṇa) formulates as follows:
The properties of the cups (*grahadharma*) are indeed mentioned without reference to a specific context by means of the two [cups], the *Aṃśu* and the *Ādābhya*.
[The question is] whether they exist due to the general context (*prakaraṇa*) or the first [option], or whether here the latter [is correct] due to the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Without reference to a specific context, two cups are heard: "He takes the *Aṃśu*," and... [etc.]
And there is the statement: "He draws the Adābhya.
For those two [vessels], the duties pertaining to the cups (grahadharmas), such as placing them down and wiping them, do not exist.
Why?
If it is argued that [the details] are restricted by the context (prakaraṇa) precisely to the cups dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others because they were studied starting from those very points—
this is not so;
for by the sentence "The cups are set down" (grahāḥ sādyante), their status as properties of the cups (grahadharma) is understood, and thus those two cups also cannot be excluded.
Furthermore, the offerings to Indra-Vāyu and the others are not the possessors of the context;
for it is the Jyotiṣṭoma that possesses the context.
Therefore, those two [offerings] have their own respective shares.
(Regarding the twelfth section [of the third chapter], the adhikaraṇa on the subsidiary nature of the *citriṇī* and other bricks to the fire-altar, the sūtra states:
"In the absence of a specific context, it is a subsidiary to the fire-altar, just like that. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.35)
He formulates the twelfth topic:

"The properties of the bricks, such as being unbroken and so forth, are not appropriate for the *citriṇī* and other [bricks], or are they? Since there is also a statement made here outside of a specific context (*anārabhyokta*), therefore they do not apply. (MJaiNy 3.6.20)

Even from such a sentence, because of its connection with the primary *apūrva*, those qualities such as indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) exist in the case of the *agnicayana* bricks like the *citriṇī*s and others. [MJaiNy 3.6.21] — It is heard in a non-contextual (*anārabhya*) passage: "He lays down the *citriṇī* bricks."
In the section concerning the fire-altar (agniprakaraṇa), the properties of the bricks are heard in the injunction: "One should make them unbroken and not black.

In the preceding case [of the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups], although the originative injunctions for the Aṃśu and Adābhya are taught outside of any specific context (anārabhyādhīta), the applicatory injunction is taught within the context (prakaraṇādhīta).
However, for the specific types of bricks named Citriṇī and so forth, even the applicatory injunction is taught outside of any specific context.
And that [text] assigns those bricks containing various colors (*citriṇī*) to other altars (*citi*).
However, attributes such as "unbrokenness" (*akhaṇḍatva*) are prescribed among the six altars specifically in the first altar.
Therefore, since they are not appropriate for the bricks containing various colors and so forth—this being the position reached—[the following is stated].

We reply: Even though neither the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*) nor the applicatory injunction (*viniyojaka-vākya*) is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*), nevertheless, because the phrase "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar" refers to the previously introduced *agni-apūrva*, the *citriṇī* bricks and others are applied—by means of that very connection—to it even by a sentence not recited within the context; and these are the properties of the bricks which serve as the instruments for the *agni*.
But these are not the properties of the first layer;
therefore, they exist even in the bricks such as the *citriṇī*, which serve as means for accomplishing the fire-altar.
(Thirteenth [adhikaraṇa]: On the point that the acts such as pressing belong to the Soma alone; the sūtra:
"The occasional [rite] should have a different injunction because it is not equal [to the regular rite].
Jaimini 3.6.36.

He formulates the thirteenth section: "Are the injunctions for pressing and so forth applicable to the cup designated as the result, or not? Since the occasional rite is equal to the obligatory one, there is an injunction for it. (MJaiNy 3.6.22)

Since the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have already achieved their purpose in the permanent [sacrifice], they need not be performed again when [the rite] arises due to a subsequent occasion; rather, they should be obtained there by way of extension (*atideśa*). A *phalacamasa* is that in which the ground of the fruit, shaped like a banyan bud, is chewed.
And that [sacrifice] is occasional (naimittika),
because it is prescribed contingent upon a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya;
Soma, however, is obligatory (nitya).
This is because [the rule] "one should sacrifice with soma" is enjoined independently of even the sequence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
Just as that eternal *soma* possesses the status of being a means for the sacrifice, so too does the *phalacamasa* possess that same status.

Therefore, since injunctions such as "he presses the Soma" and "he buys the Soma," which are rules for the consecration of the sacrificial substance, apply to the *phalacamas* just as they do to the Soma—this being the prima facie view—we reply: the constant consecrations, such as heating (*abhivāsa*), having fulfilled their purpose by consecrating the constant Soma, do not require another object of consecration.
However, the *phalacamas*, being a modification of Soma, occurs later.
Consequently, the ritual procedures (*saṃskāra*) do not apply there, as they are independent [of those specific details];
yet, this does not imply an absence of *saṃskāras*,
for they are established there by means of the general injunction (*codaka*).
Therefore, the injunctions pertain exclusively to the Soma.
(Section 14: On the Performance of Primary Ritual Duties Even with Substitutes;
Sūtras 37–39) And the substitute is like that [the original].
(Jaimini 3.6.37) Because it is like that, due to the identity of the purpose. (Jaimini 3.6.38)
And because it does not possess the characteristics of the Śāstra. [Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.39] The fourteenth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:

The rule regarding a substitute such as *nīvāra* rice is either unequal or equal; it is unequal as before, yet there is equality because of the similarity in form, since it possesses the nature of *vrīhi*. Regarding this: it will be stated that when *vrīhi* grains, which are prescribed by the injunction "one should sacrifice with *vrīhi*," are unavailable, *nīvāra* rice must be accepted as a substitute. However, the question arises whether this rule for a substitute is dissimilar to the original injunction or similar to it. It is dissimilar because the substitute is not the very substance (*dravya*) prescribed by the primary injunction; nevertheless, there is equality because of the similarity in appearance, insofar as the substitute possesses the generic character (*jāti*) of being a grain suitable for sacrifice. Thus, the rule for the substitute is both unequal and equal.

If it is argued that, according to the previous principle, injunctions such as threshing, having fulfilled their purpose with respect to *vrīhi* rice, do not subsequently apply to *nīvāra* and other grains that appear later—
this is not so;
for the word *vrīhi* denotes a substance endowed with a specific genus or a specific form.

Even though *nīvāra* grains do not possess the status of being the referent of the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) by way of their genus (*jāti*), the injunction "one threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) still applies because they possess the form of rice.

Just as the injunction applies even to grains that lack substance due to damage by water, fire, or other factors—even when excellent rice of the same genus is unavailable—so too may the injunction apply to *nīvāra* grains that lack the [specific] genus, since they constitute a part of the primary [referent]. (MJaiNyC 3.6.24)
(Regarding the fifteenth section, concerning the performance of the primary ritual characteristics even when substitutes are employed, the sūtra states:
"The scriptural mention of qualities is for the purpose of restriction. (Jaimini 3.6.40)
He formulates the fifteenth section:
"Is the pressing of *pūtīka* plants unequal or equal [to the Soma-pressing]?
It is not equal because it is contingent; it is equal because it serves as a substitute. (MJaiNy 3.6.25)
It is heard in scripture: "If one should not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants.

In that case, since the Pūtīka stalk fragments are enjoined by taking the absence of Soma as the occasion (nimitta), the injunctions regarding the pressing and purchase of Soma are not equivalent [to those for the Pūtīkas], because they are occasional (naimittika) in nature, like the fruit-cup (phalacamasa).
Not so;
for it serves as a substitute, like wild rice (*nīvāra*).
But surely, if it is a substitute, since it is desired by its own nature, no injunction would be required?
If it is argued that for this very reason no injunction is heard regarding wild rice (*nīvāra*), we say no;
for it will be stated in the sixth [book] that the purpose of an injunction is restrictive (*niyama*).
Therefore, the injunctions concerning pressing and purchasing apply equally to both *soma* and *pūtīka*.
(Regarding the section on the subsidiary status of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites to the *agniṣṭoma* in the sixteenth [chapter], Sūtras 41–47:
"But the *saṃsthās* are governed by the same injunctions, because there is no distinction in their context" (Jaimini 3.6.41).
"And the designation is likewise equal" (Jaimini 3.6.42).
But the modifications [occur] when there is a connection with desire, because of the constancy and equality [of the original].
(Jaimini 3.6.43) Or rather, they will belong to the archetype because of the double mention. (Jaimini 3.6.44) But there is a combination because of the explicit statement. (Jaimini 3.6.45)
And because of the prohibition of the previous marks;
[Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.46]. The designation of one [deity] is due to a specific quality; [Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.47].
The sixteenth section (adhikaraṇa) formulates the following:
In the Ukthya and other sacrifices, is the injunction for the constituent parts such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā equal [to that of the Jyotiṣṭoma], or not?
Because they belong to the same context (prakaraṇa) and possess fruit, there is equality. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 3.6.26)
The Ukthya and other sacrifices are modifications (*vikāra*) due to their connection with specific desires; therefore, their procedure (*prakriyā*) follows from that.
Their injunction applies both to the Jyotiṣṭoma in its entirety and specifically to that which consists of the Agniṣṭoma.
The Jyotiṣṭoma, though itself one, is differentiated by the differences in its concluding rites (*samāpti*).

When completed with the *yajñāyajñiya* hymn, it is called the *agniṣṭoma*; after that hymn, when completed with the *ukthya* hymn, it is called the *ukthya*. The same applies to the *ṣoḍaśin* and the others.
In the context of such a Jyotiṣṭoma, which possesses seven terminuses (saṃsthās), the injunctions for its constituent parts— such as the Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi, the Prāyaṇīyeṣṭi, and others— are recorded.
And just as that injunction applies to the Agniṣṭoma, which is the first specific terminus of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it applies in exactly the same way to the Ukthya and the other terminuses as well.
Why?
Because the connection with the context is the same.
Furthermore, just as the Agniṣṭoma, being the primary fruit, is connected with the injunctions for its subsidiaries, [so too is this case].
The same applies to the Ukthya and the other forms as well.

Their results are likewise recorded in scripture: "One desiring cattle should take the Ukthya," "One desiring vigor should praise with the Ṣoḍaśin," and "One desiring progeny should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Atirātra.
Therefore, since the injunction regarding the auxiliary parts is common to all seven forms (saṃsthās), this being the position reached—
We reply: as for this result that has been cited for the Ukthya and other rites, it indicates their status as modifications (*vikāra*).

According to the maxim, "A desired quality (*guṇa*) being heard in scripture enters by modifying the permanent element," just as the quality of using the *godohana* vessel enters by modifying the constant water-carrying performed with the *camasa* vessel.
Thus, the *ukthya* quality, by modifying the constant *agniṣṭoma* termination, brings about the state of being another termination.

Therefore, the *ukthya* and other qualities are modifications of the *agniṣṭoma*; consequently, the context (*prakaraṇa*) does not pertain to all terminations in common, but rather belongs exclusively to the *agniṣṭoma*.

If it is argued that— since it has been stated, "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"— this is the context (prakaraṇa) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and not of the Agniṣṭoma termination (saṃsthā), we reply: certainly so.
The Jyotiṣṭoma never deviates from being an Agniṣṭoma,
because the Ukthya and other forms are also included within the Agniṣṭoma;
however, it does deviate from being an Ukthya and so forth.
Even without those [sacrificial sessions], the Jyotiṣṭoma can exist as the Agniṣṭoma;
therefore, this context belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma in its Agniṣṭoma form, and thus it establishes the injunctions for the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other subsidiaries therein.
In the Ukthya and other forms, the subsidiaries are extended by means of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
Thus ends the sixth quarter of the third chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* composed by the venerable Mādhava.
Now begins the seventh quarter of the third chapter.

(In the first section [of this quarter], concerning the status of the *barhis* grass and other elements as belonging to both the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and their subsidiaries, there are Sūtras 1–5.)
Jaimini 3.7.1: Due to the distinction of context, it is not connected with the primary sacrifice.
Jaimini 3.7.2: Or rather, it belongs to all [the subsidiaries], because being a subsidiary is not prompted by that [context].
Jaimini 3.7.3: If it is argued that it applies even from afar.
"For that sentence [is not for that purpose], because it has that as its meaning" (Jaimini 3.7.4);
"and because of the observation of an indicative mark" (Jaimini 3.7.5).
He formulates the first section of the seventh pāda as follows:
MJaiNy 3.7.1–2:
Whether the altar and so forth are subsidiary parts of the primary sacrifice (*mukhya*) or even of the *prayāja* offerings and other subsidiaries,
that scriptural statement (*vākya*), when joined with the context (*prakriyā*), is the indicator of their status as subsidiary parts of the primary sacrifice.
Even though the altar (*vedi*) and so forth are primary elements, they possess the status of being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *prayāja* offerings and the like;
for the *prayāja* and other such rites exist for the sake of the primary, and because [the altar] is separated from its own *apūrva* by the intervention of those [subsidiary rites].

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He places the sacrificial oblations on the altar" and "He places the sacrificial oblations on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)."
Likewise, its constituent elements (dharmas) are heard in such [injunctions] as "he digs the altar" and "he cuts the sacrificial grass," and so forth.
The primary oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are the *puroḍāśa* for Agni and others; the secondary oblations, however, are those intended for the *prayāja* offerings and the like.

In this regard, if it is argued that the altar (*vedi*) and so forth, accompanied by their respective properties, are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) specifically to the principal oblations (*mukhya-havis*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), based on the statement "He places the oblations on the altar," and thus they are subsidiary to all oblations—
[we reply] that the sentence must be restricted by the context.
For if the sentence were independent, without dependence on the context, [it would follow that the altar is subsidiary to everything].

In that case, since the sacrifice would not exist if it were to terminate merely with the placing [of the offering] on the altar, it would be purposeless; furthermore, this act of placing on the altar would undesirably apply even to the *haviḥ* offerings belonging to the Soma sacrifice.
Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that the altar and so forth are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the primary *haviḥ*—

We reply: Let it be that the altar (*vedi*) and other such items are subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the oblations (*havis*) which serve as the means for accomplishing the primary *apūrva*, thereby avoiding both futility and over-extension.

Since the oblations of the *prayāja* offerings and others are themselves means for accomplishing the primary *apūrva* by way of their own intermediate *apūrvas*, it is likewise logical that the altar and other items are subsidiary to them as well.
This being the case, there will be no excessive restriction of the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
(Regarding the second section, concerning the fact that the consecrations of the master are for the sake of the principal rite, the sūtra states:
"But because of the connection with the fruit, that which is connected to the master is for the sake of the principal rite. (Jaimini 3.7.6).
The second section is formulated as follows:
Does the benefit [arising from] acts such as shaving pertain to both the principal and the subsidiary [acts], or only to the principal?
Let it pertain to both, because [the benefit] resides in the entirety of the agent.
The scriptural consecration is connected with the primary agent who enjoys the fruit;
even in the absence of such consecration, agency is observed [in others], yet that [consecration] does not exist in him.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, consecrations for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—such as the shaving of hair and beard, the vow of drinking milk, and so forth—are prescribed.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the offering of oblations with Soma by means of the cups (grahas) is the primary element,
while the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma and so forth are auxiliary elements.
In this context, these acts such as shaving (vapanādi) serve to benefit both the primary and the auxiliary elements.
Why?
Because it is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*).
For the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is consecrated by acts such as shaving, by virtue of being the agent.

If it is argued that just as its agency exists primarily with respect to the principal act, so too does it exist with respect to the subsidiary act, and therefore there is benefit for both; [we reply: no.
Not so;
for there are two aspects of the sacrificer: his being the agent of the ritual action and his being the enjoyer of the fruit.
In those two cases, the enjoyment of the fruit is unseen,
while the accomplishment of the action is seen.

This being so, since the benefit produced by acts such as sowing is also unseen, sowing and the like ultimately result in being directly instrumental in the means for the enjoyer’s experience of the fruit.
It is observed that ritual actions are being accomplished even by officiating priests who lack purificatory rites such as tonsure, as well as by farmers and others;
therefore, in those cases, the assistance produced by such rites as tonsure does not exist in the form of agency.
Consequently, for this sacrificer who is to enjoy the unseen fruit, that scriptural purificatory rite which is of an unseen nature is applicable to the primary action, not to the subsidiary parts.
In this case, there is no sentence as in the previous instance,
by which one might suspect that acts such as shaving (vapanādi) provide assistance toward the subsidiary elements that accomplish the successive results;
rather, the context (prakaraṇa) pertains only to the primary [sacrifice].
But not of the subsidiaries;
therefore, there is no benefit for them in those [cases].

(Regarding the third section, concerning the fact that the sacrificial altar and other elements of the Soma sacrifice serve as subsidiaries to both the primary and the auxiliary rites; Sūtras 7 and 9:

"And because of the connection with the desire to perform [the rite]. (Jaimini 3.7.7) "But since the scriptural statement of the fruit is connected to that [desire], therefore there should be a desire to perform it in its entirety. (Jaimini 3.7.9)
START MJaiNy 3.7.5-6: The third section formulates the problem as follows:
Is the sacrificial altar used at the Soma sacrifice intended for the primary purpose alone, or does it serve both purposes, or is it restricted to the primary one?
Because that which is intended to be performed is primary, and because its performance is possible through the altar (vedi).

Because it is the cause of the primary excellence and because it is intended as a constituent part (*aṅga*) [of the sacrifice], it is like the primary act; therefore, that altar (*vedi*) is beneficial even for the constituent parts (*aṅgas*).
Having included the altar of the New Moon sacrifice within its center, the *prācīnavaṃśa* pavilion is situated.
Then, in the eastern direction, there is a specific area of ground sufficient for the *sadas*, the *havirdhāna*, and so forth;
together with those [structures] beginning with the *sadas*, it is called the *saumikī vedī* (the Soma-altar).
This indeed provides assistance specifically to the principal Soma sacrifice.
But it does not apply to the non-primary subsidiaries, such as the Agniṣomīya and others. Why? Because the primary [sacrifice] alone is intended to be performed.
Nor should it be said that "the constituent parts (aṅgas) are also intended to be performed," because the very nature of the intention to perform them is already expressed by the Veda itself.
Thus it is heard: "The [altar] is thirty-six steps long toward the east."
"It is twenty-four finger-breadths in length at the front and thirty at the back; we shall be able to manage with this much."

The meaning of this is as follows: having determined, "On a portion of ground measured by this length being heard and by these two transverse measurements, we shall be able to perform the Soma sacrifice which is the cause of the fruit," one should act accordingly;
this very desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) has the primary object [of the sacrifice] as its domain.

Because of the presentation of both the measurement and the capacity with the words "we shall be able in this much space," that presentation would be useless in the case of the subsidiary animal sacrifices and the *iṣṭis*, since they can be performed even without the aforementioned measurement as they do not require structures such as the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds;
however, the performance of the *Soma* sacrifice is possible only on the altar (*vedi*) as described.
It is not otherwise.
Therefore, when it is argued that "that altar serves only the primary [sacrifice]," we reply:
in the statement "we shall be able in this much," the capacity for the performance of both the subsidiaries and the primary is expressed.
Because such [an action] alone is a complete cause for the fruit;
therefore, since the desire to perform (*cikīrṣā*) is equal for both primary subsidiaries, the altar serves the purpose of both.
Nor should it be suspected here that there is a similarity to the acts of sowing and so forth.
Because it was stated there that there is an absence of visible utility [in that case],

whereas here, however, there is a visible utility beginning with the placing of the oblation; and since that utility is equal for both the primary and the subsidiary acts, it serves the purpose of both.
(Section 8/10: On the fourth [topic], that the *anumantraṇa* is an auxiliary to both the subsidiary and the principal acts.
By virtue of being so designated; because it designates a quality (*guṇa*), the designation applies to all [acts]. Jaimini 3.7.8–10.
In the third chapter, seventh section, verses 7–8, the fourth topic is formulated as follows:
"One should touch the *paurṇamāsī* [offering] with the *caturhotṛ* formula during the touching of the clarified butter and other materials."
The mantra is primary even when it is a subordinate part [of a rite], because there is a word denoting it as primary.

Because the word denotes the object (*karman*), and because touching is excluded therein, the mantra—due to the change of case ending—applies to both the primary subsidiary and the oblation. In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One should touch the full moon sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* [formula]."
"By means of the Pañcahotṛ [offering] one should offer in this [earth]," it is said.
The mantra beginning with "The earth is the Hotṛ" is the Caturhotṛ;
for in that mantra, four constituent elements of the sacrifice are mentioned.
Alternatively, a certain person who had become one with that mantra through identification was addressed by Prajāpati as "Caturhūta" and gave an answer; thus, that person is called Caturhūta.
By virtue of his name, the mantra itself is also called "Caturhūta.
With the intention that "it is improper to mention the actual names of those worthy of worship," the word *hotṛ* is used in place of the word *hūta*.
This entire matter is heard in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa: "He addressed himself, saying, 'O Self, O Self! To him, the Fourfold Invocation (caturhūta) replied."
He became the Caturhūta;
indeed, this one is named Caturhūta.
Although he is the Caturhūta, they call him "Caturhotṛ" by way of indirect designation.
"For the gods, as it were, delight in what is out of sight.
The mantra beginning with "Agni is the Hotṛ" is the Pañcahotṛ;
in that case as well, the aforementioned method is to be understood.
In this regard, it is argued that the mantra intended for the touching of the sacrificial oblations such as clarified butter (*ājya*) applies only to the primary oblation,
because the terms *paurṇamāsī* (Full Moon) and *amāvāsyā* (New Moon) refer specifically to the primary oblations; such being the prima facie view—
We reply: the words *paurṇamāsī* and *āmāvāsya* denote rituals (*karman*), not sacrificial oblations (*havis*).
Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be a touching (*upasparśana*) of two rituals.
Now, if— due to a shift in case endings— the sense of the locative were explained as expressing time,
then, since the connection with time would be equally primary for both [the *mukhya* and the *aṅga*], the mantra would be employed in the touching of both kinds of oblations.
(Regarding the fifth section [of the third book], concerning the fact that initiation and sacrificial fees serve the purpose of the primary sacrifice, the two sūtras state:
"But initiation and the sacrificial fee belong to the primary sacrifice because of a direct scriptural statement" (Jaimini 3.7.11).
"And because the cessation [of certain rites] is observed" (Jaimini 3.7.12).
Starting with *Mīmāṃsājaiṇī* 3.7.9–10, the fifth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"The initiation by means of the staff (*daṇḍadīkṣā*) consists of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of one hundred and twelve [cows]."
Or rather, it is for the sake of both meanings, because the statement "of the Soma" is possible in its primary sense.
"It does not pertain to the two primary components; thus, it is not a mockery of the traditional sequence. Therefore, this statement is established as referring to the principal matter.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, initiation and sacrificial fees are prescribed: "He initiates with a staff," and so forth.
And there is the statement: "Its sacrificial fee consists of twelve hundred.
In that context, the initiation (dīkṣā) assists both the primary [sacrifice] and its subsidiary parts;
likewise, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) does as well.

Nor should it be argued that in the sentence "The initiation belongs to Soma, the sacrificial fee belongs to Soma," the genitive case indicates only a primary relationship and not a subsidiary relationship.
The initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) are directly connected with the Soma sacrifice alone;
that Soma, in turn, is connected with the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*). Thus, by way of this succession, there is also a connection between the initiation and the sacrificial fee and the auxiliary rites.
Therefore, since the initiation and so forth serve both purposes, [this is] the position reached.
We reply: the meaning expressed by the genitive case is indeed an immediate relation;
however, when that is impossible, a mediated relation is somehow accepted. But in this case, since that [immediate relation] is possible, a mediated one is not appropriate.
Therefore, initiation and the like are for the sake of the principal [sacrifice].
(On the sixth [topic]—the section concerning the altar not being an auxiliary to the sacrificial post, Sūtras 13–14):

Likewise, the altar belongs to the sacrificial post; or rather, it is merely a location, because it forms a single syntactical unit with that which is taught [as the primary element]. Jaimini 3.7.13–14.
In the sixth section, beginning with *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 3.7.11–12, [the author] formulates the problem:
"Does one erect half [of the sacrificial post] within the altar as a constituent part of the post, or should it serve merely as a mark?"
In this context, a portion of the altar is enjoined as the location by virtue of being an auxiliary to the sacrificial post.
In the injunction of that [measure], the sentence "half outside the altar" would be split;
rather, in this context, the extent of the space for the being-measured sacrificial post (yūpa) is indicated.
Regarding the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, having introduced the topic with "he erects the sacrificial post," it is heard: "He erects half within the altar..."
Regarding the statement "half outside the altar" (*ardhaṃ bahirvedi*):

if one desires to know what extent of width is required for the pit (*avaṭa*) to establish the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), then, in order to determine that, the thickness of the base of the post must be measured with the fingers and so forth.
If it is argued that the portion of that being-measured post which lies within the altar is prescribed as the part to be adorned (*alaṅga*).
Not so;

just as the prepared inner portion is enjoined by the sentence "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*), in the same way, the prepared outer portion must be enjoined by the sentence "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*).
In that case, the sentence would be split. However,

when it is understood that here it is precisely an unprepared, non-worldly (*alaukika*) space, characterized by the interior and exterior parts of the altar (*vedi*), that is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and not a prepared portion of the altar.
(Regarding the section on the non-subordinate status of the *sāmidhenī* verses to the *havirdhāna* cart in the seventh [chapter], Sūtras 15–17:
"Because of the statement regarding the two *havirdhāna* carts, 'They recite those *sāmidhenī* verses after that' (Jaim_3.7.15), [it might be argued that the *sāmidhenīs* are subordinate to them].
"Or rather, it is merely a matter of location, for the purposeful act (*arthakarma*) is directly perceived as belonging to the *soma* (Jaim_3.7.16)."
"And the designation is likewise. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.17). [The author] formulates the seventh section as follows:
"One standing at the *havirdhāna* [shed] should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses;
here, they are subsidiary to the *havirdhāna*. Or rather, it is the location of the *havirdhāna* that is indicated by this [injunction]."

[Objection: "Subsidiarity [of the *sāmidhenīs*] would arise from the sentence; [Response: It is not so. Because of the original context (*prakṛti*), the location subsequent to the fire is already obtained; by parsimony (*lāghava*), the proximity to the cart (*śakaṭasaṃnidhi*) is what is indicated.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "And when they press [the Soma], they recite the *sāmidhenī* verses there."

Between the two carts named *havirdhāna*, which are situated in the southern and northern portions of the *havirdhāna* shed, that which is the southern cart is designated here by the words "that" (*yat*) and "this" (*tat*).
Near it occurs the pressing of the *soma*.
The word "also" (*uta*) is used here in the sense of "then" (*atha*).
"Now, they should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses in that *havirdhāna* shed where they press the Soma.
Here, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs* is understood to belong to the southern *havirdhāna*.

And here, one should not suspect the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) as in the previous case, because the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*) is clearly apparent— this being the position reached, we reply: since the *sāmidhenī* verses are subsidiary to the *iṣṭi*, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*) in this context.
In the archetype (prakṛti), the western region of the Āhavanīya fire is the location for the *sāmidhenī* verses;
here, however, because the Uttaravedi serves as the Āhavanīya, the Havirdhāna shed stands to its west.
Since that location is already obtained through extension (*codaka*), the status of the location as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs* need not be enjoined.

However, since there is no fixed rule regarding proximity to either the southern or the northern *havirdhāna* cart, the term *havirdhāna* is used as an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) to restrict [the location] to the vicinity of the southern *havirdhāna* alone;

this being the case, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) because only a restrictive rule (*niyamamātra*) is enjoined. In your view, however, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) to the *sāmidhenī* verses—which is absolutely unestablished—is enjoined for the southern *havirdhāna* as indicated by the act of pressing (*abhiṣava*); thus, there is complexity (*gaurava*).
Therefore, it is characterized by its location.

(Eighth [Adhikaraṇa]: On the performance of the auxiliary acts by another; Sūtras 18–20) The fruit of the scripture accrues to the performer, because that is its defining characteristic; therefore, there should be personal performance. (Jaimini 3.7.18) But in the case of the disposal (utsarga), because it is subordinate, the one who performs the subsidiary acts may be another or himself. (Jaimini 3.7.19)

Or it may be someone else, because of the scriptural injunction regarding purchase and because of the contradiction with respect to one's own self. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.20). The eighth section formulates [the argument] as follows:
Either the entire [rite] must be performed by the sacrificer, or the act of relinquishment (tyāga) alone;
for it is consistent with the scriptural statement regarding the fruit accruing to the agent that he be the performer of everything.
The status of being an agent exists even for the instigator; otherwise, the purchase [of the officiants] would be in vain.
Therefore, in that case, there is merely the renunciation [of the fee] by the sacrificer, whereas elsewhere the officiant possesses agency.

In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," oneness is understood through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the enjoyer of heaven and the performer of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, Pāṇini, by the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.72), prescribes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.

Consequently, since the fruit cannot arise without the performance of the ritual along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), it follows that everything must be performed by the sacrificer himself—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

To this we reply: even in the absence of performing all the constituent parts, the sacrificer possesses the status of the "agent" (*kartṛtva*) in every respect by virtue of being the instigator (*prayojaka*).
This is because such usage is observed in the expression "he plows with six ploughs.
If everything were performed by the sacrificer alone,
then the hiring of officiating priests (ṛtvij) would be rendered useless.
Therefore—the sacrificer must perform only the act of renunciation (*tyāga*).
In other instances, the performance of the subsidiary and primary rites is carried out by the priest who has been hired.
This being so, since the status of being the agent of everything—both directly and through intermediaries—is possible for the sacrificer, his attainment of the fruit is not contradicted.
(Regarding the ninth section on the restriction of the specific number of priests who have been hired:
Sūtras 21–24) In that case, the number of performers should be determined by the requirements of the purpose, as there is no restrictive rule due to the absence of specification.
(Jaimini 3.7.21) Or rather, because of the distinction in the scriptural texts, there should be one [priest] for each specific name. (Jaimini 3.7.22)
If it is argued that [the distinction] is due to a difference in the action of a single [deity], [we reply]: No, for [the distinction occurs] at the time of origination. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.23–24)
The ninth section formulates [the following]: Is there no restriction on the number of purchased agents, or is there? No;
because there is no distinction, there must be as many as are required for the task. (MJaiNy 3.7.17)
Although no specific number of those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have been purchased by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is explicitly heard in the scripture,
nevertheless, that number must be understood according to the requirements of the ritual tasks.
And those specific ritual actions are heard in scripture as being connected with specific agents: "The Adhvaryu divides [the cake] in front;
the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the Manthin cup; the Neṣṭṛ leads the wife forward."
The Unnetṛ draws up the cups;
the Prastotṛ chants the Prastāva;
the Udgātṛ chants the Udgītha.
The Pratihartṛ chants the Pratihāra; the Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā;
the Hotṛ recites the Prātaranuvāka.
"The Maitrāvaruṇa gives the direction,
the Acchāvāka performs the offering, and the Grāvastut recites the Grāvastotrīya."
In this manner, the duties of the four— namely the Brahman, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Agnīdhra, and the Potṛ— are to be illustrated. Therefore,
as many officiating priests (ṛtvij) as there are duties must be chosen.
(Regarding the tenth section on the distinctness of the *camasādhvaryu* priests, the sūtra states:
"And the *camasādhvaryus* [are distinct] because they are designated by them. Jaimini 3.7.25.
The tenth section formulates the problem:
Are the *camasādhvaryus* other than the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or are they among them?

[Objection: They are not [other], because of the etymological designation [of the term]. [Reply: It is not so, because they are distinguished from them by the use of the genitive case. (MJaiNy 3.7.18)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "He chooses the Camasādhvaryus.
These Camasādhvaryus are not distinct from those priests, headed by the Adhvaryu, who were mentioned previously according to their respective functions.
Why?
Because through a derivative designation (*yaugika-saṃjñā*), there is the cognition of non-difference [between the two].
Just as Devadatta himself becomes a "cook" (*pācaka*) due to his connection with the act of cooking.
If it is argued that those headed by the *adhvaryu* are themselves the *camasādhvaryus* because of their connection with the *camasa* cups,
it is not so;
for the *camasādhvaryus* belong to those who perform the rites from the middle.
For the *hotrakas*,
there are the *camasādhvaryus*, as they appear as distinct [officiants] in the recitation; among those who perform the central rites are the *adhvaryu*, the *hotṛ*, and others.
The *hotraka*s—namely the Pratiprasthātṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, and others—are distinct from those [principal] officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). 3.7.18.

(Regarding the eleventh section, concerning the rule for the plurality of the *camasādhvaryu* priests, the Sūtra states: "But because of the scriptural mention of 'many' at the time of their origination. (Jaimini 3.7.26)
The eleventh section formulates the following:
"One should choose them"—is there no plurality here, or is there? As in the case of the single [Soma] vessel, there is none.

If it is argued that this is not so because of the disparity [with other cases], we say no; for in the original injunction (*utpatti*), plurality is explicitly heard. *Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara* 3.7.19.

If it is argued that the plurality heard in the injunction "one should choose the *camasādhvaryus*" is not intended to be significant, because it resides in the objective (*uddeśya*)— just like the singularity [of the cup] in the case of the *graha*— then [the following is said].
Not so;
because of the difference in the nature of the vessels (*graha*).
The statement "he cleanses the vessels" is not the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the vessels.
However, this very sentence is the originative injunction for the *camasādhvaryu*s;
therefore, because they are to be taken up [as participants], the plurality inherent in them is intended to be significant.

(The Sūtra in the section concerning the restriction to the number ten for the Camasādhvaryus in the twelfth [adhyāya]: "The number ten [is established] because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Jaimini 3.7.27)

He formulates the twelfth section: "Is there a fixed number for them, or is there not? Because there is no restrictive rule [regarding their number], [one might think there is none]. But because there are ten cups, there are ten *camasādhvaryu* priests. (MJaiNy 3.7.20)
The meaning is clear.

(Thirteenth Section: On the Non-Distinctness of the Śamitṛ; Sūtras 28–29) And the Śamitṛ [is distinct] because of the difference in words. (Jaimini 3.7.28) Or rather, he is not distinct because of the context, since there is no connection with the original injunction. (Jaimini 3.7.29)

The thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa) of MJaiNy 3.7.21 formulates [the following]: Is the *śamitṛ* (the immolator) other than those [officiants], or not other? He is other, because of the distinctness of the designation (*saṃjñā*).
"There is no other [person] due to the absence of a restrictive injunction; the difference in designation is merely etymological.

(JS 3.7.21) If it is argued that because the designation *śamitṛ* heard in the mantra "O *śamitṛ*s, approach the sacrifice" is mentioned separately, there must be a *śamitṛ* distinct from those already mentioned—this is not so.
Because there is no separate act of choosing [the victim],
the difference in designation is justified by the connection with the ritual slaughter of the animal (*paśusaṃjñapana*).
Even though this mantra is recited in the section of the *Adhvaryu* priest (*adhvaryukāṇḍa*), [it belongs to the Hotṛ].
Nevertheless, because it is heard that the Adhvaryu must turn away, the Pratiprasthātṛ and others who are the Adhvaryu’s subordinates are the Śamitṛs.
For this very reason, it is stated in the scripture: "The Adhvaryu turns away from the animal while it is being slaughtered. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 3.7.21)
(Regarding the fourteenth [topic]: the section on non-distinctness after approaching—sūtra:
"And Upaga [is to be included] because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.30)
He formulates the fourteenth section:
"Should there be others as singers [of the Prastāva], like those mentioned previously, or not?
As it is in the world, so it should be here too; [the answer is] not so, because of the indicative mark that 'the Adhvaryu is not [a singer]'. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 3.7.22)
If it is argued that just as in the world there are secondary singers standing at the side of the principal singers and leaders, so it is here as well— do not say so.
If there were other singers (upagātṛs) besides those already mentioned,
then, since the Adhvaryu would not be applicable [in that context], the prohibition "the Adhvaryu should not sing as an upagātṛ" would be purposeless.
Therefore, the distinction in terminology is merely etymological and applies only to those already mentioned.
(Regarding the fifteenth section on the distinctness of the Soma-seller, the sūtra states:
But the seller is another person, because the act [of selling] is not enjoined [as part of the sacrifice]. Jaimini 3.7.31.
He formulates the fifteenth section:

"Among these, is there one Soma-seller, or not? Because of the absence of formal appointment (*varaṇa*), there is only one; since the act of selling does not serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), it is distinct. [MJaiNy_3.7.23]
Only the purchase is heard in scripture as a subsidiary element of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice,
not the sale;
and priests do not perform what is not prescribed.
Therefore, the seller is someone other than that [the father].
(Regarding the section on the non-universal application of the title "officiant" in the sixteenth [chapter], Sūtras 32–35:

All [the priests] possess the status of an *ṛtvij* because of their performance of the ritual acts, as there is no distinction [among them]. (Jaimini 3.7.32) Or rather, it is not so, because of the restrictive enumeration. (Jaimini 3.7.33)
If it is argued that [the qualification applies] to one half [of the year], [the response is:
no; there is no entitlement for all [twice-born men]. (Jaimini 3.7.34–35)
The sixteenth section formulates the following inquiry: Is the name "ṛtvij" (sacrificial priest) common to all [officiants], or only to some?
Since they all equally perform sacrifice during the ritual season (*ṛtu*), that name applies to them all. (MJaiNy 3.7.24)
In the *Saumya-adhvara*, there are seven [priests] and ten, according to such enumerations;

the name is not the same for all, as for some it is established through etymological derivation (*yoga-rūḍhi*). The basis for the application of the word *ṛtvij* (priest) is "sacrificing during the [proper] season" (*ṛtau yajana*).
If it is argued that this [designation] exists among the *canasādhvaryu*s just as it does among Brahmā and the others— and therefore the name "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) applies equally to all—
this is not so.
Because it contradicts the scriptural statement regarding the number:
"In the Soma sacrifice, the Adhvara, the sacrificial rite, there are seventeen officiating priests," so it is heard in the scripture.

Therefore, without overstepping the principles of yoga and also relying on the conventional usage established by the scriptures, it should be understood that this name applies to only certain [sacrifices].
(Seventeenth [adhikaraṇa]: On the fact that only those beginning with Brahmā, as mentioned in the statement regarding the fee for initiation, are the seventeen officiating priests; Sūtras 36–37.
"But there is a restriction by means of the fees, because of the connection with the Vedic text" (Jaimini 3.7.36).
"And because, having stated their status as sacrificers, the initiation is prescribed for them" (Jaimini 3.7.37).
The seventeenth section begins with *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtra* 3.7.26:
"Even those things which are enumerated, whether they are restricted or not specifically so," [should be understood as such].
The first [alternative] does not apply to the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and especially not to the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Those who are numbered as seventeen should be selected at will from among the Brahmans and others, as well as from among the *camasādhvaryu* priests.
If it is argued that this is because no specific detail is heard [in the text],
it is not so;
for specific details are indeed heard in the passage concerning the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and in the passage concerning the consecration (dīkṣā).

Having stated, "He gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij)," the specific details thereof are heard through such passages as, "He gives to the Agnīdh," "He gives to the Brahman," and so forth. Furthermore, in that same context, immediately after the statement, "Those who are the sacrificers (yajamāna), they are the officiating priests," the following is recited: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brahman; thereafter, the Udgātṛ."
Then, after the Pratiprasthātṛ has initiated the Hotṛ, he initiates those who receive half-shares: the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin for the Brahman,
and the Prastotṛ for the Udgātṛ.
The cup for Mitra and Varuṇa belongs to the Hotṛ.
Then, after the Neṣṭṛ has initiated him, he initiates those belonging to the third group: the Agnīdhra for the Brahman, and the Pratihartṛ for the Udgātṛ.
The Acchāvāka [is initiated] by the Hotṛ;
then the Unnetṛ, having initiated him, initiates those who have completed a quarter [of the vow]: the Potṛ by the Brahman, and the Subrahmaṇya by the Udgātṛ.
"The Grāvastut [is initiated] by the Hotṛ; then another Brāhmaṇa initiates him"—the meaning of this is: "The Adhvaryu performs what is prescribed in the Yajurveda;
he has three assistants who are Brāhmaṇas: the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin..."
The Agnīdh and the Potṛ;
the Udgātṛ performs the chanting, and he has three assistants: the Prastotṛ, the [Udgātṛ], and the Pratihartṛ.
The Pratihartṛ and the Subrahmaṇya;
the Hotṛ performs the recitation.
He has three assistants: the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Acchāvāka, and the Grāvastut.
Among the four groups, those who are the first receive the full sacrificial fee.

Those who are second receive half of that—thus they are called "half-sharers" (ardhinaḥ). Those who are third receive a third part—thus they are called "third-sharers" (tṛtīyinaḥ). And those who are fourth receive a fourth part—thus they are called "quarter-sharers" (pādinaḥ).
"Each of those persons consecrates these [materials] in the order not [explicitly] stated.

Here, in this injunction regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), it should be understood as a rule that the sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) specified— beginning with the *adhvaryu*— are intended, and not the *camasādhvaryus*.
(Regarding the eighteenth [topic]—the section on the priests being seventeen with the master as the seventeenth—the sūtra states:
"The master is the seventeenth, because of the commonality of the ritual action. Jaimini 3.7.38.
He formulates the eighteenth topic:
"Whether it be the Sadasya or the Sacrificer, the seventeenth [priest] is chosen on account of being appointed. He performs some action for the Sadasya, but not truly for the Master. (MJaiNy_3.7.27)
When the sixteen officiants, beginning with the *adhvaryu* and the *brahmā*, have been established, some other priest who completes the number seventeen is required;
he shall be the *sadasya* here.
One who is situated among the members of the assembly is a *sadasya*.
And it cannot be argued that there is an absence of such a prohibition, because in some recensional branches (*śākhā*) that prohibition is indeed recorded;
therefore, the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) is restricted to the *sadasya*— if this is your position.
Not so;
that *sadasya* performs nothing at all,
because there is no injunction stating, "The *sadasya* should do this."
Furthermore, the term *ṛtvij* (priest) is not applicable to him [the sacrificer] without the performance of the ritual action for the purpose of sacrificing at the proper seasons;
however, it is appropriate in the case of the sacrificer because he performs the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Therefore, the rule of seventeen priests (*sāptadaśya*) is properly applied to the sacrificer.

(Regarding the nineteenth [topic]— the section on the restriction of the agency of the Adhvaryu and others in the duties of the Adhvaryu and so forth— and the twentieth [topic]— the section on the fact that the fire-altar serves all purposes, both the archetype and the ectype— the sūtras are 39–Jaim_3.7.42).

All those purposes [are accomplished] because they are applied; and the fires [are established] because they have their own specific time. (Jaimini 3.7.39) There should be a restriction of the ritual action due to its connection with that [fire], because that connection serves a purpose. (Jaimini 3.7.40) Its specification is by means of direct instruction and technical name. (Jaimini 3.7.41)
And likewise, there is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 3.7.42.
[The author] formulates the nineteenth section as follows:

Their duty is not fixed, nor is it fixed; for since the first [is possible], by what means could there be a restriction here as to "who is capable" and "what [should be done]"? This would be determined by the designation (*samākhyā*).
Thus, for those such as the Adhvaryu and others, the duty is not fixed.
If it is argued that all [causes] are capable of producing everything everywhere, and that the context (*prakaraṇa*) cannot be a restrictive factor because it is common to all cases—
this is not so.
Because the designation (samākhyā) is the determining factor:
in whatever ritual action the designation "Ādhvaryava" occurs, that action belongs to the Adhvaryu.
The same applies elsewhere as well.
(Regarding the twentieth [adhikaraṇa]—on the fact that the fires serve both as archetypes and modifications for all purposes—the portion of the stated sūtra:
And the fires [serve] all purposes, because they have their own specific time. 3.7.31.
He formulates the discussion regarding the *viśādhikaraṇa*:
"Is the meaning [of the word] restricted to the archetype (*prakṛti*), or is it for all purposes? Let the fire be the first, as in the case of the *parṇa*."

The principle of the *parṇa* [wood] would apply to what is extended (*atidiṣṭa*), but when something is directly enjoined (*upadiṣṭa*), it applies universally. If it is argued: "Just as the injunction regarding the *parṇa* wood—'He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood hears no evil report'—is for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too, since the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not mentioned in connection with a specific rite (*anārabhya-adhīta*), the fire such as the *āhavanīya* established thereby is for the sake of the archetype."
Not so;
for there is a disparity.
According to the statement regarding the *parṇa* wood, the ladle (*juhū*) serves as the medium through which the quality of being made of *parṇa* enters into the sacrifice.
And that *juhū* ladle, being prescribed in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) itself, is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to all the modified rites (*vikṛti*).
As for the *āhavanīya* and other fires, the oblation (*homa*) is the means of access to them in the place of the sacrifice;
and that [oblation], being prescribed in some cases in the archetype itself, is extended by analogy to the modified rites.
For example, in the case of oblations such as the *prayāṇa* and *nāriṣṭha*,
in such a context the sentence "they offer in the *āhavanīya*" prescribes the fire only for the archetype (*prakṛti*);
however, in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), it is extended by means of the oblation itself.
Therefore, in this case, the principle of the leaves (parṇanyāya) applies.
As for the oblation that is taught in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*),
such as the *āmanahoma* in the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice;

In that case, since the *homa* which serves as a door (*dvāra*) is taught in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is impossible to maintain that the door-bearer (*dvārī*) is also enjoined by the sentence in the modified sacrifice just as it was in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, the fire (*vahni*) is for all purposes.
(Section 21: On the Sublation by Designation;
Sūtras 43–45) The recitation of the *praiṣa* and *anuvacana* belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa, because of the direct instruction.
Or rather, it is the *puro’nuvākyā* that belongs to him, because of its proximity to the *praiṣa*. Jaimini 3.7.43–44.
And because the Hotṛ is seen at the morning recitation (*prātar-anuvāka*). (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.45).
[The author] formulates the twenty-first section as follows:

That the Maitrāvaruṇa priest gives the *preṣya* command and the *anubrūhi* invitation constitutes his "authorization" (*bādhana*) applies everywhere, not only in some specific instances, because of the designation (*samākhyā*) such as "belonging to the Hotṛ" and so forth.

"Let it be so because of the statement. No, because we perceive the mention of their being together; where the *praisha* (direction) and the *anuvacana* (recitation) are mentioned as being conjoined, there is a sublation [of the individual application].
In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The Maitrāvaruṇa directs and recites after."
This sentence prescribes that the *praiṣas* (directions) and *anuvacanās* (recitations) are to be performed by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest.
By this sentence, the *samākhyā* (title-based designation) is set aside;

for we observe that the *praiṣas* such as "Recite for Agni being enkindled" (*agnaye samidhyamānāyānubrūhi*) and "Recite for the sacrificial post being anointed" (*yūpāyājyamānāyānubrūhi*) are performed by the Adhvaryu—hence the ritualists maintain that "the *praiṣas* belong to the Adhvaryu."
[The name is] *samākhyā* (designation).
Likewise,

because we observe that recitations such as "Forward, O strengths, seeking heaven" (*pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ*) and "The seekers of the gods anoint you at the sacrifice" (*añjanti tvāmadhvare devayantaḥ*) have the *hotṛ* priest as their performer.
The technical designation of the ritualists is that "the *anuvacanāni* are the *hautra* [duties].
And the *praiṣas* and *anuvacanās* are of two kinds: combined and separate;
those cited previously were the separate ones.

At the end of the recitation mantra beginning with "hotā yakṣad agniṃ samidham," the direction (praiṣa) "hotaryaja" is prescribed; these directions and recitations are taken together. And in all these cases—whether the directions and recitations are separate or combined—the stronger syntactical connection (vākya) overrides the name (samākhyā).
If it is argued that one should abandon both the Hotṛ’s agency and the Adhvaryu’s agency and instead accept the Maitrāvaruṇa’s agency alone, we reply as follows:

In the statement "He gives the command and recites after," the two *ca* particles indicate that the giving of the command (*praiṣa*) and the subsequent recitation (*anuvacana*) are to be combined within this sentence.
Therefore, it is precisely these two combined actions that override the conventional designations (*samākhyā*).
But when they are separate, it must be accepted that the performance belongs to the Hotṛ and others, according to their respective designations.
(Regarding the twenty-second section, concerning the performance of the cup-offerings by the *camasādhvaryu* priests, Sūtras 46–49: Sūtra 46:
The *camasādhvaryus* [should offer] the cups, because of their designation (*samākhyāna*). Sūtra 47: Or rather, the *adhvaryu* [should offer them], because that is the logical rule (*nyāya*).
And because another [use] is seen for the *camasa* cup;
they should be understood as being for that [other purpose] when [the primary function] is impossible. (Jaimini 3.7.48–49)
The twenty-second section formulates the argument:
"Does the Camasādhvaryu offer with the cups, or is it the Adhvaryu himself?
Let the first alternative hold because of the specific designation; no, for that is not so, due to the designation 'Adhvaryu'. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 3.7.32)

Because a specific distinction is independent [of others], while another requires it, the *adhvaryu* should offer the oblation if he is capable; otherwise, even another may do so. If it is argued that, because of the specific designation "cup-attendant" (*camasādhvaryu*), only the cup-attendants themselves should offer with the cups—[we reply: no.
Not so;
for the designation "adhvaryu" is stronger due to its independence.
The word "adhvaryu" applies to both the sole Adhvaryu and the Camasādhvaryus, and thus exists in a general form.
The word *camasa*, however, is specific, applying only to the *camasādhvaryus*.
Without depending on that specific [designation], the word *adhvaryu* is capable of functioning as a general name for a priest (*ṛtvij*).
The word *camasa*, on the other hand, becomes a name for persons only by depending on the general term *adhvaryu*.

That being the case, by virtue of the strong and independent designation (samākhyā), "The libation is for the Adhvaryu," the Adhvaryu alone should perform the libations with the cups (camasa) as long as he is capable;
however, if he is occasionally unable due to being occupied with the libations of the vessels (graha), the Camasādhvaryus should perform them.
