(Regarding the twenty-third [topic], the section on the plurality of performers in the Śyena and Vājapeya sacrifices, Sūtras 50–51):
Jai. 3.7.50: Because of the Vedic injunction, as in the previous case, when there is a difference from the Veda, they should be according to the injunction.
Jai. 3.7.51: Or rather, by virtue of its quality, it would have its own ritual duty; because of the capacity of the entitlement, it is unmanifest with the subsidiaries in the remainder.
In the twenty-third section (adhikaraṇa), [the author] formulates [the following]:
"The Śyena sacrifice is taught in the Udgātṛveda; the Vājapeya is in the Yajurveda."
The duties of the Udgātṛ and the Adhvaryu should be performed as in the archetype; however, the former [the Udgātṛ] is the first.
For the injunction, which precedes the specific name, is indeed the same as in the archetype;
thus, the performers remain established in their respective duties, just as in the model sacrifice.
(MJaiNy 3.7.35) — Since the Śyena sacrifice is recited in the Sāmaveda, all its constituent elements are to be performed by the Udgātṛ priest.
Since the designation "Udgātṛ" applies equally to the Śyena sacrifice as it does to the Bahiṣpavamāna, Ājya, Pṛṣṭha, and other stotras,
and likewise since the Vājapeya— though recited in the Yajurveda— is to be performed entirely by the Adhvaryu priest on the basis of that designation; such being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
We reply: For the Śyena and Vājapeya sacrifices are both modifications (vikāra) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

In that case, the extended injunction (codaka) presents those various constituent elements as being to be performed by their respective persons. Once the subsidiaries have been extended [to the modification], there subsequently arises the activity of the performance-injunction (prayogavacana), which effects the performance of the primary rite together with its subsidiaries.

But a name (samākhyā) dependent on the injunctive statement (prayogavacana) is extremely weak; therefore, by the force of the stronger extended injunction (codaka), as in the archetype (prakṛti), various performers are established in their respective duties.
Thus ends the seventh pāda of the third adhyāya in the *Śrīmādhavīya Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara*.
Now begins the eighth pāda of the third adhyāya.
(In the first section [adhikaraṇa] concerning the ownership of the act of purchase, there is the following sūtra:)
The hiring of the master [of the sacrifice] is a ritual act, because the ritual act is for his sake.
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.1) In the first section of the eighth chapter, he formulates the following:
The purchase by means of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and so forth belongs either to the priests or to the masters;
however, because of the specific designation, the purchase should belong to the priests, as in other cases.
Because the Adhvaryu, Hotṛ, and other priests do not exist prior to the hiring,
the act of hiring belongs to the sacrificer, not to the officiating priest (ṛtvij).
[MJaiNy 3.8.2] — The laborers must be hired by means of the payment of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

In that regard, it has been determined that everything except the relinquishing of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) pertains to the officiating priests (*ārtvijya*). Furthermore, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of one hundred and twelve [cows], is prescribed in both the Adhvaryu Veda and the Udgātṛ Veda;
the *anvāhārya* fee is prescribed in the Adhvaryu Veda.
If it is argued that, by virtue of their designation, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the performers [of the sacrifice], this is not so;

because since the officiating priests do not exist prior to the act of hiring (*parikrayaṇa*), it is impossible for them to be the performers, and therefore the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone is the performer. MJaiNyC_3,8.1-2 //
(Regarding the second section on the Adhvaryu’s role in granting the boon, the sūtra states:
It would belong to the others because of a specific scriptural statement. Jaimini 3.8.2.

The second section formulates the problem: Should the gift of the best brick belong to the patron (*svāmin*) or to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)? It belongs to the patron, as in the previous case; but it is not so, for this [gift] belongs to the *adhvaryu* priest because of a specific scriptural injunction. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 3.8.3)
"He who should lay down this brick should give [cows] three times"—this scriptural statement (vācanika) prescribes the gift of cows by the Adhvaryu priest who performs the laying.
For there is no such thing as an excessive burden for a scriptural injunction. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Candrikā 3.8.3)
(Regarding the third section, concerning the sacrificer’s performance of the purificatory rites such as shaving, Sūtras 3–8:
But the purificatory rites, since they depend on the capacity of the person, should be restricted according to each Veda, just like the ritual acts themselves.
(Jaimini 3.8.3) However, they belong to the sacrificer because he is the primary agent, just like the ritual acts. (Jaimini 3.8.4)
And because of the designation [of it as a quality]; because it is indicated as being subordinate; and because it exists in relation to the injunction.
Because they are incomparable, they would be of unequal application. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.8) The third section formulates [the following]:
Are the preparatory rites, such as sowing and so forth, for the Adhvaryu priest or for the patron?
They belong to the Adhvaryu, because he is capable of performing them and because they are prescribed in his Veda.
Having attained fitness through the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are able to perform their respective duties;
therefore, the action [of purchasing] belongs to them, while the purification (*saṃskriyā*) pertains to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
"May the waters moisten you for life," and so forth, are the mantras of purification.
The procedures for these acts are prescribed in the Adhvaryu Veda: "He shaves his hair and beard," and "He clips his nails.
Furthermore, the Adhvaryu is capable of performing the shaving and other such tasks.
If it is argued that, therefore, those purificatory rites such as shaving belong to that Adhvaryu priest—
do not say so.
The purificatory rites such as shaving are performed to remove the impurity residing in the sacrificer and to produce his fitness for sacrifice.
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "He shaves his hair and beard.
This skin, namely the hair and beard, is indeed dead and impure;
having cast off that dead and impure skin, he becomes fit for sacrifice and approaches the sacrificial food."
For the dead skin of the sacrificer does not depart merely by the sowing of the furrows;

rather, since one who is qualified has the entitlement to perform the ritual, he subsequently hires officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as laborers when he himself becomes incapable of engaging in the activities consisting of exertion.
Even in the world, a servant is hired for the mere task of fetching medicine and such for a sick master by granting him his life.
But at that time, the servant does not consume the medicine;
therefore, while the other ritual actions belong to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the consecration (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
But in some cases,
because of a scriptural statement, let there be a purificatory rite even for the officiating priests.
(Regarding the fourth section, concerning the sacrificer's performance of austerity, sūtras 9–11:

"And austerity [is performed by the sacrificer], because it is for the sake of accomplishing the fruit, as in the world. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.9) "And the supplementary statement is likewise. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.10)
From the statement, it should apply to the others. (Jaimini 3.8.11).
[The author] formulates the fourth section as follows:
Regarding the statement "he does not eat for two days," to whom does this austerity belong?
Since it consists of suffering, the austerity belongs to the Adhvaryu priest, because it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the one who experiences it.

Because it destroys the sin that obstructs the fruit [of the sacrifice], austerity (*tapas*) is a purificatory rite (*saṃskṛti*); by virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it belongs to the master of the sacrifice (*svāmigāmi*), just like other purificatory rites.
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the austerity prescribed by such statements as "he does not eat for two days" and "he does not eat for three days" is appropriate for the *adhvaryu* priest.
If it is argued that because [the ritual] consists of suffering, it is appropriate for it to be performed by men who have been hired for wages,
and that precisely because it is suffering, it cannot be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the enjoyer of the fruit, and thus it is not fitting for the sacrificer—
this is not so.

Since austerity (*tapas*), although consisting of suffering, can serve as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificer by virtue of its capacity to destroy that sin which produces suffering and acts as an obstacle to the future fruit in the form of happiness;

regarding this point, the author of the *Kalpasūtra* has cited the following indicative mark found in a supplementary passage: "When the initiated one becomes emaciated, then he becomes fit for sacrifice (*medhya*)."
When there is nothing whatsoever within this [body], then it becomes pure;
when the blackness in his eyes disappears, [then he becomes pure].
Then he becomes pure;
when his skin and bone are joined together, then he becomes pure.
"Having drunk [the Soma], he undergoes initiation;
being emaciated, he performs the sacrifice.
Whatever of his limbs wastes away, that indeed he offers as an oblation"—so it is known.
For austerity, which is of the nature of suffering, does not destroy sin—which is the cause of suffering—without [the experience of] that suffering.
Just as there is no healing of poison-inflicted wounds without incision, so it is here.
Therefore, like the purificatory rites such as shaving, austerity belongs to the sacrificer alone.
"And because it is a subordinate quality, there would be no restriction by means of the Veda.
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.12)
The fifth section formulates the following:
"But as for the consecrations such as wearing a golden garland, they are considered [to apply] to the priests because of a scriptural statement;
should they be performed by all [the priests] according to their respective designations?"
[Objection: "It is not so, because of the force of the initial designation. [Reply: No, because they are recited in proximity to all;
since the subordinate qualities apply to each primary, the act must be performed by all as well.
(MJaiNy 3.8.8) In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The priests proceed wearing golden garlands."
In the Śyena sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The priests proceed wearing red turbans, red garments, and with the sacred thread suspended around the neck.

Although, by the previous principle, the status of being gold-garlanded and so forth—being *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites)—would have been established as pertaining to the sacrificer, nevertheless, due to this specific scriptural statement, this [wearing of red] is a *saṃskāra* for the priests.

If it is argued that, in this regard, the wearing of a golden garland must be accepted as belonging to the Adhvaryus alone because it is prescribed in the Yajurveda, and the red turban and so forth must belong to the Udgātṛs alone because they are prescribed in the Sāmaveda— on the basis of these designations (*samākhyā*)—
it is not so.

The purificatory rite of wearing golden garlands (*hiraṇyamālitva*), which is recited in proximity to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the statement "the officiating priests wearing golden garlands perform [the ritual]," is connected to all the priests because proximity (*saṃnidhi*) overrides the name (*samākhyā*). Furthermore, since the priests are primary agents due to their being the objects of the action, and because a subordinate element must be repeated for each primary agent, it must be accepted that the purificatory rite of wearing golden garlands and so forth applies to every single priest.
(Regarding the sixth section on the sacrificer's desire for rain, Sūtras 13–14:
"Likewise, the desire [belongs to the sacrificer] because of its connection with the purpose. (Jaimini 3.8.13) "It would belong to the others because of their specific designation. (Jaimini 3.8.14)
START MJaiNy 3.8.9–10:
The sixth section formulates [the following]:
"One desiring rain should construct the *sadas* low"—this is a statement of desire (*kāmanā*).
From the statement of either the Adhvaryu or the Master, it is said that [the status] belongs to the mother.
From the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending, it is understood that the officiating priest’s (*adhvaryu*) activity is for the sake of another;
therefore, when there is a conflict with the syntactical connection (*vākya*), let that [result] belong to the master [of the sacrifice], just as in the case of asceticism (*tapas*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya be rainy,' he should erect the *sadas* shed low."
The meaning is that, just as the *havirdhāna* and the *prācīnavaṃśa* are situated high both in front and behind, so too the *sadas* should not be high, but rather it should be made low.
In this case, the desire for rain belongs to the Adhvaryu priest,
because the sentence "He who desires [it], he should measure [the post]" indicates that the desire belongs to a single person in general.
And it is undisputed that the status of motherhood belongs to the Adhvaryu priest;
therefore, if you argue that he [the Adhvaryu] is the one who desires [the fruit],
it is not so.
By the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in the word "minuyāt," it is understood that the fruit of the Adhvaryu’s activity accrues to another.

Consequently, since the fruit characterized by rain accrues to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the direct statement of the *parasmaipada* is set aside by the syntactical context (*vākya*), and it should be understood that the desire belongs to the sacrificer as its agent—namely, that the Adhvaryu desires:
"May Parjanya bring about the rain desired by the sacrificer."
The sentence "he should direct it downwards" is to be explained as follows:
"The *udgātṛ* priest, being such [an expert], should desire for himself or for the sacrificer whatever wish he desires."

If it is argued that the desire for the fruit also belongs to the officiating priests because of the statement, "He sings for him," then let there be a fruit for the officiating priests as well in that meditation on the *udgītha*, on account of that scriptural declaration.
(Regarding the seventh [section], the section on the sacrificer's role in the mantras beginning with "āyurdā" [Sūtras 15–16]:
And the mantras that do not effect the ritual act are like that;
because they are seen [to be used] even when there is separation [from the act]. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.15–16)
START MJaiNy 3.8.11 Seventh Section (Adhikaraṇa): The statement of the mantra "Āyurdāḥ" is [to be performed] by which Adhvaryu, according to the designation?
If that [application] is set aside by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), then the ownership [of the result] belongs to the master; this is the view of Kāmaśrama.
This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life.

Regarding this mantra, there arises the doubt as to whether its recitation is for the Adhvaryu or for the Sacrificer (*yajamāna*); this doubt is indicated by the word "for whom" (*kasya*) in the Sūtra.
In this mantra, the connection of the fruit— expressed by the words "grant me long life"— is perceived as being with one's own self;
and that [connection] is appropriate for the sacrificer, not for the officiating priest (adhvaryu).
Therefore, even a mantra containing [the word] *kāma* belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

(Regarding the eighth section, concerning the application of both [recensions] for that which is recorded in two, the sūtra states: "In cases where there are two recensions, both [should be employed], because the dual recording is purposeful. Jaimini 3.8.17.
The eighth section formulates [the following]:
One should recite "vājasya me" to either one or two persons, because the purpose is accomplished;
since it is recited in both sections (kāṇḍas), both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer [are entitled to it]. ③.8.12.
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: this mantra, "vājasya mā prasavena," is recited in both the Adhvaryu section and the Yajamāna section.
If it is argued that since the purpose of the mantra is fulfilled when it is recited by one of them, the other should not recite it—that is not so.
Because it would otherwise follow that the recitation in one of the sections would be redundant,
it must be recited by both. Although they recite it together, there is a difference in their underlying intention.
"The meaning revealed by this mantra I shall perform," thus thinks the Adhvaryu;
"I shall not be negligent here," thus the sacrificer [thinks]. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 3.8.12)
(Regarding the ninth [topic], the section on the fact that only one who possesses supernormal knowledge (*abhijña*) should be made to recite—the Sūtra:
And the instruction (*vācana*) occurs when [the matter] is known, for one who is ignorant is not ordained [for such a role]. Jaimini 3.8.18.
The ninth section formulates the following:
Should one cause the master to recite, whether he be knowledgeable or ignorant, or only the knowledgeable one?

Since there is no distinction made, both [should recite]; or rather, because the knowledgeable one possesses ownership [of the rite], one should cause him alone to recite. (Jaimini Nyāyamālāvistara 3.8.13)
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "He causes the sacrificer to recite the *kḷpti* formulas.
The *mantras* beginning with "May [the sacrifice] prosper through the sacrifice" (*āryuyajñena kalpatām*) are the *kḷptis*.
In that regard, he should cause both to recite—the one who is conversant with the *mantras* and their meaning, as well as the one who is not.

If it is argued that this is because no such specific qualification as "one who knows" is heard in the injunction "he should cause him to recite," and because even one who is ignorant can be made to recite after being instructed at that very time—
this is not so.
Because, by the force of the injunction for Vedic study, only one who has studied the Veda and understood its meaning is eligible to be a sacrificer;
therefore, one should cause only a person possessing such knowledge to recite.
(Regarding the tenth [section], the section on the twelve pairs being the duty of the Adhvaryu, Sūtras 19–20:

The ritual acts [mentioned] in the *Yājamāna* [section] should belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), because of the designation (*samākhyāna*). Or rather, the Adhvaryu [should perform them], for he is intended for that purpose; the designation follows the prior rule of logic. Jaimini 3.8.19–20.
In the tenth section of the third chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra (3.8.14–15), the author formulates the following:
"One should let the calf approach [the mother cow], and likewise, one should place the cauldron upon the fire."
These twelve pairs of ritual acts belong either to the master of the sacrifice or to the other [the officiant].
The first [view] arises from the reading in the *Svāmikāṇḍa* (the section on the master), because the purchase is for his sake;
let the latter [view] be based on the statement in the *Mahākāṇḍa*. Here, however, only the state of being a pair (*dvaṃdvatā*) is proclaimed.
In the *Yājamānakāṇḍa* of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard: "They say that twelve pairs (*dvandvāni*) are to be prepared for the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*—he lets loose the calf... and so forth.
"He places the pot on the fire," "and he strikes [the sacrificial animal]," "and he threshes the two millstones," and so forth.
In that context, the driving away of the calves by means of a *palāśa* branch constitutes one single action.
The placing of the pot to hold the milk obtained by milking is another action; these two together constitute one pair.
Likewise, the threshing of rice grains [is another].
The striking together of the two millstones with another stone—
these two constitute the second pair of duals.
In this manner, twelve pairs of ritual actions are prescribed as those to be performed.

Since these [rites] are recited in the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamāna-kāṇḍa*), they should be performed by the sacrificer according to that designation (*samākhyā*)— this being the prima facie view—
we reply: the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) have been hired precisely for the purpose of performing those tasks which belong to the sacrificer.
Furthermore, in the Yajurveda, this is a subordinate section concerning the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), whereas the major section concerns the duties of the Adhvaryu priest alone;
it is precisely therein that these ritual rules, such as the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), are recorded.
Therefore, only the *adhvaryu* should perform them.
In the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa*, however, the manner of performance is not enjoined;
rather, it is merely recorded through enumeration that they are to be formed into pairs.
Therefore, the sacrificer, having kept that sequence in mind, is able to ensure that the Adhvaryu is free from negligence in his performance;
for this reason, the performance belongs to the Adhvaryu alone.

(Regarding the eleventh section, concerning the Hotṛ’s performance of the duties of the Adhvaryu in cases of conflict, the Sūtra states: "In case of a conflict, the one who performs the action [is the Hotṛ], because of a specific connection; the other [performs] the rest, since there would be a distinction among them based on that. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.21)
The eleventh section formulates the following:

"If one who is an Adhvaryu should act as the Hotṛ, performing the duties of the Adhvaryu, should he perform the duties of the Hotṛ [as well], or not? He does so, because there is no cause for relinquishing [the primary office]. (MJaiNy 3.8.16)
A single Hotṛ priest is not capable of performing two actions simultaneously;
therefore, he should abandon the *hautra* duties obtained from the water, as he is occupied with the work prescribed by the verbal injunction.
In the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, the Adhvaryu performs the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with a rope using the instrumental mantra, "Thou art the unencircled one" (*aparivīr asi*).
At that time, the Hotṛ recites the mantra "The youth well-dressed... while that girding is being performed.
Both of these [acts] are obtained in the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice through the succession of the *codaka* (archetypal injunctions).
Therein, the combination of the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ is prescribed: "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu."
Because the duties of the *adhvaryu* are prescribed for the *hotṛ* by the injunction "he should follow the *hotṛ*," the work of the *adhvaryu* is to be performed by the *hotṛ*.
Consequently, the *hotṛ* should perform the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-parivyāṇa*) with the instrumental mantra "thou art the encircler" (*parivīrasi*).
At that time, the *hotṛ* must not abandon his own *hautra* duties which have been obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*).
For we do not perceive any prohibition against the cause of that relinquishment.

Therefore, when it is argued that the Hotṛ priest should recite the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ" while that parivyāṇa (encircling) is being performed, we reply: it is not possible for one single Hotṛ to perform both prescribed duties simultaneously for the two priests, the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ.

Therefore, since one of the two must necessarily be abandoned, the office of the *hotṛ*—which is obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*)—should be the one abandoned; however, until the end of the sacrifice, the office of the *adhvaryu* must be performed, as it is established by the rule: "He who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*."
(Regarding the twelfth section, concerning the non-Adhvaryava nature of the placing of the sprinkling-vessels and other rites, there is the following sūtra:
"And in the case of the directions (*praiṣas*), [the action belongs to another] because of the authority over others. Jaimini 3.8.22.
He formulates the twelfth topic:
Should the Adhvaryu perform the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, or someone else?
The first [option] follows from the name [of the priest]; the other [option]—that another should do it—follows from the indicative mark [in the injunction], "Place [them]. (MJaiNy 3.8.18)
Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices: it is prescribed in the scripture that the sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇī*) is to be poured onto the altar (*vedi*) by means of some vessel.
If it is argued that this belongs to the Adhvaryu because it is mentioned in the Yajurveda, it is not so.
Because it would result in a contradiction with the *praiṣa* (direction) mantras:
"Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters;
spread this sacrificial grass (*barhis*)."

In the Adhvaryu’s injunction-mantras such as "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires; spread the sacrificial grass," the address to the Agnīdh and the use of the second person are appropriate only if that [act] is performed by someone other [than the Adhvaryu].
Therefore, it does not belong to the Adhvaryu. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāya-mālā-vistara 3.8.18)

(Thirteenth Section: On the Adhvaryu-nature of the Praiṣa-mantras; Sūtras 23–24) "But the Adhvaryu [utters them], because it is so seen. (Jaimini 3.8.23) "Or rather, it is figurative, because of the similarity of the action. (Jaimini 3.8.24)

The thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa) of the Mīmāṃsājaiminīyasūtravṛtti (MJaiNy) 3.8.19 formulates the following: "Should the *agnīdh* give the command (*preṣya*), or rather the *adhvaryu*, since there is no contradiction in the case of the *agnīdh*?"
Because of the contradiction with the designation [of the Adhvaryu], the Adhvaryu performs the purpose by means of the *praiṣa* (direction);
for it is said: "Just as he places the *prokṣaṇī* waters near the Āgnīdhra, so too let the Āgnīdhra himself recite the *praiṣa* mantra."
If it is argued that there is no contradiction, we say:
not so;
for there is a contradiction between the designation "belonging to the Adhvaryu" and the previously cited vocative case and second-person verb forms.
Nor should it be argued that the contradiction with the name (samākhyā) remains unavoidable even if the acts such as the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* water are not performed by the Adhvaryu;
for there is no such contradiction even when [the Adhvaryu] is the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) through the medium of a command (*praiṣa*).
Therefore, the mantra of the command belongs to the Adhvaryu alone.
(Regarding the fourteenth section, on the point that the fruit belongs to the master and is not to be prayed for in the mantras of the instruments [the *varco-nyāya*], the sūtras 25–27 state:
Jaimini 3.8.25: "The fruit belongs to the officiating priest in the case of the instruments, because it serves his purpose."
Or rather, it belongs to the master, because it is for his sake;
and because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.26–27)

He formulates the fourteenth topic: "In the case of 'mamāgne' (O Agni, mine), whose fruit is it here? By the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it belongs to the speaker; by direct statement (*śruti*), it belongs to the owner. Since [the ownership] has not been purchased, the indicative mark must be applied there figuratively. *Note: This verse summarizes the discussion regarding the mantra "mamāgne varco vihaveṣvastu" (O Agni, may my splendor be present at the invocations). The question is whether the result of reciting this mantra accrues to the priest who speaks it or to the sacrificer who owns the ritual materials. The conclusion is that because the sacrificer has not yet purchased the materials, the sense of ownership expressed by the word "mine" (*mama*) in the mantra is figurative with respect to him.*

The mantra "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations" (*mamāgne varco vihaveṣvastu*) is recited by the Adhvaryu priest during the *anvādhāna* (the ritual preparation) of the Āhavanīya fire. By the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of this mantra— "May that fruit characterized by splendor (*varcas*) and luster (*tejas*) belong to me in those sacrifices which have distinguished invocations (*vihava*)"— it is understood that the fruit belongs to the Adhvaryu who utters the mantra.
If this is argued,
it is not so;

for by the scriptural use of the middle voice (ātmanepada) in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," it is understood that the fruit of both the primary rite and its subsidiaries accrues to the sacrificer.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the *adhvaryu* priest, who has been hired [for a fee], to have a connection with the bitter fruit as his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Therefore, that indicative mark (*liṅga*), which contradicts both scripture (*śruti*) and logic (*nyāya*), must be treated as referring to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
For the figurative usage (*upacāra*) is: "May that splendor belong to my sacrificer."
Therefore, just as the fruit heard in the mantras containing self-benedictions (*pratyagāśīr-mantra*) recited by the sacrificer— such as "O Agni, giver of life, give me life"— is for the sacrificer,
so too the fruit heard in the instrumental mantras (*karaṇa-mantra*) recited by the Adhvaryu priest belongs to the sacrificer alone.

(Regarding the fifteenth section on the nature of the priest’s duty concerning the fruit of the ritual action within the *karaṇa-mantras*: Sūtra—) But the fruit is for the sake of the ritual action, because it is meaningful with respect to the master [of the sacrifice]. Jaimini 3.8.28.
He formulates the fifteenth section:
"Do not cause me distress"—in reference to which master [is this said], as before?
It refers to the Adhvaryu, because that [act] is useful for the master's ritual duty.
At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, having taken up the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles filled with clarified butter for the purpose of the *āghāra* oblation, he holds them with his hand near his navel.
Thereupon, this ritual formula (*karaṇamantra*) is recited by the Adhvaryu: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you; move apart! Do not scorch me; O makers of the world, prepare a place for me.
"O Agni and Viṣṇu, who are here in the form of the *sruc* and *sruva*, as I, the Adhvaryu, hold you near my navel, may I not step upon you—I have not committed an overstepping against you."
"And may you two not be separated from me;
therefore, do not cause me, who possess a body, to suffer—that is, do not produce heat in my body in the form of fever and the like.
By making a place, you two should prepare a location for the Āghāra libations and the Homa," is the meaning.

If it is argued that, according to the principle of the previously mentioned *varcas* [rite], the absence of distress belongs only to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and not to the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*),
do not say so.
When the Adhvaryu priest is not afflicted by distress, the master’s ritual work is completed without obstacle.

Therefore—the absence of distress in the Adhvaryu, even though it has occurred in him, is the fruit for the sacrificer (yajamāna) alone—and thus there is no figurative application (*upacāra*) of the word "I" (*mad*) here.
(Regarding the sixteenth [topic], the section on the dual application of the verse beginning with "bhadram," the sūtra states:
"And because of the designation. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.29)
The sixteenth section formulates the following:
To which master does this [formula], "May it be auspicious for us both," apply?
Because of the hearing of the dual number, it applies to these two: the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, within the Havirdhāna shed, beneath the two wooden boards that serve as the supports for the pressing of the Soma, there are four pits called *uparava*. These are dug to the depth of one *aratni*, joined together at their lower parts, and separated from one another by a distance of one *prādeśa* at their upper parts; they are situated in the four intermediate directions, beginning with the southeast (*āgneyī*).
In one of those pits, the sacrificer extends his right hand;
likewise, the Adhvaryu extends his own hand in another pit and grasps the sacrificer’s hand from below.
At that time, the sacrificer asks about the fruit with the mantra: "What is here? (kim atra).
The Adhvaryu priest responds with the mantra beginning with "bhadram-".
Thereupon, the sacrificer, by means of the mantra beginning with "tannau saha-", appropriates that fruit as his own.
Therefore, that [fruit] belongs to the sacrificer alone.
If this is argued,
it is not so;
for by the dual form "nau," [the two boats are indicated].
And by the word "together" (*saha*), it is accepted precisely as something that pertains to both.
(Regarding the seventeenth section, the adhikaraṇa on whether the preparation of a substance is for the sake of both the subsidiary and the principal acts; Sūtras 30–31):

Jai. 3.8.30: The preparation of a substance [is for the sake of] all rites, because there is no distinction in the context. Jai. 3.8.31: But because of the specific mention, it does not apply to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
START MJaiNy 3.8.23–24: The seventeenth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
Regarding the properties residing in the archetype (prakṛti), their extension (atideśa) to the ectype (vikṛti) [is established].
Or rather, [the difference] is due to attainment; for the first [alternative is not tenable], because no specific distinction can be defined.
The properties that perform a function in the archetype (*prakṛti*) would not exist in the ectype (*vikṛti*), nor would others;
for the strewing of grass in the sacrificial post-hole is not a function of the archetypal sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

It was established previously that in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the properties of the altar (*vedi*) and the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), such as the placing of the oblation (*havirāsādana*) and so forth, are for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary rites.

When it is argued that since those properties are being extended by way of modification (*atideśa*), they should all be extended because there is no restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), we reply: the purpose (*kārya*) is the restrictive factor here.
For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the placement of the sacrificial oblation (*havirāsādana*) is the function of the altar.
And that [quality], being obtained even in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), brings about the sacrificial duties (vedidharmas) such as digging for its own establishment;
however, the function consisting of the spreading [of grass] in the pit for the sacrificial post (yūpāvaṭāstaraṇa) does not exist in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti),
because there is no pit for the sacrificial post in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Furthermore, even when [the grass] is enjoined for the function of spreading in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because that function is not the original one, it does not bring about the original purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) such as cutting and so forth.
Therefore, only those properties belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*) which accomplish the purpose are extended to the modified sacrifice.

(Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.32: In the eighteenth section concerning the performance of the *pavitra* with the *paribhojanīya* sacrificial grass, the sūtra states: "And in case of conflict, because of the specific scriptural statement, the unmanifested [procedure] applies to the remainder."

He formulates the eighteenth topic: "Is that which is the *barhis* for the purpose of the *pavitra*, or not? It is the first [alternative], because its existence is possible; it is exhausted by being consecrated for the spreading, but the *pavitra* may come from elsewhere. (MJaiNy_3.8.25)
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they prescribe: "He makes two purifiers (pavitra) from darbha grass, uncut at both ends and a span in length.

Now, if it is argued that since the sacrificial grass (barhis) prepared by the act of cutting for the purpose of spreading over the altar can serve as the purifier, the purifier should therefore perform the function of the sacrificial grass, just like the spreading itself—then [the response follows].
Not so;

for all the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that has been consecrated is exhausted precisely by the act of spreading. Indeed, it is not reasonable to arbitrarily restrict the spreading—enjoined by the rule "he spreads on the altar"—to only a single portion of the sacrificial grass.

Therefore, just as one strews the sacrificial pit with *barhis* grass that has not been consecrated, so too the preparation of the *pavitra* must be accomplished using *darbha* grass known by the name *paribhojanīya*, which is devoid of ritual consecrations such as cutting prescribed by the scriptures.
(Regarding the nineteenth section, concerning the disposal of the ordinary *puroḍāśa* and other offerings, there is the following sūtra:
"But there is the removal of a single portion, because of its connection with what is already present. — Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.33.
The nineteenth section formulates the following:
One should place a fragment of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) into the cup for Indra and Vāyu; should this cake be a new one, or rather the *savanīya* cake? 3.8.26.
Because the sacrifice is performed for the sake of one who has already attained success (*siddha*), that ritual act is not to be performed by preparing a new [offering];
rather, its function is fulfilled by the *savanīya* [cake], since it is the object to be consecrated, as indicated by the accusative case ending.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "He places a fragment of the *puroḍāśa* cake in the vessel of the Aindravāyava [cup]."

In this regard, if it is argued that although a scrap of the *stravaṇīya* sacrificial cake has already been produced, nevertheless, because it was consecrated for the purpose of the sacrificer— just like the consecrated sacrificial grass (*barhis*)— it is exhausted, and therefore one must prepare some new sacrificial cake and perform the act of throwing its scrap into the *aindravāyava* vessel.
Not so;
this depositing must be performed with a fragment of the *savanīya* sacrificial cake.
Why? Because:
Because it is something to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*).
In the phrase "he places the chip" (*śakalaṃ nidadhāti*), its status as something to be consecrated is understood through the accusative case.
For the consecration of what remains after a sacrifice consists in the form of a ritual disposal (*pratipatti*).
And here, the entire [cake] is not for the purpose of sacrifice,
because a portion of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)— namely, the size of the *avadāna*— is left over;
just as in this case there is a fragment of a previously prepared sacrificial cake.
Likewise, in the cases "the curdled milk in the Āśvin cup" and "the whey in the Maitrāvaruṇa cup," the pouring in is also of that which remains from the previous [offering]. // MJaiNyC_3,8.26-27 //
(Regarding the twenty-second section, concerning the fact that the quality of being performed silently (*upāṃśutva*) in the *tāmyeṣṭi* pertains to the primary rite; Sūtras 34–35):
Sūtra 34: In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) serves all purposes, because it follows the model of the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
Sūtra 35: Or rather, it serves the purpose of the principal rite alone, because the subsidiary is not independently enjoined.

In the twenty-first section of the third chapter, verse 28–29, the author formulates the following: Should optional sacrifices be performed silently (*upāṃśu*), and if so, is this [silence] for both the subsidiaries and the principal rites?
Or rather, it is the primary [element] alone; therefore, no distinction is stated here between the two.
Since only the principal rites are objects of desire, it is with respect to them alone that the objection is raised;
because the subsidiaries do not possess that quality, the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) belongs to the principal acts.
This is recorded in the tradition: "The *iṣṭis* performed for specific desires belong to the *Yajñātharvaṇa*."
"Those [offerings] are to be performed in a low voice (upāṃśu).
Just like the rites prescribed in the Atharvaveda, the optional sacrifices (kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ) at the great sacrifices (yajña) are connected with cows;
therefore, it is appropriate that they be performed in a low voice—this is the meaning.
If it is argued that, just as the injunction is common to both the subsidiary and the principal acts regarding the characteristics of the altar and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),
so too is it for the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*),
since no specific distinction is recorded here.
Not so;
for in this context, it is the very fact of being optional (*kāmyatva*) that serves as the sole restrictive factor. However, the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) do not possess the quality of being optional.
Since those [subsidiary acts] which bring about the perfection of the instruments have no direct connection with the fruit,
therefore the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) applies only to the primary act that directly accomplishes the fruit;
however, regarding the subsidiaries, there is a specific mode of intonation according to each respective Veda.
(Regarding the twenty-first section, concerning the use of clarified butter as the sacrificial offering for the parts of the hawk [śyena] sacrifice, Sūtras 36–38:
Sūtra 36: Because there is no distinction in proximity, [the rule applies] to its constituent parts when [the primary act] is impossible.
Sūtra 37: If it is argued that the same applies even to the fire-installation (ādhāna).
"No, because it is not part of the context, since the subsidiary [element] does not have that as its cause. (Jaimini 3.8.38).
He formulates the twenty-first section as follows:

The fresh butter (navanīta) is the ghee (ājya) for the hawk; it should reside in the principal part, as the ghee to be prescribed is that which has not yet been [otherwise] obtained, namely the fresh butter located in the leather bag.
The primary modification of Soma is clarified butter (ājya) obtained through the force of the extended injunction (codaka) regarding the subsidiary rites;
by referring to this clarified butter as being in the state of a leather bag (dṛti), the injunction prescribes fresh butter (navanīta) as its quality.
In the Śyena sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The clarified butter is fresh butter from a leather bag."

It might be argued that "this clarified butter (ājya)— the original substance of which is butter (navanīta) long held in a leather bag— is to be enjoined for the primary rite, because it has not been previously obtained through any other means of knowledge";
but this is not so, because the primary Śyena sacrifice, being a modification of the Soma sacrifice, has no requirement for clarified butter.

In the subsidiary sacrifices (aṅga-iṣṭi) which are specific modifications, the quality of the aforementioned fresh butter (navanīta) is prescribed as a modification of the clarified butter (ājya) obtained through the rule of extension (codaka), serving as its material cause (prakṛti-dravya).
(Regarding the twenty-second section, concerning the fact that clarified butter (*navanīta*) is the sacrificial fat for all parts of the *sarvaśyena* sacrifice, Sūtras 39–41:
"Or rather, it applies at that time, because of the observation of indicative marks" (Jaimini 3.8.39);
"Or rather, it applies to all [the parts], because there is no distinction" (Jaimini 3.8.40).
The observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) regarding what has been stated by logic. Jaimini 3.8.41.
[The author] formulates the twenty-second section:
Regarding the quality prescribed for the subsidiaries belonging to the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), it applies either to all of them or only to the first;
because of its specific connection with the subsidiary, there is a syntactical connection (*vākya*) with all the subsidiaries.

This quality of using a leather bag (*dṛti*) and fresh butter (*navanīta*) which is enjoined for the subsidiaries of the Śyena sacrifice applies only to those subsidiaries belonging to the time of the pressing—namely, the forms of the Savanīya animal sacrifices and their corresponding sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

But it does not apply to the subsidiaries such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* which persist over a period of time. The subject of dispute— the specific quality— pertains only to those subsidiaries occurring at the time of the *sutyā*,
because it is a distinctive feature of the Śyena sacrifice.
It is like the concomitance of animals (*paśusāhitya*).

Just as the concomitance of animals enjoined by the rule "He sacrifices the animals together" is specified as a particular feature only in the *Śyena* sacrifice, and thus remains restricted to the *savanīya* animals belonging to the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*),
so too is the case with the fresh butter (*navanīta*)— this being the position reached [by the opponent].

We reply: Since the sentence "That which is clarified butter (ājya) is fresh butter (navanīta)" is understood to refer to all the auxiliary substances (aṅga) that are clarified butter, the inference [of its being restricted to specific parts] is vitiated by the fallacy of being superseded by a later cognition (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa). Therefore, that fresh butter applies to all the auxiliaries. // MJaiNyC_3.8.32 //

(Section 23: On the fact that the *savanīya* offerings consist of meat; Sūtras 42–44) "But the *savanīyas* consist of meat, because of the specific injunction. (Jaimini 3.8.42) "If it is argued that a figurative application is improper when the primary substance is not present," (Jaimini 3.8.43)
It may be so, on account of the natural gender, as in the case of Vairāja;
thus [Jaimini] formulates the twenty-third section.
In the Śākyāyana sacrifice, the term "puroḍāśās" refers to meat by force;
this applies everywhere in the Savanīya sacrifice, just as it does everywhere regarding clarified butter (navanīta).

The *tarasas* (omentum) are to be the *savanīya* offerings; since their proximity is prescribed by scripture, the flesh-nature of the *puroḍāśa* is therefore restricted to those very [offerings]. This is the Śākyāyana view, which is to be performed during thirty-six years.

In this regard, it is heard [in scripture]: "The householder, having settled for the day, goes out on a hunt; the strength (tarasa) of those animals he kills becomes the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) to be offered."
In this regard, if it is argued that just as butter is present in all parts [of the body], so too the nature of flesh is present in all sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), we say:
not so.
For in that case, under the interpretation of the statement "those which are *puroḍāśas* are *tarasas*," there would be a remote connection (*vyavahitānvaya*),
because the word *savanīya* intervenes between the words *tarasa* and *puroḍāśa*.
But here, the proximity (*saṃnidhi*) of these two— *tarasāḥ* and *savanīyāḥ*— is heard in the text.

That being the case, by the sentence "Those which are *savanīya* are made of meat," which is supported by the context (*saṃnidhi*), the quality of being meat is restricted specifically to the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
Thus ends the eighth quarter of the third chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* composed by the venerable Mādhava;
and with this, the third chapter is completed.
